Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a weak, rejected view, which implies belief in two terms, and the Mu'tazilites clung to something similar.

The majority read ﴿wa-lā yunqaṣu﴾ ("nor is it reduced") in the passive voice. Ya'qub, Salam, Abd al-Warith, and Harun, both transmitted from Abu Amr, read ﴿wa-lā yanqusu﴾ in the active voice. Al-Hasan read ﴿min 'umrihi illā fī kitābin﴾ ("of his life, except in a Book"). Ibn Abbas said: this is the Preserved Tablet. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by "the Book of God" is meant the knowledge of God, or the record of the person. End of quotation.

﴿Nor are the two seas alike﴾: this is another verse by which every intelligent person may be shown that it is something in which no idol has any share. The explanation of ﴿this is sweet, palatable﴾ and ﴿this is salt, bitter﴾ has already been given in Surah Al-Furqan. Here, between the two categories, is an attribute of the Arabs, and between it and His saying ﴿pleasant to drink﴾ (sā'igun sharābuhu). The majority read ﴿sā'igun﴾ as an active participle from ﴿sāgha﴾. Isa read ﴿sayyi'un﴾ on the pattern fay'il, like ﴿mayyitun﴾; the same is transmitted from Abu Amr and Asim. Isa also read ﴿sayghun﴾, a lightened form of the doubled verb, like ﴿mayt﴾, the lightened form of ﴿mayyit﴾. The majority read ﴿milḥun﴾; Abu Nahik and Talha read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this is an irregular dialect. It is possible that it is a shortened form of ﴿mālih﴾, with the alif dropped for lightness. It is also said: "water is milḥ" in irregular usage, but in common usage it is mamlūḥ. Al-Zamakhshari said: the two seas, the sweet and the salt, are set forth as parables for the believer and the disbeliever. Then he said, by way of digression (istitrad, a shift to a related topic) in describing the two seas and what is connected with them: "of His blessing and His bounty."

﴿And from each﴾: al-Zamakhshari explained words from the verse that were repeated in Surah Al-Nahl. Then he said: it may also bear a meaning other than the digression, namely that the two kinds are compared to the two seas, and then the salt sea is preferred over the disbeliever, in that it shares with the sweet sea in benefits such as fish and pearls, and the sailing of ships upon it, whereas the disbeliever is empty of benefit. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 74], and the verse. End of quotation.

﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾: he means trade, the Hajj, the campaign, or every journey that has a lawful aim.

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾: the explanation of these phrases has already been given. When He mentioned many things that indicate His overwhelming power, such as sending the winds, creating from dust and what is joined to it, causing the night to enter the day, and subjecting the sun and the moon, He pointed out that the One who has these wondrous acts is God. So He said: ﴿That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs sovereignty﴾. These are successive predicates. The subject is ﴿dhālikum﴾ ("that"), and ﴿Allāhu rabbukum﴾ ("God is your Lord") are two predicates; ﴿lahu al-mulk﴾ ("to Him belongs sovereignty") is a subject-predicate sentence in connection with His saying: ﴿And those you call upon besides Him possess not even a thin membrane of a date pit﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also permissible, in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), to make the name of God an attribute of the demonstrative pronoun, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan, a noun in apposition that clarifies the preceding word), with ﴿rabbukum﴾ as the predicate, were it not that the meaning rejects it. End of quotation. As for its being an attribute, that is not permissible, because ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper noun (ism 'alam), and a proper noun is not described by an attribute, nor is it a generic noun like "man," in which an attribute could be imagined. As for his saying "were it not that the meaning rejects it," it is not evident that the meaning rejects it, because it would then be informing that the one indicated by those attributes and the mentioned acts is your Lord, that is, your owner or your reformer. This is a fitting and acceptable meaning.

Those whom you call upon besides Him are the idols. The majority read ﴿tad'ūna﴾ ("you call upon") with the second-person prefix; Isa, Salam, and Ya'qub read it with the third-person prefix. The author of al-Kamil, Abu al-Qasim ibn Jabbara, said: ﴿yad'ūna﴾ with the third person is transmitted by al-Lu'lu'i from Abu Amr and Salam, al-Nahawandi from Qutayba, Ibn al-Jalla' from Nusayr, Ibn Habib and Ibn Yunus from al-Kisa'i, and Abu Umara from Hafs. The word ﴿qiṭmīr﴾ has already been explained. Juwaybir, on the authority of his men, and al-Dahhak said: it is the cap at the top of the date. Mujahid said: it is the wrapping of the pit. It is also said: it is what lies between the cap of the date and the pit. It is also said: the skin of garlic. Whichever it is, it is a figure for the smallest thing. The poet said:

*Your father wears down his sandal, squatting, yet the poor man does not possess even a thin membrane of a date pit.*

﴿They do not hear your call﴾: because they are inanimate. ﴿And if they heard﴾: this is on the supposition of a hypothesis. ﴿They would not respond to you﴾: because they do not claim any divinity for themselves, and they disown it. It is also said: they would not benefit you. He added the verbal noun (maṣdar) to ﴿shirkikum﴾ ("your associating"), meaning by your associating them with God in your worship of them, as in His saying: ﴿You did not worship us﴾ [Yunus: 28]. Thus it is an annexation to the doer. As for His saying ﴿yakfurūna﴾ ("they will disown"), it may mean that, by what appears there of their stillness and sluggishness when a speaker moves and every arguer contests, this comes in the manner of figurative speech (tajawwuz), as in the words of Dhu al-Rumma:

*I stood at a dwelling of Mayya, speaking, its traces addressing me while I address it.*

*And I water it until, from what I pour out, its stones and its playgrounds almost speak to me.*

﴿And none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾. Qatada and other exegetes said: the All-Aware here means God Himself, who is the Truthful in report, who has informed of this, so there is no doubt in its occurrence. Ibn Atiyyah said: it may be that His saying ﴿and none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾ is part of the continuing description of the idols, as if He said: none informs you like one who informs you about himself, that is, they do not speak truthfully in disowning your associating them with God. So by "the All-Aware" in this similitude is meant, as it were: none informs you about himself like one who has informed about himself, and they have informed about themselves by disbelieving in these (their worshippers). Al-Zamakhshari said: none informs you of the matter like one who informs, who is All-Aware of it, meaning that the one who is aware of the matter is the one who informs you of the truth rather than the other informants about it. The meaning is: what I have told you about the state of the idols is the truth, because I am aware of what I inform about. The author of al-Tajrid said: it admits of two aspects. First, that this is an address to the Messenger when he was informed that on the Day of Resurrection the wood and the stone will speak and deny their worshippers, a matter that cannot be known by pure reason without God's informing of it. God said: ﴿They will disown their associating﴾, that is, they will disown them on the Day of Resurrection. This statement, though what it reports is a wondrous matter, is as it has said, because the informant is All-Aware. Second, that it is an address not restricted to anyone in particular, that is: what has been mentioned is as it has been mentioned; none informs you, O listener, whoever you are, like one who is All-Aware.

[p. 302] ﴿And Allah is He who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus is the Resurrection.﴾ ﴿Whoever desires honour—then to Allah belongs all honour. To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it. As for those who plot evil deeds, for them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish.﴾ ﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then He made you into pairs. No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And no one is granted long life or has his life shortened except that it is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter. From each you eat fresh flesh, and you extract ornaments to wear. And you see the ships ploughing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a speck of a date-pit membrane.﴾ ﴿If you invoke them, they do not hear your call, and even if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association of them. And none can inform you like the All-Knowing.﴾

When He mentioned some matters of the heavenly realm and the sending of the angels, He mentioned some matters of the earthly realm: the winds and their sending. In this there is an argument against those who deny the resurrection. He pointed them to the example they witness, namely that bringing the dead to life is like this. It is mentioned in a hadith: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'How does Allah give life to the dead, and what is the sign of that in His creation?' He said: 'Have you passed by a valley that was barren, then you passed by it and it was stirring green?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Thus Allah gives life to the dead, and that is His sign in His creation.'"

It has been said that ﴿arsala﴾ (He sent) has the meaning of yursilu (He sends), and for that reason ﴿fatuthiru﴾ (so they stir up) is conjoined to it. It has also been said: the present tense was used to narrate a state in which the stirring of the clouds by the winds takes place, and to evoke that wondrous image which indicates the divine power. From the same usage is ﴿fatusbihu al-ardu mukhdarrah﴾ (then the earth becomes green). Al-Zamakhshari said: "They do likewise with every act in which there is a kind of distinguishing particularity by a state that is strange, or in which the addressee is suspected, or other than that, as Ta'abbata Sharran said:

"That I have met the ghoul, as she plunges with meteors like a page, with a wide expanse,
So I struck her without dismay, and she fell, a prostrate one, onto both her hands and her neck."

He intended to depict for his people the state in which he encouraged his cousin to strike the ghoul, as if he were making them see it and informing them of its reality, as a witnessing of wonder at his boldness toward every terror and his steadfastness at every hardship. Likewise, the driving of the clouds to the dead land and the giving of life to the earth by rain after its death. Since this is among the proofs of the overwhelming power, it was said: ﴿fa-saqna﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ (We drive and We give life), diverted by them from the form of the third person to what is more inherent in particularity and more indicative of it." End of quotation.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: "That is, He sent it in the past tense, because what is attributed to Allah and what He does, by His saying 'Be,' does not remain for a time or a part of a time. So He did not use the future form, due to the necessity of its occurrence and the speed of its coming into being. And because He has finished with everything, He has determined the sending at known times and to specified places. And since He attributed the stirring to the wind, which is formed over a period of time, He said ﴿fatuthiru﴾; and He attributed ﴿arsala﴾ to the third person (the absent one), and in ﴿fa-saqnahu﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ to the first person (the speaker). Because in the first He introduced Himself by an act of His acts, which is the sending; then when He was known, He said: 'I am the One you know: I drove the clouds, so I gave life to the earth.' So in the first there is an introduction through the wondrous act, and in the second a reminder of the resurrection. And ﴿fa-saqnahu﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ in the past form support what we have mentioned of the difference between ﴿fatuthiru﴾ and ﴿arsala﴾." End of quotation.

This distinction he mentioned between ﴿arsala﴾ and ﴿fatuthiru﴾ does not appear clearly. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Rum: ﴿Allah is He who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [al-Rum: 48], and in al-A'raf: ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]: how did the present tense come with the verb of sending? This is only a variation in speech and a manipulation of eloquence. As for the shift from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun glorifying Himself, it is of the category of iltifat (shift in address). Likewise in al-A'raf: ﴿We drove it to a dead land, and We sent down water by it, and brought forth thereby fruits of every kind﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]. As for his statement "and what He does, etc." and that every act, although it is attributed to other than Him metaphorically, is truly His act, there is no difference between what He attributes to His essence and what He attributes to other than Himself, because all of that is His bringing into existence and His creation. (Commentary continues.)

Al-nushur (the resurrection, the rising) is the verbal noun of nashara, said of the dead when he comes back to life. Al-A'sha said:

"Until people say, at what they see: 'How wondrous, for the dead one who rises!'"

Al-nushur is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), and the preposition and its object before it are in a position of jarr (genitive). The comparison occurs in several respects: when the dead earth accepts the life fitting for it, so likewise the limbs accept life. Or: just as the wind gathers pieces of cloud, so likewise the parts of limbs and the fragments of things are gathered. Or: just as He drives the winds and the clouds to the dead land, so He drives the spirit and life to the body.

﴿Man kana yuridu al-izzah﴾: that is, desires victory over others (al-mughalabah). ﴿Fa-lillahi al-izzah﴾: that is, it does not belong to anyone else and is not completed except by Him, and the one who seeks to overcome is overcome. Mujahid inclined to this view, and said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾ by worshipping idols. This is an illustration of His saying: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81]. Qatadah said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾ and its straight path, and loves to attain it, ﴿then to Allah belongs honour﴾: that is, through Him and by His command; His honour is not attained except by obeying Him. Al-Farra' said: whoever desires knowledge of honour, ﴿then to Allah belongs honour﴾: that is, He is the one characterized by it. It has also been said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾: that is, honour that is not followed by humiliation and is not turned toward humiliation. Al-Zamakhshari said: the disbelievers used to gain honour through the idols, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81]. And those who believed with their tongues without their hearts agreeing used to gain honour through the polytheists, as He said: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. Do they seek honour with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139]. Thus He made clear that there is no honour except for Allah and for His allies, and He said: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. End of quotation.

There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139], although the apparent meaning is that it belongs to Him and not to anything else, and His saying ﴿honour belongs to Allah and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], although it implies sharing. This is because honour in reality belongs to Allah essentially, to the Messenger through his nearness to Allah, and to the believers through the Messenger. So the one judged first is other than the one judged second.

Man is a conditional particle (ism shart), and the response clause must contain a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun when it is not an adverb. The response is elided, and its estimated form is according to those earlier sayings. According to Mujahid's view: "then he is overcome." According to Qatadah's view: "then let him seek it from Allah." According to al-Farra's view: "then let him attribute that to Allah." According to the fourth view: "then he does not attain it." The response was omitted, being dispensed with by His saying ﴿then to Allah belongs all honour﴾, since it indicates it. The most apparent of these views is Qatadah's: "let him seek it from the One to whom honour belongs, who disposes of it as He wills," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You grant honour to whom You will and You humble whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Jami'an (all) is put in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (al-muraad), and what is meant is the honour of this world and the honour of the Hereafter.

﴿Al-kalim al-tayyib﴾ (the good word) is tawhid, tahmid, the remembrance of Allah, and the like. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It has also been said: praise with good for the righteous believers. Ka'b said: "Indeed, 'Subhan Allah,' 'al-hamdu lillah,' 'la ilaha illa Allah,' and 'Allahu akbar' have a humming around the Throne like the humming of bees, with mention of their speaker."

The majority read (yas'adu), in the active voice from sa'ida, with ﴿al-kalim al-tayyib﴾ in the nominative, so al-kalim is the plural of kalimah. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sulami, and Ibrahim read yus'idu from as'ada, with al-kalam al-tayyib in the passive voice. End of quotation. Zayd ibn 'Ali read yas'adu from sa'ida, with al-kalam (speech) as subject, meaning "ascended." The ascent of speech to Him, exalted is He, is metaphorical both in the agent and in the one to whom it ascends, because He, exalted is He, is not in a direction, and because words are utterances that are not described as ascending, since ascent belongs to bodies. Rather, it is a metaphor for acceptance and for describing it as perfect, as one says: "His heel was raised and his rank was elevated," and from it: "they went up to the judge" and "the matter was raised to him," and there is no height in direction there.

The majority read: ﴿wal-'amalu al-salihu yarfa'uhu﴾ (and righteous deed raises it). So al-'amal (deed) is a mubtada' (subject), and yarfa'uhu is the khabar (predicate). The subject of yarfa'uhu is a pronoun referring to al-'amal al-salih, and the object pronoun refers to al-kalim, meaning: it raises the good word. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. Al-Hasan said: the statement is presented to the deed; if the statement agrees with the deed, it is accepted, and if it disagrees, it is rejected. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: when the servant remembers Allah and says a good word and performs His obligations, his statement is raised together with his deed; and when he speaks but does not perform His obligations, his statement is rejected in favor of his deed. It was also said: his deed is more fitting for him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a view refuted by the creed of the People of the Sunnah, and it is not authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas. The truth is that the one who performs his obligations, when he remembers Allah and says a good word, is recorded for him and accepted; he has his good deeds and his bad deeds are upon him, and Allah accepts from everyone who guards against shirk. Abu Salih and Shahr ibn Hawshab said the reverse of this view: the subject pronoun refers to al-kalim, and the object pronoun to al-'amal al-salih, meaning: the good word raises it. Qatadah said: the subject is a pronoun referring to Allah, and the hi (its) refers to al-'amal al-salih, meaning: Allah raises it to Himself, that is, accepts it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the most preferred of the views. From Ibn 'Abbas: "al-'amal al-salih raises its doer and honours him," so he made it with an elided mudaf (genitive construction). In my view it is permissible that al-'amal be conjoined to al-kalim al-tayyib, meaning that both ascend to Allah, and yarfa'uhu is a resumed statement (isti'naf ikhbar), meaning: Allah raises them. He made the pronoun singular because the two are shared in ascending, and a pronoun may take the place of a demonstrative, so its form is singular while what is meant is the dual. It is as if it were said: their ascent is not from themselves, rather it is by Allah's raising them.

'Isa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: wal-'amala al-saliha, with both in the accusative by ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun, governing the object). The subject is a pronoun referring to al-kalim or to Allah. Makara is intransitive. (Al-sayyi'at) is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, meaning "evil plottings," or of a mudaf to a verbal noun, meaning he attributed the plotting to the evil deeds, or he made yamkurun include the meaning of "earning," so that al-sayyi'at is the direct object. When al-sayyi'at is an adjective of a verbal noun, or of a mudaf to a verbal noun, the apparent meaning is that it refers to the plottings of Quraysh in the Dar al-Nadwah, when they discussed one of three plots, which are mentioned in al-Anfal: to confine him, or to kill him, or to expel him. And ﴿ula'ika﴾ (those) refers to those who devised those plots.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 35, verses 9–14 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Yabūr﴾ means it will be corrupted and destroyed, "apart from the plotting of God against them," when He expelled them from Mecca, killed them, and threw them into the well of Badr. He thus gathered all their schemes upon them and fulfilled His saying: ﴿They plot, and God plots, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30], and His saying: ﴿The evil plot encompasses only its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. The word ﴿al-makr al-sayyi'﴾ is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and ﴿yabūr﴾ is its predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate). The whole sentence is a predicate for ﴿wa-makru ūlā'ika﴾ ("and the plotting of those"). Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa permitted that ﴿huwa﴾ be a separating pronoun (fasl, a pronoun placed between subject and predicate to mark the division), with ﴿yabūr﴾ as the predicate and ﴿makru ūlā'ika﴾ as the subject. Yet, as far as we know, no one has taken this view except Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani in his commentary on his Sharh al-Idah, where he permitted in ﴿kāna Zaydun huwa yaqūmu﴾ that ﴿huwa﴾ be a separating pronoun. This view was rejected.

﴿And God created you from dust﴾: from the point of view that He created our father Adam from dust.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: that is, by procreation.

﴿Then He made you pairs﴾: that is, kinds, males and females, as He said: ﴿He gives to whom He wills females and males﴾ [Al-Shura: 50]. Qatada said: He decreed marriage among you, and He joined some of you with others. The ﴿min﴾ in ﴿min mu'ammar﴾ ("of one granted a long life") is superfluous. He called him "one granted a long life" by what he will become, namely one who has a long lifespan. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿min 'umrihi﴾ ("of his life") refers to ﴿mu'ammar﴾ both in form and in meaning. Ibn Abbas and others said: it refers to ﴿mu'ammar﴾ as a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a category), and what is meant is other than the one who is granted a long life. Thus the verse contains two persons: one of them is granted a hundred years, and something is reduced from the other. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik, that what is meant is one person, that is, he counts what has passed of his life; when a year passes, he records that, then another year, and so this is the reduction. The poet said:

*Your life is breaths that are counted; every time a breath of yours passes, you have lost a part by it.*

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the meaning of ﴿nor is anything reduced from his life﴾ is that no one's life is cut short by a cause that God's power does not permit; had He willed, He would have delayed that cause. It is reported that when Umar, may God be pleased with him, was stabbed, he said: "If he prayed to God, He would have increased his term." The Muslims denied this and said: God, exalted is He, says: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [Al-A'raf: 34], and so they argued with this verse. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a weak, rejected view, which implies belief in two terms, and the Mu'tazilites clung to something similar.

The majority read ﴿wa-lā yunqaṣu﴾ ("nor is it reduced") in the passive voice. Ya'qub, Salam, Abd al-Warith, and Harun, both transmitted from Abu Amr, read ﴿wa-lā yanqusu﴾ in the active voice. Al-Hasan read ﴿min 'umrihi illā fī kitābin﴾ ("of his life, except in a Book"). Ibn Abbas said: this is the Preserved Tablet. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by "the Book of God" is meant the knowledge of God, or the record of the person. End of quotation.

﴿Nor are the two seas alike﴾: this is another verse by which every intelligent person may be shown that it is something in which no idol has any share. The explanation of ﴿this is sweet, palatable﴾ and ﴿this is salt, bitter﴾ has already been given in Surah Al-Furqan. Here, between the two categories, is an attribute of the Arabs, and between it and His saying ﴿pleasant to drink﴾ (sā'igun sharābuhu). The majority read ﴿sā'igun﴾ as an active participle from ﴿sāgha﴾. Isa read ﴿sayyi'un﴾ on the pattern fay'il, like ﴿mayyitun﴾; the same is transmitted from Abu Amr and Asim. Isa also read ﴿sayghun﴾, a lightened form of the doubled verb, like ﴿mayt﴾, the lightened form of ﴿mayyit﴾. The majority read ﴿milḥun﴾; Abu Nahik and Talha read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this is an irregular dialect. It is possible that it is a shortened form of ﴿mālih﴾, with the alif dropped for lightness. It is also said: "water is milḥ" in irregular usage, but in common usage it is mamlūḥ. Al-Zamakhshari said: the two seas, the sweet and the salt, are set forth as parables for the believer and the disbeliever. Then he said, by way of digression (istitrad, a shift to a related topic) in describing the two seas and what is connected with them: "of His blessing and His bounty."

﴿And from each﴾: al-Zamakhshari explained words from the verse that were repeated in Surah Al-Nahl. Then he said: it may also bear a meaning other than the digression, namely that the two kinds are compared to the two seas, and then the salt sea is preferred over the disbeliever, in that it shares with the sweet sea in benefits such as fish and pearls, and the sailing of ships upon it, whereas the disbeliever is empty of benefit. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 74], and the verse. End of quotation.

﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾: he means trade, the Hajj, the campaign, or every journey that has a lawful aim.

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾: the explanation of these phrases has already been given. When He mentioned many things that indicate His overwhelming power, such as sending the winds, creating from dust and what is joined to it, causing the night to enter the day, and subjecting the sun and the moon, He pointed out that the One who has these wondrous acts is God. So He said: ﴿That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs sovereignty﴾. These are successive predicates. The subject is ﴿dhālikum﴾ ("that"), and ﴿Allāhu rabbukum﴾ ("God is your Lord") are two predicates; ﴿lahu al-mulk﴾ ("to Him belongs sovereignty") is a subject-predicate sentence in connection with His saying: ﴿And those you call upon besides Him possess not even a thin membrane of a date pit﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also permissible, in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), to make the name of God an attribute of the demonstrative pronoun, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan, a noun in apposition that clarifies the preceding word), with ﴿rabbukum﴾ as the predicate, were it not that the meaning rejects it. End of quotation. As for its being an attribute, that is not permissible, because ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper noun (ism 'alam), and a proper noun is not described by an attribute, nor is it a generic noun like "man," in which an attribute could be imagined. As for his saying "were it not that the meaning rejects it," it is not evident that the meaning rejects it, because it would then be informing that the one indicated by those attributes and the mentioned acts is your Lord, that is, your owner or your reformer. This is a fitting and acceptable meaning.

Those whom you call upon besides Him are the idols. The majority read ﴿tad'ūna﴾ ("you call upon") with the second-person prefix; Isa, Salam, and Ya'qub read it with the third-person prefix. The author of al-Kamil, Abu al-Qasim ibn Jabbara, said: ﴿yad'ūna﴾ with the third person is transmitted by al-Lu'lu'i from Abu Amr and Salam, al-Nahawandi from Qutayba, Ibn al-Jalla' from Nusayr, Ibn Habib and Ibn Yunus from al-Kisa'i, and Abu Umara from Hafs. The word ﴿qiṭmīr﴾ has already been explained. Juwaybir, on the authority of his men, and al-Dahhak said: it is the cap at the top of the date. Mujahid said: it is the wrapping of the pit. It is also said: it is what lies between the cap of the date and the pit. It is also said: the skin of garlic. Whichever it is, it is a figure for the smallest thing. The poet said:

*Your father wears down his sandal, squatting, yet the poor man does not possess even a thin membrane of a date pit.*

﴿They do not hear your call﴾: because they are inanimate. ﴿And if they heard﴾: this is on the supposition of a hypothesis. ﴿They would not respond to you﴾: because they do not claim any divinity for themselves, and they disown it. It is also said: they would not benefit you. He added the verbal noun (maṣdar) to ﴿shirkikum﴾ ("your associating"), meaning by your associating them with God in your worship of them, as in His saying: ﴿You did not worship us﴾ [Yunus: 28]. Thus it is an annexation to the doer. As for His saying ﴿yakfurūna﴾ ("they will disown"), it may mean that, by what appears there of their stillness and sluggishness when a speaker moves and every arguer contests, this comes in the manner of figurative speech (tajawwuz), as in the words of Dhu al-Rumma:

*I stood at a dwelling of Mayya, speaking, its traces addressing me while I address it.*

*And I water it until, from what I pour out, its stones and its playgrounds almost speak to me.*

﴿And none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾. Qatada and other exegetes said: the All-Aware here means God Himself, who is the Truthful in report, who has informed of this, so there is no doubt in its occurrence. Ibn Atiyyah said: it may be that His saying ﴿and none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾ is part of the continuing description of the idols, as if He said: none informs you like one who informs you about himself, that is, they do not speak truthfully in disowning your associating them with God. So by "the All-Aware" in this similitude is meant, as it were: none informs you about himself like one who has informed about himself, and they have informed about themselves by disbelieving in these (their worshippers). Al-Zamakhshari said: none informs you of the matter like one who informs, who is All-Aware of it, meaning that the one who is aware of the matter is the one who informs you of the truth rather than the other informants about it. The meaning is: what I have told you about the state of the idols is the truth, because I am aware of what I inform about. The author of al-Tajrid said: it admits of two aspects. First, that this is an address to the Messenger when he was informed that on the Day of Resurrection the wood and the stone will speak and deny their worshippers, a matter that cannot be known by pure reason without God's informing of it. God said: ﴿They will disown their associating﴾, that is, they will disown them on the Day of Resurrection. This statement, though what it reports is a wondrous matter, is as it has said, because the informant is All-Aware. Second, that it is an address not restricted to anyone in particular, that is: what has been mentioned is as it has been mentioned; none informs you, O listener, whoever you are, like one who is All-Aware.

[p. 302] ﴿And Allah is He who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus is the Resurrection.﴾ ﴿Whoever desires honour—then to Allah belongs all honour. To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it. As for those who plot evil deeds, for them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish.﴾ ﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then He made you into pairs. No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And no one is granted long life or has his life shortened except that it is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter. From each you eat fresh flesh, and you extract ornaments to wear. And you see the ships ploughing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a speck of a date-pit membrane.﴾ ﴿If you invoke them, they do not hear your call, and even if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association of them. And none can inform you like the All-Knowing.﴾

When He mentioned some matters of the heavenly realm and the sending of the angels, He mentioned some matters of the earthly realm: the winds and their sending. In this there is an argument against those who deny the resurrection. He pointed them to the example they witness, namely that bringing the dead to life is like this. It is mentioned in a hadith: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'How does Allah give life to the dead, and what is the sign of that in His creation?' He said: 'Have you passed by a valley that was barren, then you passed by it and it was stirring green?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Thus Allah gives life to the dead, and that is His sign in His creation.'"

It has been said that ﴿arsala﴾ (He sent) has the meaning of yursilu (He sends), and for that reason ﴿fatuthiru﴾ (so they stir up) is conjoined to it. It has also been said: the present tense was used to narrate a state in which the stirring of the clouds by the winds takes place, and to evoke that wondrous image which indicates the divine power. From the same usage is ﴿fatusbihu al-ardu mukhdarrah﴾ (then the earth becomes green). Al-Zamakhshari said: "They do likewise with every act in which there is a kind of distinguishing particularity by a state that is strange, or in which the addressee is suspected, or other than that, as Ta'abbata Sharran said:

"That I have met the ghoul, as she plunges with meteors like a page, with a wide expanse,
So I struck her without dismay, and she fell, a prostrate one, onto both her hands and her neck."

He intended to depict for his people the state in which he encouraged his cousin to strike the ghoul, as if he were making them see it and informing them of its reality, as a witnessing of wonder at his boldness toward every terror and his steadfastness at every hardship. Likewise, the driving of the clouds to the dead land and the giving of life to the earth by rain after its death. Since this is among the proofs of the overwhelming power, it was said: ﴿fa-saqna﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ (We drive and We give life), diverted by them from the form of the third person to what is more inherent in particularity and more indicative of it." End of quotation.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: "That is, He sent it in the past tense, because what is attributed to Allah and what He does, by His saying 'Be,' does not remain for a time or a part of a time. So He did not use the future form, due to the necessity of its occurrence and the speed of its coming into being. And because He has finished with everything, He has determined the sending at known times and to specified places. And since He attributed the stirring to the wind, which is formed over a period of time, He said ﴿fatuthiru﴾; and He attributed ﴿arsala﴾ to the third person (the absent one), and in ﴿fa-saqnahu﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ to the first person (the speaker). Because in the first He introduced Himself by an act of His acts, which is the sending; then when He was known, He said: 'I am the One you know: I drove the clouds, so I gave life to the earth.' So in the first there is an introduction through the wondrous act, and in the second a reminder of the resurrection. And ﴿fa-saqnahu﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ in the past form support what we have mentioned of the difference between ﴿fatuthiru﴾ and ﴿arsala﴾." End of quotation.

This distinction he mentioned between ﴿arsala﴾ and ﴿fatuthiru﴾ does not appear clearly. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Rum: ﴿Allah is He who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [al-Rum: 48], and in al-A'raf: ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]: how did the present tense come with the verb of sending? This is only a variation in speech and a manipulation of eloquence. As for the shift from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun glorifying Himself, it is of the category of iltifat (shift in address). Likewise in al-A'raf: ﴿We drove it to a dead land, and We sent down water by it, and brought forth thereby fruits of every kind﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]. As for his statement "and what He does, etc." and that every act, although it is attributed to other than Him metaphorically, is truly His act, there is no difference between what He attributes to His essence and what He attributes to other than Himself, because all of that is His bringing into existence and His creation. (Commentary continues.)

Al-nushur (the resurrection, the rising) is the verbal noun of nashara, said of the dead when he comes back to life. Al-A'sha said:

"Until people say, at what they see: 'How wondrous, for the dead one who rises!'"

Al-nushur is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), and the preposition and its object before it are in a position of jarr (genitive). The comparison occurs in several respects: when the dead earth accepts the life fitting for it, so likewise the limbs accept life. Or: just as the wind gathers pieces of cloud, so likewise the parts of limbs and the fragments of things are gathered. Or: just as He drives the winds and the clouds to the dead land, so He drives the spirit and life to the body.

﴿Man kana yuridu al-izzah﴾: that is, desires victory over others (al-mughalabah). ﴿Fa-lillahi al-izzah﴾: that is, it does not belong to anyone else and is not completed except by Him, and the one who seeks to overcome is overcome. Mujahid inclined to this view, and said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾ by worshipping idols. This is an illustration of His saying: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81]. Qatadah said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾ and its straight path, and loves to attain it, ﴿then to Allah belongs honour﴾: that is, through Him and by His command; His honour is not attained except by obeying Him. Al-Farra' said: whoever desires knowledge of honour, ﴿then to Allah belongs honour﴾: that is, He is the one characterized by it. It has also been said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾: that is, honour that is not followed by humiliation and is not turned toward humiliation. Al-Zamakhshari said: the disbelievers used to gain honour through the idols, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81]. And those who believed with their tongues without their hearts agreeing used to gain honour through the polytheists, as He said: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. Do they seek honour with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139]. Thus He made clear that there is no honour except for Allah and for His allies, and He said: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. End of quotation.

There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139], although the apparent meaning is that it belongs to Him and not to anything else, and His saying ﴿honour belongs to Allah and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], although it implies sharing. This is because honour in reality belongs to Allah essentially, to the Messenger through his nearness to Allah, and to the believers through the Messenger. So the one judged first is other than the one judged second.

Man is a conditional particle (ism shart), and the response clause must contain a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun when it is not an adverb. The response is elided, and its estimated form is according to those earlier sayings. According to Mujahid's view: "then he is overcome." According to Qatadah's view: "then let him seek it from Allah." According to al-Farra's view: "then let him attribute that to Allah." According to the fourth view: "then he does not attain it." The response was omitted, being dispensed with by His saying ﴿then to Allah belongs all honour﴾, since it indicates it. The most apparent of these views is Qatadah's: "let him seek it from the One to whom honour belongs, who disposes of it as He wills," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You grant honour to whom You will and You humble whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Jami'an (all) is put in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (al-muraad), and what is meant is the honour of this world and the honour of the Hereafter.

﴿Al-kalim al-tayyib﴾ (the good word) is tawhid, tahmid, the remembrance of Allah, and the like. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It has also been said: praise with good for the righteous believers. Ka'b said: "Indeed, 'Subhan Allah,' 'al-hamdu lillah,' 'la ilaha illa Allah,' and 'Allahu akbar' have a humming around the Throne like the humming of bees, with mention of their speaker."

The majority read (yas'adu), in the active voice from sa'ida, with ﴿al-kalim al-tayyib﴾ in the nominative, so al-kalim is the plural of kalimah. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sulami, and Ibrahim read yus'idu from as'ada, with al-kalam al-tayyib in the passive voice. End of quotation. Zayd ibn 'Ali read yas'adu from sa'ida, with al-kalam (speech) as subject, meaning "ascended." The ascent of speech to Him, exalted is He, is metaphorical both in the agent and in the one to whom it ascends, because He, exalted is He, is not in a direction, and because words are utterances that are not described as ascending, since ascent belongs to bodies. Rather, it is a metaphor for acceptance and for describing it as perfect, as one says: "His heel was raised and his rank was elevated," and from it: "they went up to the judge" and "the matter was raised to him," and there is no height in direction there.

The majority read: ﴿wal-'amalu al-salihu yarfa'uhu﴾ (and righteous deed raises it). So al-'amal (deed) is a mubtada' (subject), and yarfa'uhu is the khabar (predicate). The subject of yarfa'uhu is a pronoun referring to al-'amal al-salih, and the object pronoun refers to al-kalim, meaning: it raises the good word. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. Al-Hasan said: the statement is presented to the deed; if the statement agrees with the deed, it is accepted, and if it disagrees, it is rejected. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: when the servant remembers Allah and says a good word and performs His obligations, his statement is raised together with his deed; and when he speaks but does not perform His obligations, his statement is rejected in favor of his deed. It was also said: his deed is more fitting for him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a view refuted by the creed of the People of the Sunnah, and it is not authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas. The truth is that the one who performs his obligations, when he remembers Allah and says a good word, is recorded for him and accepted; he has his good deeds and his bad deeds are upon him, and Allah accepts from everyone who guards against shirk. Abu Salih and Shahr ibn Hawshab said the reverse of this view: the subject pronoun refers to al-kalim, and the object pronoun to al-'amal al-salih, meaning: the good word raises it. Qatadah said: the subject is a pronoun referring to Allah, and the hi (its) refers to al-'amal al-salih, meaning: Allah raises it to Himself, that is, accepts it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the most preferred of the views. From Ibn 'Abbas: "al-'amal al-salih raises its doer and honours him," so he made it with an elided mudaf (genitive construction). In my view it is permissible that al-'amal be conjoined to al-kalim al-tayyib, meaning that both ascend to Allah, and yarfa'uhu is a resumed statement (isti'naf ikhbar), meaning: Allah raises them. He made the pronoun singular because the two are shared in ascending, and a pronoun may take the place of a demonstrative, so its form is singular while what is meant is the dual. It is as if it were said: their ascent is not from themselves, rather it is by Allah's raising them.

'Isa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: wal-'amala al-saliha, with both in the accusative by ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun, governing the object). The subject is a pronoun referring to al-kalim or to Allah. Makara is intransitive. (Al-sayyi'at) is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, meaning "evil plottings," or of a mudaf to a verbal noun, meaning he attributed the plotting to the evil deeds, or he made yamkurun include the meaning of "earning," so that al-sayyi'at is the direct object. When al-sayyi'at is an adjective of a verbal noun, or of a mudaf to a verbal noun, the apparent meaning is that it refers to the plottings of Quraysh in the Dar al-Nadwah, when they discussed one of three plots, which are mentioned in al-Anfal: to confine him, or to kill him, or to expel him. And ﴿ula'ika﴾ (those) refers to those who devised those plots.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 35, verses 9–14 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Yabūr﴾ means it will be corrupted and destroyed, "apart from the plotting of God against them," when He expelled them from Mecca, killed them, and threw them into the well of Badr. He thus gathered all their schemes upon them and fulfilled His saying: ﴿They plot, and God plots, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30], and His saying: ﴿The evil plot encompasses only its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. The word ﴿al-makr al-sayyi'﴾ is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and ﴿yabūr﴾ is its predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate). The whole sentence is a predicate for ﴿wa-makru ūlā'ika﴾ ("and the plotting of those"). Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa permitted that ﴿huwa﴾ be a separating pronoun (fasl, a pronoun placed between subject and predicate to mark the division), with ﴿yabūr﴾ as the predicate and ﴿makru ūlā'ika﴾ as the subject. Yet, as far as we know, no one has taken this view except Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani in his commentary on his Sharh al-Idah, where he permitted in ﴿kāna Zaydun huwa yaqūmu﴾ that ﴿huwa﴾ be a separating pronoun. This view was rejected.

﴿And God created you from dust﴾: from the point of view that He created our father Adam from dust.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: that is, by procreation.

﴿Then He made you pairs﴾: that is, kinds, males and females, as He said: ﴿He gives to whom He wills females and males﴾ [Al-Shura: 50]. Qatada said: He decreed marriage among you, and He joined some of you with others. The ﴿min﴾ in ﴿min mu'ammar﴾ ("of one granted a long life") is superfluous. He called him "one granted a long life" by what he will become, namely one who has a long lifespan. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿min 'umrihi﴾ ("of his life") refers to ﴿mu'ammar﴾ both in form and in meaning. Ibn Abbas and others said: it refers to ﴿mu'ammar﴾ as a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a category), and what is meant is other than the one who is granted a long life. Thus the verse contains two persons: one of them is granted a hundred years, and something is reduced from the other. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik, that what is meant is one person, that is, he counts what has passed of his life; when a year passes, he records that, then another year, and so this is the reduction. The poet said:

*Your life is breaths that are counted; every time a breath of yours passes, you have lost a part by it.*

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the meaning of ﴿nor is anything reduced from his life﴾ is that no one's life is cut short by a cause that God's power does not permit; had He willed, He would have delayed that cause. It is reported that when Umar, may God be pleased with him, was stabbed, he said: "If he prayed to God, He would have increased his term." The Muslims denied this and said: God, exalted is He, says: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [Al-A'raf: 34], and so they argued with this verse. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a weak, rejected view, which implies belief in two terms, and the Mu'tazilites clung to something similar.

The majority read ﴿wa-lā yunqaṣu﴾ ("nor is it reduced") in the passive voice. Ya'qub, Salam, Abd al-Warith, and Harun, both transmitted from Abu Amr, read ﴿wa-lā yanqusu﴾ in the active voice. Al-Hasan read ﴿min 'umrihi illā fī kitābin﴾ ("of his life, except in a Book"). Ibn Abbas said: this is the Preserved Tablet. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by "the Book of God" is meant the knowledge of God, or the record of the person. End of quotation.

﴿Nor are the two seas alike﴾: this is another verse by which every intelligent person may be shown that it is something in which no idol has any share. The explanation of ﴿this is sweet, palatable﴾ and ﴿this is salt, bitter﴾ has already been given in Surah Al-Furqan. Here, between the two categories, is an attribute of the Arabs, and between it and His saying ﴿pleasant to drink﴾ (sā'igun sharābuhu). The majority read ﴿sā'igun﴾ as an active participle from ﴿sāgha﴾. Isa read ﴿sayyi'un﴾ on the pattern fay'il, like ﴿mayyitun﴾; the same is transmitted from Abu Amr and Asim. Isa also read ﴿sayghun﴾, a lightened form of the doubled verb, like ﴿mayt﴾, the lightened form of ﴿mayyit﴾. The majority read ﴿milḥun﴾; Abu Nahik and Talha read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this is an irregular dialect. It is possible that it is a shortened form of ﴿mālih﴾, with the alif dropped for lightness. It is also said: "water is milḥ" in irregular usage, but in common usage it is mamlūḥ. Al-Zamakhshari said: the two seas, the sweet and the salt, are set forth as parables for the believer and the disbeliever. Then he said, by way of digression (istitrad, a shift to a related topic) in describing the two seas and what is connected with them: "of His blessing and His bounty."

﴿And from each﴾: al-Zamakhshari explained words from the verse that were repeated in Surah Al-Nahl. Then he said: it may also bear a meaning other than the digression, namely that the two kinds are compared to the two seas, and then the salt sea is preferred over the disbeliever, in that it shares with the sweet sea in benefits such as fish and pearls, and the sailing of ships upon it, whereas the disbeliever is empty of benefit. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 74], and the verse. End of quotation.

﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾: he means trade, the Hajj, the campaign, or every journey that has a lawful aim.

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾: the explanation of these phrases has already been given. When He mentioned many things that indicate His overwhelming power, such as sending the winds, creating from dust and what is joined to it, causing the night to enter the day, and subjecting the sun and the moon, He pointed out that the One who has these wondrous acts is God. So He said: ﴿That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs sovereignty﴾. These are successive predicates. The subject is ﴿dhālikum﴾ ("that"), and ﴿Allāhu rabbukum﴾ ("God is your Lord") are two predicates; ﴿lahu al-mulk﴾ ("to Him belongs sovereignty") is a subject-predicate sentence in connection with His saying: ﴿And those you call upon besides Him possess not even a thin membrane of a date pit﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also permissible, in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), to make the name of God an attribute of the demonstrative pronoun, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan, a noun in apposition that clarifies the preceding word), with ﴿rabbukum﴾ as the predicate, were it not that the meaning rejects it. End of quotation. As for its being an attribute, that is not permissible, because ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper noun (ism 'alam), and a proper noun is not described by an attribute, nor is it a generic noun like "man," in which an attribute could be imagined. As for his saying "were it not that the meaning rejects it," it is not evident that the meaning rejects it, because it would then be informing that the one indicated by those attributes and the mentioned acts is your Lord, that is, your owner or your reformer. This is a fitting and acceptable meaning.

Those whom you call upon besides Him are the idols. The majority read ﴿tad'ūna﴾ ("you call upon") with the second-person prefix; Isa, Salam, and Ya'qub read it with the third-person prefix. The author of al-Kamil, Abu al-Qasim ibn Jabbara, said: ﴿yad'ūna﴾ with the third person is transmitted by al-Lu'lu'i from Abu Amr and Salam, al-Nahawandi from Qutayba, Ibn al-Jalla' from Nusayr, Ibn Habib and Ibn Yunus from al-Kisa'i, and Abu Umara from Hafs. The word ﴿qiṭmīr﴾ has already been explained. Juwaybir, on the authority of his men, and al-Dahhak said: it is the cap at the top of the date. Mujahid said: it is the wrapping of the pit. It is also said: it is what lies between the cap of the date and the pit. It is also said: the skin of garlic. Whichever it is, it is a figure for the smallest thing. The poet said:

*Your father wears down his sandal, squatting, yet the poor man does not possess even a thin membrane of a date pit.*

﴿They do not hear your call﴾: because they are inanimate. ﴿And if they heard﴾: this is on the supposition of a hypothesis. ﴿They would not respond to you﴾: because they do not claim any divinity for themselves, and they disown it. It is also said: they would not benefit you. He added the verbal noun (maṣdar) to ﴿shirkikum﴾ ("your associating"), meaning by your associating them with God in your worship of them, as in His saying: ﴿You did not worship us﴾ [Yunus: 28]. Thus it is an annexation to the doer. As for His saying ﴿yakfurūna﴾ ("they will disown"), it may mean that, by what appears there of their stillness and sluggishness when a speaker moves and every arguer contests, this comes in the manner of figurative speech (tajawwuz), as in the words of Dhu al-Rumma:

*I stood at a dwelling of Mayya, speaking, its traces addressing me while I address it.*

*And I water it until, from what I pour out, its stones and its playgrounds almost speak to me.*

﴿And none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾. Qatada and other exegetes said: the All-Aware here means God Himself, who is the Truthful in report, who has informed of this, so there is no doubt in its occurrence. Ibn Atiyyah said: it may be that His saying ﴿and none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾ is part of the continuing description of the idols, as if He said: none informs you like one who informs you about himself, that is, they do not speak truthfully in disowning your associating them with God. So by "the All-Aware" in this similitude is meant, as it were: none informs you about himself like one who has informed about himself, and they have informed about themselves by disbelieving in these (their worshippers). Al-Zamakhshari said: none informs you of the matter like one who informs, who is All-Aware of it, meaning that the one who is aware of the matter is the one who informs you of the truth rather than the other informants about it. The meaning is: what I have told you about the state of the idols is the truth, because I am aware of what I inform about. The author of al-Tajrid said: it admits of two aspects. First, that this is an address to the Messenger when he was informed that on the Day of Resurrection the wood and the stone will speak and deny their worshippers, a matter that cannot be known by pure reason without God's informing of it. God said: ﴿They will disown their associating﴾, that is, they will disown them on the Day of Resurrection. This statement, though what it reports is a wondrous matter, is as it has said, because the informant is All-Aware. Second, that it is an address not restricted to anyone in particular, that is: what has been mentioned is as it has been mentioned; none informs you, O listener, whoever you are, like one who is All-Aware.

[p. 302] ﴿And Allah is He who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and give life thereby to the earth after its death. Thus is the Resurrection.﴾ ﴿Whoever desires honour—then to Allah belongs all honour. To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it. As for those who plot evil deeds, for them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish.﴾ ﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then He made you into pairs. No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And no one is granted long life or has his life shortened except that it is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter. From each you eat fresh flesh, and you extract ornaments to wear. And you see the ships ploughing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful.﴾ ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a speck of a date-pit membrane.﴾ ﴿If you invoke them, they do not hear your call, and even if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association of them. And none can inform you like the All-Knowing.﴾

When He mentioned some matters of the heavenly realm and the sending of the angels, He mentioned some matters of the earthly realm: the winds and their sending. In this there is an argument against those who deny the resurrection. He pointed them to the example they witness, namely that bringing the dead to life is like this. It is mentioned in a hadith: "It was said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'How does Allah give life to the dead, and what is the sign of that in His creation?' He said: 'Have you passed by a valley that was barren, then you passed by it and it was stirring green?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Thus Allah gives life to the dead, and that is His sign in His creation.'"

It has been said that ﴿arsala﴾ (He sent) has the meaning of yursilu (He sends), and for that reason ﴿fatuthiru﴾ (so they stir up) is conjoined to it. It has also been said: the present tense was used to narrate a state in which the stirring of the clouds by the winds takes place, and to evoke that wondrous image which indicates the divine power. From the same usage is ﴿fatusbihu al-ardu mukhdarrah﴾ (then the earth becomes green). Al-Zamakhshari said: "They do likewise with every act in which there is a kind of distinguishing particularity by a state that is strange, or in which the addressee is suspected, or other than that, as Ta'abbata Sharran said:

"That I have met the ghoul, as she plunges with meteors like a page, with a wide expanse,
So I struck her without dismay, and she fell, a prostrate one, onto both her hands and her neck."

He intended to depict for his people the state in which he encouraged his cousin to strike the ghoul, as if he were making them see it and informing them of its reality, as a witnessing of wonder at his boldness toward every terror and his steadfastness at every hardship. Likewise, the driving of the clouds to the dead land and the giving of life to the earth by rain after its death. Since this is among the proofs of the overwhelming power, it was said: ﴿fa-saqna﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ (We drive and We give life), diverted by them from the form of the third person to what is more inherent in particularity and more indicative of it." End of quotation.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: "That is, He sent it in the past tense, because what is attributed to Allah and what He does, by His saying 'Be,' does not remain for a time or a part of a time. So He did not use the future form, due to the necessity of its occurrence and the speed of its coming into being. And because He has finished with everything, He has determined the sending at known times and to specified places. And since He attributed the stirring to the wind, which is formed over a period of time, He said ﴿fatuthiru﴾; and He attributed ﴿arsala﴾ to the third person (the absent one), and in ﴿fa-saqnahu﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ to the first person (the speaker). Because in the first He introduced Himself by an act of His acts, which is the sending; then when He was known, He said: 'I am the One you know: I drove the clouds, so I gave life to the earth.' So in the first there is an introduction through the wondrous act, and in the second a reminder of the resurrection. And ﴿fa-saqnahu﴾ and ﴿fa-ahyayna﴾ in the past form support what we have mentioned of the difference between ﴿fatuthiru﴾ and ﴿arsala﴾." End of quotation.

This distinction he mentioned between ﴿arsala﴾ and ﴿fatuthiru﴾ does not appear clearly. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Rum: ﴿Allah is He who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾ [al-Rum: 48], and in al-A'raf: ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]: how did the present tense come with the verb of sending? This is only a variation in speech and a manipulation of eloquence. As for the shift from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun glorifying Himself, it is of the category of iltifat (shift in address). Likewise in al-A'raf: ﴿We drove it to a dead land, and We sent down water by it, and brought forth thereby fruits of every kind﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]. As for his statement "and what He does, etc." and that every act, although it is attributed to other than Him metaphorically, is truly His act, there is no difference between what He attributes to His essence and what He attributes to other than Himself, because all of that is His bringing into existence and His creation. (Commentary continues.)

Al-nushur (the resurrection, the rising) is the verbal noun of nashara, said of the dead when he comes back to life. Al-A'sha said:

"Until people say, at what they see: 'How wondrous, for the dead one who rises!'"

Al-nushur is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), and the preposition and its object before it are in a position of jarr (genitive). The comparison occurs in several respects: when the dead earth accepts the life fitting for it, so likewise the limbs accept life. Or: just as the wind gathers pieces of cloud, so likewise the parts of limbs and the fragments of things are gathered. Or: just as He drives the winds and the clouds to the dead land, so He drives the spirit and life to the body.

﴿Man kana yuridu al-izzah﴾: that is, desires victory over others (al-mughalabah). ﴿Fa-lillahi al-izzah﴾: that is, it does not belong to anyone else and is not completed except by Him, and the one who seeks to overcome is overcome. Mujahid inclined to this view, and said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾ by worshipping idols. This is an illustration of His saying: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81]. Qatadah said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾ and its straight path, and loves to attain it, ﴿then to Allah belongs honour﴾: that is, through Him and by His command; His honour is not attained except by obeying Him. Al-Farra' said: whoever desires knowledge of honour, ﴿then to Allah belongs honour﴾: that is, He is the one characterized by it. It has also been said: ﴿Whoever desires honour﴾: that is, honour that is not followed by humiliation and is not turned toward humiliation. Al-Zamakhshari said: the disbelievers used to gain honour through the idols, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81]. And those who believed with their tongues without their hearts agreeing used to gain honour through the polytheists, as He said: ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers. Do they seek honour with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139]. Thus He made clear that there is no honour except for Allah and for His allies, and He said: ﴿And honour belongs to Allah and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. End of quotation.

There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139], although the apparent meaning is that it belongs to Him and not to anything else, and His saying ﴿honour belongs to Allah and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], although it implies sharing. This is because honour in reality belongs to Allah essentially, to the Messenger through his nearness to Allah, and to the believers through the Messenger. So the one judged first is other than the one judged second.

Man is a conditional particle (ism shart), and the response clause must contain a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun when it is not an adverb. The response is elided, and its estimated form is according to those earlier sayings. According to Mujahid's view: "then he is overcome." According to Qatadah's view: "then let him seek it from Allah." According to al-Farra's view: "then let him attribute that to Allah." According to the fourth view: "then he does not attain it." The response was omitted, being dispensed with by His saying ﴿then to Allah belongs all honour﴾, since it indicates it. The most apparent of these views is Qatadah's: "let him seek it from the One to whom honour belongs, who disposes of it as He wills," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You grant honour to whom You will and You humble whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Jami'an (all) is put in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (al-muraad), and what is meant is the honour of this world and the honour of the Hereafter.

﴿Al-kalim al-tayyib﴾ (the good word) is tawhid, tahmid, the remembrance of Allah, and the like. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It has also been said: praise with good for the righteous believers. Ka'b said: "Indeed, 'Subhan Allah,' 'al-hamdu lillah,' 'la ilaha illa Allah,' and 'Allahu akbar' have a humming around the Throne like the humming of bees, with mention of their speaker."

The majority read (yas'adu), in the active voice from sa'ida, with ﴿al-kalim al-tayyib﴾ in the nominative, so al-kalim is the plural of kalimah. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sulami, and Ibrahim read yus'idu from as'ada, with al-kalam al-tayyib in the passive voice. End of quotation. Zayd ibn 'Ali read yas'adu from sa'ida, with al-kalam (speech) as subject, meaning "ascended." The ascent of speech to Him, exalted is He, is metaphorical both in the agent and in the one to whom it ascends, because He, exalted is He, is not in a direction, and because words are utterances that are not described as ascending, since ascent belongs to bodies. Rather, it is a metaphor for acceptance and for describing it as perfect, as one says: "His heel was raised and his rank was elevated," and from it: "they went up to the judge" and "the matter was raised to him," and there is no height in direction there.

The majority read: ﴿wal-'amalu al-salihu yarfa'uhu﴾ (and righteous deed raises it). So al-'amal (deed) is a mubtada' (subject), and yarfa'uhu is the khabar (predicate). The subject of yarfa'uhu is a pronoun referring to al-'amal al-salih, and the object pronoun refers to al-kalim, meaning: it raises the good word. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. Al-Hasan said: the statement is presented to the deed; if the statement agrees with the deed, it is accepted, and if it disagrees, it is rejected. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: when the servant remembers Allah and says a good word and performs His obligations, his statement is raised together with his deed; and when he speaks but does not perform His obligations, his statement is rejected in favor of his deed. It was also said: his deed is more fitting for him. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a view refuted by the creed of the People of the Sunnah, and it is not authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas. The truth is that the one who performs his obligations, when he remembers Allah and says a good word, is recorded for him and accepted; he has his good deeds and his bad deeds are upon him, and Allah accepts from everyone who guards against shirk. Abu Salih and Shahr ibn Hawshab said the reverse of this view: the subject pronoun refers to al-kalim, and the object pronoun to al-'amal al-salih, meaning: the good word raises it. Qatadah said: the subject is a pronoun referring to Allah, and the hi (its) refers to al-'amal al-salih, meaning: Allah raises it to Himself, that is, accepts it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is the most preferred of the views. From Ibn 'Abbas: "al-'amal al-salih raises its doer and honours him," so he made it with an elided mudaf (genitive construction). In my view it is permissible that al-'amal be conjoined to al-kalim al-tayyib, meaning that both ascend to Allah, and yarfa'uhu is a resumed statement (isti'naf ikhbar), meaning: Allah raises them. He made the pronoun singular because the two are shared in ascending, and a pronoun may take the place of a demonstrative, so its form is singular while what is meant is the dual. It is as if it were said: their ascent is not from themselves, rather it is by Allah's raising them.

'Isa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: wal-'amala al-saliha, with both in the accusative by ishtighal (the verb being occupied with a pronoun, governing the object). The subject is a pronoun referring to al-kalim or to Allah. Makara is intransitive. (Al-sayyi'at) is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, meaning "evil plottings," or of a mudaf to a verbal noun, meaning he attributed the plotting to the evil deeds, or he made yamkurun include the meaning of "earning," so that al-sayyi'at is the direct object. When al-sayyi'at is an adjective of a verbal noun, or of a mudaf to a verbal noun, the apparent meaning is that it refers to the plottings of Quraysh in the Dar al-Nadwah, when they discussed one of three plots, which are mentioned in al-Anfal: to confine him, or to kill him, or to expel him. And ﴿ula'ika﴾ (those) refers to those who devised those plots.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 35, verses 9–14 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Yabūr﴾ means it will be corrupted and destroyed, "apart from the plotting of God against them," when He expelled them from Mecca, killed them, and threw them into the well of Badr. He thus gathered all their schemes upon them and fulfilled His saying: ﴿They plot, and God plots, and God is the best of plotters﴾ [Al-Anfal: 30], and His saying: ﴿The evil plot encompasses only its own people﴾ [Fatir: 43]. The word ﴿al-makr al-sayyi'﴾ is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and ﴿yabūr﴾ is its predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate). The whole sentence is a predicate for ﴿wa-makru ūlā'ika﴾ ("and the plotting of those"). Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa permitted that ﴿huwa﴾ be a separating pronoun (fasl, a pronoun placed between subject and predicate to mark the division), with ﴿yabūr﴾ as the predicate and ﴿makru ūlā'ika﴾ as the subject. Yet, as far as we know, no one has taken this view except Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani in his commentary on his Sharh al-Idah, where he permitted in ﴿kāna Zaydun huwa yaqūmu﴾ that ﴿huwa﴾ be a separating pronoun. This view was rejected.

﴿And God created you from dust﴾: from the point of view that He created our father Adam from dust.

﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾: that is, by procreation.

﴿Then He made you pairs﴾: that is, kinds, males and females, as He said: ﴿He gives to whom He wills females and males﴾ [Al-Shura: 50]. Qatada said: He decreed marriage among you, and He joined some of you with others. The ﴿min﴾ in ﴿min mu'ammar﴾ ("of one granted a long life") is superfluous. He called him "one granted a long life" by what he will become, namely one who has a long lifespan. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿min 'umrihi﴾ ("of his life") refers to ﴿mu'ammar﴾ both in form and in meaning. Ibn Abbas and others said: it refers to ﴿mu'ammar﴾ as a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a category), and what is meant is other than the one who is granted a long life. Thus the verse contains two persons: one of them is granted a hundred years, and something is reduced from the other. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik, that what is meant is one person, that is, he counts what has passed of his life; when a year passes, he records that, then another year, and so this is the reduction. The poet said:

*Your life is breaths that are counted; every time a breath of yours passes, you have lost a part by it.*

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the meaning of ﴿nor is anything reduced from his life﴾ is that no one's life is cut short by a cause that God's power does not permit; had He willed, He would have delayed that cause. It is reported that when Umar, may God be pleased with him, was stabbed, he said: "If he prayed to God, He would have increased his term." The Muslims denied this and said: God, exalted is He, says: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [Al-A'raf: 34], and so they argued with this verse. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a weak, rejected view, which implies belief in two terms, and the Mu'tazilites clung to something similar.

The majority read ﴿wa-lā yunqaṣu﴾ ("nor is it reduced") in the passive voice. Ya'qub, Salam, Abd al-Warith, and Harun, both transmitted from Abu Amr, read ﴿wa-lā yanqusu﴾ in the active voice. Al-Hasan read ﴿min 'umrihi illā fī kitābin﴾ ("of his life, except in a Book"). Ibn Abbas said: this is the Preserved Tablet. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by "the Book of God" is meant the knowledge of God, or the record of the person. End of quotation.

﴿Nor are the two seas alike﴾: this is another verse by which every intelligent person may be shown that it is something in which no idol has any share. The explanation of ﴿this is sweet, palatable﴾ and ﴿this is salt, bitter﴾ has already been given in Surah Al-Furqan. Here, between the two categories, is an attribute of the Arabs, and between it and His saying ﴿pleasant to drink﴾ (sā'igun sharābuhu). The majority read ﴿sā'igun﴾ as an active participle from ﴿sāgha﴾. Isa read ﴿sayyi'un﴾ on the pattern fay'il, like ﴿mayyitun﴾; the same is transmitted from Abu Amr and Asim. Isa also read ﴿sayghun﴾, a lightened form of the doubled verb, like ﴿mayt﴾, the lightened form of ﴿mayyit﴾. The majority read ﴿milḥun﴾; Abu Nahik and Talha read it with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: this is an irregular dialect. It is possible that it is a shortened form of ﴿mālih﴾, with the alif dropped for lightness. It is also said: "water is milḥ" in irregular usage, but in common usage it is mamlūḥ. Al-Zamakhshari said: the two seas, the sweet and the salt, are set forth as parables for the believer and the disbeliever. Then he said, by way of digression (istitrad, a shift to a related topic) in describing the two seas and what is connected with them: "of His blessing and His bounty."

﴿And from each﴾: al-Zamakhshari explained words from the verse that were repeated in Surah Al-Nahl. Then he said: it may also bear a meaning other than the digression, namely that the two kinds are compared to the two seas, and then the salt sea is preferred over the disbeliever, in that it shares with the sweet sea in benefits such as fish and pearls, and the sailing of ships upon it, whereas the disbeliever is empty of benefit. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 74], and the verse. End of quotation.

﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾: he means trade, the Hajj, the campaign, or every journey that has a lawful aim.

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾: the explanation of these phrases has already been given. When He mentioned many things that indicate His overwhelming power, such as sending the winds, creating from dust and what is joined to it, causing the night to enter the day, and subjecting the sun and the moon, He pointed out that the One who has these wondrous acts is God. So He said: ﴿That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs sovereignty﴾. These are successive predicates. The subject is ﴿dhālikum﴾ ("that"), and ﴿Allāhu rabbukum﴾ ("God is your Lord") are two predicates; ﴿lahu al-mulk﴾ ("to Him belongs sovereignty") is a subject-predicate sentence in connection with His saying: ﴿And those you call upon besides Him possess not even a thin membrane of a date pit﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also permissible, in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab), to make the name of God an attribute of the demonstrative pronoun, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan, a noun in apposition that clarifies the preceding word), with ﴿rabbukum﴾ as the predicate, were it not that the meaning rejects it. End of quotation. As for its being an attribute, that is not permissible, because ﴿Allah﴾ is a proper noun (ism 'alam), and a proper noun is not described by an attribute, nor is it a generic noun like "man," in which an attribute could be imagined.
