Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read ﴿wa-mā tastawī al-aḥyā'﴾ with the feminine *ta'*. The majority read it with a *ya'*. The ordering of these things negated as being equal is in the utmost eloquence. He mentioned the blind and the seeing as an example of the believer and the disbeliever. Then the seeing person, even if he is keen-sighted, sees only in light, so He mentioned what the disbeliever is in, namely the darkness of disbelief, and what the believer is in, namely the light of faith. Then He mentioned their outcome, which is the shade: the believer, by his faith, is in shade and ease, while the disbeliever, by his disbelief, is in heat and hardship.

Then He mentioned another parable concerning the believer and the disbeliever, beyond the case of the blind and the seeing, since the blind may share with the seeing some kind of perception, whereas the disbeliever does not perceive in a beneficial way; he is like the dead. For this reason He repeated the verb, saying ﴿And the living are not equal, nor the dead﴾, as if He had placed it in the position of a question, and He repeated "lā" in what He mentioned to emphasize the opposition. Darkness opposes and contrasts with light, and shade and heat are likewise; but the blind and the seeing are not like that, because one and the same person may be seeing, then afterward blindness befalls him, so there is no opposition except from the standpoint of the attribute. The opposition between shade and heat is permanent, because what is meant by shade is the absence of heat and cold; since the opposition there is more complete, it was emphasized by repetition. As for the living and the dead, inasmuch as one and the same body may be a locus of life, then it becomes a locus of death, the opposition between them is more complete than the opposition between the blind and the seeing, because these two may share some kind of perception, whereas the living does not. The dead differs from the living in reality, not merely in attribute, as explained in the Divine Wisdom. The more noble was placed first in two examples, namely the shade and the living, and was placed last in two examples, namely the seeing and the light. This is not said for the sake of rhymed prose (saj'), because the miraculous nature of the Qur'an does not lie in mere wording, but in its meaning as well. The poet may advance and postpone for the sake of rhyme, whereas the Qur'an's meaning is sound and its wording eloquent. Before the mission they were in misguidance, so they were like the blind, and their path was darkness. When the Messenger came and some people were guided by him, they became seeing, and their path was light. Then, when He mentioned the outcome and the final return, He placed what is connected with mercy before what is connected with wrath, as has come: "My mercy precedes My wrath." So He placed the shade before the heat.

Then the persistent disbeliever after the mission became more astray than the blind, and resembled the dead in not perceiving the truth. So He said ﴿And the living are not equal﴾, those who believed in what Allah sent down, ﴿nor the dead﴾, those to whom the clear verses were recited and who did not benefit from them. These were after the faith of those who believed, so He placed them later, because the life of the believers existed before the death of the disbeliever. He made the blind and the seeing singular, because He matched the genus with the genus, since among individuals of the blind there may be some who equal some individuals of the seeing, like a blind man who has such intelligence that he equals a dull seeing man. So the difference between the two genera is certain, not between individuals. The darknesses were made plural, because the paths of disbelief are many; and light was made singular, because monotheism and the truth are one, and the difference between each individual of those (plural) and this one is such that He said: the darknesses do not find in them anything equal to this light. As for the living and the dead, the difference between them is greater, since there is no dead person who equals a living one in perception. So He mentioned that the living are not equal to the dead, whether you match genus with genus or individual with individual. End of the words of Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi, with some abridgement.

Then He consoled His Messenger, saying ﴿Indeed Allah makes hear whom He wills﴾, meaning: the causing of these people to hear is subject to Our will, and by "hearing" He meant that by which response to faith occurs. When He had mentioned that ﴿the living are not equal nor the dead﴾, He said ﴿And you are not one who can make hear those in the graves﴾, meaning these people, because of their not listening to the hearing of the truth, are in the position of those who have died and then remain in their graves. Just as one who has died cannot accept from you the word of truth, so too are these, for they are dead of heart. Al-Ashhab and al-Hasan read "bi-musmi‘i man" with an idafa; the majority read it with tanwin.

﴿You are only a warner﴾, meaning: your duty is only to convey and warn. If the one warned is among those whom Allah wills to guide, he hears and is guided; and if he is among those whom Allah wills to misguide, then it is not upon you, for He, exalted is He, is the One who guides and misguides. "Bi'l-haqq" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the agent, meaning "being truthful"; or from the object, meaning "truthfully"; or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a sending with the truth," i.e., accompanied. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is related to "bashīr" and "nadhīr," so "nadhīr" is with respect to "bashīr" with the true promise, and "nadhīr" with the threat. End of quotation. It is not possible that "bi'l-haqq" relate to both "bashīr" and "nadhīr" together; rather his words should be interpreted as meaning that there is an omitted element, the sense being: a bringer of good tidings with the true promise, and a warner with the true threat, so he omitted the counterpart because its counterpart indicates it.

﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾. "Ummah" means a large group. The meaning is that the call to Allah has not ceased for any nation, either directly through their prophets, and what is transmitted up to the time of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ; and the verses indicating that Quraysh had not received a warner mean that no warner had come to them directly, nor had their nearer forefathers. Or it means that warning ceased, and then not. When the traces of warning began to fade, Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ; and what the scholars of kalam mention about the condition of the people of the intervals (al-fatarat) is by way of supposition, since that is actual, and there is no nation upon the face of the earth that has not known the call to Allah and His worship. He suffices with mentioning "nadhīr" without "bashīr," because it is accompanied by it in His saying ﴿as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, so this indicates that it is intended, and it was omitted for the sake of that indication.

﴿And if they deny you﴾ is a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ, and the discussion of the parallels to these sentences has preceded at the end of Al ʿImran. His saying ﴿then how was My denunciation?﴾ is a threat to Quraysh with what befell the deniers of their messengers.

(p-307) ﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation.﴾ ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah.﴾ ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls to its burden, nothing of it will be carried, even by a near relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer. Whoever purifies himself, purifies himself only for his own soul, and to Allah is the final return.﴾ ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike,﴾ ﴿nor are the darkness and the light,﴾ ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat.﴾ ﴿Nor are the living and the dead alike. Indeed Allah makes whom He wills hear, but you cannot make those in the graves hear.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner. And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had also denied. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with the Psalms, and with the Book that gives light.﴾ ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved, and how was My rejection!﴾

This is a verse of admonition and reminder, and that all people are in need of Allah's beneficence and favour in all their conditions. No one is independent of Him for even the blink of an eye, while He is absolutely independent of the whole creation. He described them as "the poor" (fuqara') in order to show them how intensely they are in need of Him, since they are the category of the poor. Even though the whole world is in need of Him, because of their weakness they are treated as if they were the entirety of this category. Had He used the indefinite form, the meaning would have been "you are [some] poor," but the definite form makes the poor stand in contrast to the Self-Sufficient. He is described as "the Praiseworthy" to indicate that He is generous and bountiful, so He is praised for the blessings He bestows and deserves to be praised.

Having stated that He is absolutely self-sufficient, He mentioned what indicates His independence from the creation and that He has no need of them, saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away﴾, meaning: if He wills to take you away, He will take you away. This contains a threat of destroying them.

﴿And that﴾, that is, taking you away and bringing a new creation, ﴿is not difficult﴾, meaning it is not impossible for Him, since He is characterised by complete power, so nothing He wills is impossible for Him. The meaning of ﴿a new creation﴾ is that He will replace you, in line with His saying ﴿And if you turn away, He will substitute a people other than you﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. Ibn 'Abbas said: He will create after you those who worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. This meaning has also come in connection with the mention of taking away after describing Him as self-sufficient, in His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can take you away and make successors after you of whomever He wills﴾ [al-An'am: 133]. The taking away is also linked, and concluded at the end of the verse, with the mention of the power that indicates this, in His saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others; and Allah is ever capable of that﴾ [al-Nisa': 133].

It is reported that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to some of the believers: "Disbelieve in Muhammad, and I will bear your burden," so this verse was revealed. Allah informed that no one carries another's burden. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: this verse concerns sins and crimes. It is said: "wazara al-shay'" means he carried the thing, and *wazira* (a bearer) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "a soul bearing [a burden]". He mentioned the adjective without mentioning the noun it qualifies, restricting himself to it, because the meaning is that every soul is seen only as bearing its own burden, not the burden of another. So He does not seize a soul for the sin of another soul, unlike the tyrants of this world who seize the neighbour for the neighbour, the friend for the friend, and the relative for the relative. Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever among the rulers goes to the extreme of seizing a relative for the crime of his relative, as the act of Ziyad and similar people, that is injustice, because the one seized may have helped the criminal through support and association, or by knowing of his condition and approving of it, and thus he has taken a share of the crime. End of quote. It seems Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted the actions of Ziyad and what he did in Islam; his conduct was close to that of al-Hajjaj. There is no contradiction between this verse and the one in al-'Ankabut, because that one concerns misguided people who misguide others: they bear the burdens of leading people astray together with the burdens of their own error, so all of that is their burden, and there is nothing of the burden of others in it. Do you not see His words: ﴿And they will not bear anything of their sins﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12]?

﴿And if a heavily laden soul calls﴾, that is, a soul weighed down by its load, ﴿to its burden, nothing of it will be carried﴾, meaning there will be no help or rescue on that day for one who seeks rescue, and no assistance, to the extent that a soul whose burdens have weighed it down, if it calls someone to lighten some of its burden, will not be answered, even if the one called is one of its close relatives, such as a father, son or brother. The previous verse is about the justice of Allah in His judgement and that He does not seize a soul for the sin of another, while this one is about negating assistance. *Al-himl* (load) originally means what is carried on the back in physical things, and it is extended metaphorically to abstract things such as sins and the like. Thus every burden is considered as attached to the back, as in His saying ﴿And they carry their burdens on their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31], just as every acquisition is attributed to the hand.

The majority of readers read ﴿yuḥmal﴾ (is carried) with a *ya'* and in the passive voice. Abu al-Sammal, on the authority of Talha, and Ibrahim ibn Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read it with a *ta'* at the beginning and a *kasra* on the *mim*. This reading requires that *shay'* be in the accusative, just as the majority reading requires it to be in the nominative. The subject of *yuḥmal* in this reading is a pronoun referring to the omitted object of *tad'u* (calls), meaning: "And if a heavily laden soul calls another soul to its burden, that other soul will not carry anything of it." The subject of *kāna* (the verb "to be") is a pronoun referring to the understood one called, from His saying ﴿And if he calls﴾. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement. He said: the called one was left unspecified so that it would include and cover every person called. He said: If you ask, "how can there be a pronoun for something implied, and how can a general noun be the close relative of the heavily laden one?" I say: this is of the generality that occurs by way of substitution. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the subject of *kāna* is an implied pronoun, its estimated form being "wa-law kāna" (even if there were). End of quote, meaning: even if the one called was a close relative of the one called upon, the one called will not carry anything of it. The pronoun is mentioned in agreement with the meaning, because His saying ﴿heavily laden﴾ does not refer only to the feminine form of meaning, but to every person, so it is as if it were said: "And if he calls a heavily laden person."

It was also read as *wa-law kāna dhu qurba* (even if there were a near relative), with *kāna* being complete (*tāmma*, i.e., used with the meaning "to occur, to exist"), meaning: "even if a near relative were present at that time and she called him, he would not carry anything of it." The Arabs say: "qad kāna laban," meaning "there came to be milk," i.e., it appeared and came about. Al-Zamakhshari said: the structure of the sentence fits incomplete *kāna* (*nāqisa*, i.e., used as a copula) better, because the meaning is: when the heavily laden soul calls someone to its burden, that person will not carry any of it, even if the one it calls is a near relative. This is a sound meaning and well connected. If you said "even if a near relative were found," it would fall apart and lose its coherence and cohesion. End of quote. This is a coherent construction under the interpretation we mentioned. Its explanation is *kāna*, which is in the active voice; the passive form is taken as an explanation of meaning, not as a synonym. Its synonyms are *ḥadatha* (happened), *ḥaḍara* (was present) or *waqa'a* (occurred), as the grammarians explained it.

When what contains the threat and some of the terrors of the Resurrection had preceded, that was a warning. So He mentioned that warning benefits and profits only those who fear Allah.

﴿Unseen﴾ (*bil-ghayb*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a grammatical term meaning the state of the subject or object at the time of the action) from the subject or the object: they fear their Lord while heedless of His punishment, or they fear His punishment while it is absent from them. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means in secret. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means, while He is in the state of being unseen by them, and what they have is only the message.

The majority read ﴿wa-man tazakkā﴾ (and whoever purifies himself) as a past-tense verb, and ﴿fa-innamā yatazakkā﴾ (then he purifies only) as a present-tense verb from *tazakkā*. The meaning is: whoever purifies himself by performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, the fruit of that returns to himself. His purification is only for himself and not for anyone else. *Tazakkī* includes fear and the establishment of prayer. Al-Abbas, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿wa-man yazzakkā fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with a *ya'* at the beginning and a doubled *zay* in both, and these are present-tense verbs whose original form is *wa-man yatazakkā*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*, just as it was assimilated into the *dhal* in His saying ﴿yadhdhakkarūn﴾ [al-An'am: 126]. Ibn Mas'ud and Talha read ﴿wa-manizzakkā﴾, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay* and a *hamzat al-wasl* (connecting hamza, a hamza used at the beginning of a word and dropped in continuous speech) added at the beginning. Talha also read ﴿fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*.

﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ is a promise to whoever purifies himself, of reward.

﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, the verse. It is a rebuke of the disbelievers and an illustration. The blind is the disbeliever and the seeing is the believer. Or the blind is the idol and the seeing is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, exalted, meaning that the one they worship and the one the believers worship are not alike. The darkness and the light, and the shade and the scorching heat, are illustrations of truth and falsehood and of the reward and punishment that each leads to. The living and the dead are an illustration of those who entered Islam and those who did not enter it. *Al-ḥarūr* is the intensity of the sun's heat. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-ḥarūr* is the samum (a hot, dry wind), except that the samum occurs by day, while *al-ḥarūr* occurs by night and day; it was also said: by night. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Ru'ba said: *al-ḥarūr* is by night, and *al-samum* by day, but that is not as he said. The matter is as al-Farra' and others related: that *al-samum* is specific to the day. It is said: *al-ḥarūr* is the heat of the night and the heat of the day. End of quote. Ru'ba's statement is not refuted, because language is taken from him, and he reported the language of his people. Some said: the shade here is Paradise, and the scorching heat is Hell. The verb *yastawī* (to be equal) is among those verbs that do not suffice with one subject. The repetition of *lā* (not) in the negation is for emphasis of its meaning, as in His saying ﴿The good deed and the bad deed are not equal﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the repetition of *lā* is only in the form of repetition, as if he said: "nor are the darkness and the light, nor the light and the darkness," so mention of the first items is sufficient without the second, and the mentioned part of the speech indicates what is left out. End of quote. What was mentioned does not need this supposition, because when He negates the equality of darkness and light, what is the benefit of supposing a second negation of their equality and adding two elisions? You say: "Zayd did not stand, nor 'Amr," so you emphasise the meaning of negation with *lā*; likewise here.

Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read ﴿wa-mā tastawī al-aḥyā'﴾ with the feminine *ta'*. The majority read it with a *ya'*. The ordering of these things negated as being equal is in the utmost eloquence. He mentioned the blind and the seeing as an example of the believer and the disbeliever. Then the seeing person, even if he is keen-sighted, sees only in light, so He mentioned what the disbeliever is in, namely the darkness of disbelief, and what the believer is in, namely the light of faith. Then He mentioned their outcome, which is the shade: the believer, by his faith, is in shade and ease, while the disbeliever, by his disbelief, is in heat and hardship.

Then He mentioned another parable concerning the believer and the disbeliever, beyond the case of the blind and the seeing, since the blind may share with the seeing some kind of perception, whereas the disbeliever does not perceive in a beneficial way; he is like the dead. For this reason He repeated the verb, saying ﴿And the living are not equal, nor the dead﴾, as if He had placed it in the position of a question, and He repeated "lā" in what He mentioned to emphasize the opposition. Darkness opposes and contrasts with light, and shade and heat are likewise; but the blind and the seeing are not like that, because one and the same person may be seeing, then afterward blindness befalls him, so there is no opposition except from the standpoint of the attribute. The opposition between shade and heat is permanent, because what is meant by shade is the absence of heat and cold; since the opposition there is more complete, it was emphasized by repetition. As for the living and the dead, inasmuch as one and the same body may be a locus of life, then it becomes a locus of death, the opposition between them is more complete than the opposition between the blind and the seeing, because these two may share some kind of perception, whereas the living does not. The dead differs from the living in reality, not merely in attribute, as explained in the Divine Wisdom. The more noble was placed first in two examples, namely the shade and the living, and was placed last in two examples, namely the seeing and the light. This is not said for the sake of rhymed prose (saj'), because the miraculous nature of the Qur'an does not lie in mere wording, but in its meaning as well. The poet may advance and postpone for the sake of rhyme, whereas the Qur'an's meaning is sound and its wording eloquent. Before the mission they were in misguidance, so they were like the blind, and their path was darkness. When the Messenger came and some people were guided by him, they became seeing, and their path was light. He placed first what was earlier in the one characterized by disbelief and his way, over what was later in the one characterized by faith and his way. Then, when He mentioned the outcome and the final return, He placed what is connected with mercy before what is connected with wrath, as has come: "My mercy precedes My wrath." So He placed the shade before the heat.

Then the persistent disbeliever after the mission became more astray than the blind, and resembled the dead in not perceiving the truth. So He said ﴿And the living are not equal﴾, those who believed in what Allah sent down, ﴿nor the dead﴾, those to whom the clear verses were recited and who did not benefit from them. These were after the faith of those who believed, so He placed them later, because the life of the believers existed before the death of the disbeliever. He made the blind and the seeing singular, because He matched the genus with the genus, since among individuals of the blind there may be some who equal some individuals of the seeing, like a blind man who has such intelligence that he equals a dull seeing man. So the difference between the two genera is certain, not between individuals. The darknesses were made plural, because the paths of disbelief are many; and light was made singular, because monotheism and the truth are one, and the difference between each individual of those (plural) and this one is such that He said: the darknesses do not find in them anything equal to this light. As for the living and the dead, the difference between them is greater, since there is no dead person who equals a living one in perception. So He mentioned that the living are not equal to the dead, whether you match genus with genus or individual with individual. End of the words of Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi, with some abridgement.

Then He consoled His Messenger, saying ﴿Indeed Allah makes hear whom He wills﴾, meaning: the causing of these people to hear is subject to Our will, and by "hearing" He meant that by which response to faith occurs. When He had mentioned that ﴿the living are not equal nor the dead﴾, He said ﴿And you are not one who can make hear those in the graves﴾, meaning these people, because of their not listening to the hearing of the truth, are in the position of those who have died and then remain in their graves. Just as one who has died cannot accept from you the word of truth, so too are these, for they are dead of heart. Al-Ashhab and al-Hasan read "bi-musmi‘i man" with an idafa; the majority read it with tanwin.

﴿You are only a warner﴾, meaning: your duty is only to convey and warn. If the one warned is among those whom Allah wills to guide, he hears and is guided; and if he is among those whom Allah wills to misguide, then it is not upon you, for He, exalted is He, is the One who guides and misguides. "Bi'l-haqq" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the agent, meaning "being truthful"; or from the object, meaning "truthfully"; or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a sending with the truth," i.e., accompanied. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is related to "bashīr" and "nadhīr," so "nadhīr" is with respect to "bashīr" with the true promise, and "nadhīr" with the threat. End of quotation. It is not possible that "bi'l-haqq" relate to both "bashīr" and "nadhīr" together; rather his words should be interpreted as meaning that there is an omitted element, the sense being: a bringer of good tidings with the true promise, and a warner with the true threat, so he omitted the counterpart because its counterpart indicates it.

﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾. "Ummah" means a large group. The meaning is that the call to Allah has not ceased for any nation, either directly through their prophets, and what is transmitted up to the time of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ; and the verses indicating that Quraysh had not received a warner mean that no warner had come to them directly, nor had their nearer forefathers. Or it means that warning ceased, and then not. When the traces of warning began to fade, Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ; and what the scholars of kalam mention about the condition of the people of the intervals (al-fatarat) is by way of supposition, since that is actual, and there is no nation upon the face of the earth that has not known the call to Allah and His worship. He suffices with mentioning "nadhīr" without "bashīr," because it is accompanied by it in His saying ﴿as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, so this indicates that it is intended, and it was omitted for the sake of that indication.

﴿And if they deny you﴾ is a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ, and the discussion of the parallels to these sentences has preceded at the end of Al ʿImran. His saying ﴿then how was My denunciation?﴾ is a threat to Quraysh with what befell the deniers of their messengers.

(p-307) ﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation.﴾ ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah.﴾ ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls to its burden, nothing of it will be carried, even by a near relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer. Whoever purifies himself, purifies himself only for his own soul, and to Allah is the final return.﴾ ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike,﴾ ﴿nor are the darkness and the light,﴾ ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat.﴾ ﴿Nor are the living and the dead alike. Indeed Allah makes whom He wills hear, but you cannot make those in the graves hear.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner. And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had also denied. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with the Psalms, and with the Book that gives light.﴾ ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved, and how was My rejection!﴾

This is a verse of admonition and reminder, and that all people are in need of Allah's beneficence and favour in all their conditions. No one is independent of Him for even the blink of an eye, while He is absolutely independent of the whole creation. He described them as "the poor" (fuqara') in order to show them how intensely they are in need of Him, since they are the category of the poor. Even though the whole world is in need of Him, because of their weakness they are treated as if they were the entirety of this category. Had He used the indefinite form, the meaning would have been "you are [some] poor," but the definite form makes the poor stand in contrast to the Self-Sufficient. He is described as "the Praiseworthy" to indicate that He is generous and bountiful, so He is praised for the blessings He bestows and deserves to be praised.

Having stated that He is absolutely self-sufficient, He mentioned what indicates His independence from the creation and that He has no need of them, saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away﴾, meaning: if He wills to take you away, He will take you away. This contains a threat of destroying them.

﴿And that﴾, that is, taking you away and bringing a new creation, ﴿is not difficult﴾, meaning it is not impossible for Him, since He is characterised by complete power, so nothing He wills is impossible for Him. The meaning of ﴿a new creation﴾ is that He will replace you, in line with His saying ﴿And if you turn away, He will substitute a people other than you﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. Ibn 'Abbas said: He will create after you those who worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. This meaning has also come in connection with the mention of taking away after describing Him as self-sufficient, in His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can take you away and make successors after you of whomever He wills﴾ [al-An'am: 133]. The taking away is also linked, and concluded at the end of the verse, with the mention of the power that indicates this, in His saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others; and Allah is ever capable of that﴾ [al-Nisa': 133].

It is reported that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to some of the believers: "Disbelieve in Muhammad, and I will bear your burden," so this verse was revealed. Allah informed that no one carries another's burden. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: this verse concerns sins and crimes. It is said: "wazara al-shay'" means he carried the thing, and *wazira* (a bearer) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "a soul bearing [a burden]". He mentioned the adjective without mentioning the noun it qualifies, restricting himself to it, because the meaning is that every soul is seen only as bearing its own burden, not the burden of another. So He does not seize a soul for the sin of another soul, unlike the tyrants of this world who seize the neighbour for the neighbour, the friend for the friend, and the relative for the relative. Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever among the rulers goes to the extreme of seizing a relative for the crime of his relative, as the act of Ziyad and similar people, that is injustice, because the one seized may have helped the criminal through support and association, or by knowing of his condition and approving of it, and thus he has taken a share of the crime. End of quote. It seems Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted the actions of Ziyad and what he did in Islam; his conduct was close to that of al-Hajjaj. There is no contradiction between this verse and the one in al-'Ankabut, because that one concerns misguided people who misguide others: they bear the burdens of leading people astray together with the burdens of their own error, so all of that is their burden, and there is nothing of the burden of others in it. Do you not see His words: ﴿And they will not bear anything of their sins﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12]?

﴿And if a heavily laden soul calls﴾, that is, a soul weighed down by its load, ﴿to its burden, nothing of it will be carried﴾, meaning there will be no help or rescue on that day for one who seeks rescue, and no assistance, to the extent that a soul whose burdens have weighed it down, if it calls someone to lighten some of its burden, will not be answered, even if the one called is one of its close relatives, such as a father, son or brother. The previous verse is about the justice of Allah in His judgement and that He does not seize a soul for the sin of another, while this one is about negating assistance. *Al-himl* (load) originally means what is carried on the back in physical things, and it is extended metaphorically to abstract things such as sins and the like. Thus every burden is considered as attached to the back, as in His saying ﴿And they carry their burdens on their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31], just as every acquisition is attributed to the hand.

The majority of readers read ﴿yuḥmal﴾ (is carried) with a *ya'* and in the passive voice. Abu al-Sammal, on the authority of Talha, and Ibrahim ibn Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read it with a *ta'* at the beginning and a *kasra* on the *mim*. This reading requires that *shay'* be in the accusative, just as the majority reading requires it to be in the nominative. The subject of *yuḥmal* in this reading is a pronoun referring to the omitted object of *tad'u* (calls), meaning: "And if a heavily laden soul calls another soul to its burden, that other soul will not carry anything of it." The subject of *kāna* (the verb "to be") is a pronoun referring to the understood one called, from His saying ﴿And if he calls﴾. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement. He said: the called one was left unspecified so that it would include and cover every person called. He said: If you ask, "how can there be a pronoun for something implied, and how can a general noun be the close relative of the heavily laden one?" I say: this is of the generality that occurs by way of substitution. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the subject of *kāna* is an implied pronoun, its estimated form being "wa-law kāna" (even if there were). End of quote, meaning: even if the one called was a close relative of the one called upon, the one called will not carry anything of it. The pronoun is mentioned in agreement with the meaning, because His saying ﴿heavily laden﴾ does not refer only to the feminine form of meaning, but to every person, so it is as if it were said: "And if he calls a heavily laden person."

It was also read as *wa-law kāna dhu qurba* (even if there were a near relative), with *kāna* being complete (*tāmma*, i.e., used with the meaning "to occur, to exist"), meaning: "even if a near relative were present at that time and she called him, he would not carry anything of it." The Arabs say: "qad kāna laban," meaning "there came to be milk," i.e., it appeared and came about. Al-Zamakhshari said: the structure of the sentence fits incomplete *kāna* (*nāqisa*, i.e., used as a copula) better, because the meaning is: when the heavily laden soul calls someone to its burden, that person will not carry any of it, even if the one it calls is a near relative. This is a sound meaning and well connected. If you said "even if a near relative were found," it would fall apart and lose its coherence and cohesion. End of quote. This is a coherent construction under the interpretation we mentioned. Its explanation is *kāna*, which is in the active voice; the passive form is taken as an explanation of meaning, not as a synonym. Its synonyms are *ḥadatha* (happened), *ḥaḍara* (was present) or *waqa'a* (occurred), as the grammarians explained it.

When what contains the threat and some of the terrors of the Resurrection had preceded, that was a warning. So He mentioned that warning benefits and profits only those who fear Allah.

﴿Unseen﴾ (*bil-ghayb*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a grammatical term meaning the state of the subject or object at the time of the action) from the subject or the object: they fear their Lord while heedless of His punishment, or they fear His punishment while it is absent from them. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means in secret. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means, while He is in the state of being unseen by them, and what they have is only the message.

The majority read ﴿wa-man tazakkā﴾ (and whoever purifies himself) as a past-tense verb, and ﴿fa-innamā yatazakkā﴾ (then he purifies only) as a present-tense verb from *tazakkā*. The meaning is: whoever purifies himself by performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, the fruit of that returns to himself. His purification is only for himself and not for anyone else. *Tazakkī* includes fear and the establishment of prayer. Al-Abbas, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿wa-man yazzakkā fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with a *ya'* at the beginning and a doubled *zay* in both, and these are present-tense verbs whose original form is *wa-man yatazakkā*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*, just as it was assimilated into the *dhal* in His saying ﴿yadhdhakkarūn﴾ [al-An'am: 126]. Ibn Mas'ud and Talha read ﴿wa-manizzakkā﴾, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay* and a *hamzat al-wasl* (connecting hamza, a hamza used at the beginning of a word and dropped in continuous speech) added at the beginning. Talha also read ﴿fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*.

﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ is a promise to whoever purifies himself, of reward.

﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, the verse. It is a rebuke of the disbelievers and an illustration. The blind is the disbeliever and the seeing is the believer. Or the blind is the idol and the seeing is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, exalted, meaning that the one they worship and the one the believers worship are not alike. The darkness and the light, and the shade and the scorching heat, are illustrations of truth and falsehood and of the reward and punishment that each leads to. The living and the dead are an illustration of those who entered Islam and those who did not enter it. *Al-ḥarūr* is the intensity of the sun's heat. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-ḥarūr* is the samum (a hot, dry wind), except that the samum occurs by day, while *al-ḥarūr* occurs by night and day; it was also said: by night. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Ru'ba said: *al-ḥarūr* is by night, and *al-samum* by day, but that is not as he said. The matter is as al-Farra' and others related: that *al-samum* is specific to the day. It is said: *al-ḥarūr* is the heat of the night and the heat of the day. End of quote. Ru'ba's statement is not refuted, because language is taken from him, and he reported the language of his people. Some said: the shade here is Paradise, and the scorching heat is Hell. The verb *yastawī* (to be equal) is among those verbs that do not suffice with one subject. The repetition of *lā* (not) in the negation is for emphasis of its meaning, as in His saying ﴿The good deed and the bad deed are not equal﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the repetition of *lā* is only in the form of repetition, as if he said: "nor are the darkness and the light, nor the light and the darkness," so mention of the first items is sufficient without the second, and the mentioned part of the speech indicates what is left out. End of quote. What was mentioned does not need this supposition, because when He negates the equality of darkness and light, what is the benefit of supposing a second negation of their equality and adding two elisions? You say: "Zayd did not stand, nor 'Amr," so you emphasise the meaning of negation with *lā*; likewise here.

Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read ﴿wa-mā tastawī al-aḥyā'﴾ with the feminine *ta'*. The majority read it with a *ya'*. The ordering of these things negated as being equal is in the utmost eloquence. He mentioned the blind and the seeing as an example of the believer and the disbeliever. Then the seeing person, even if he is keen-sighted, sees only in light, so He mentioned what the disbeliever is in, namely the darkness of disbelief, and what the believer is in, namely the light of faith. Then He mentioned their outcome, which is the shade: the believer, by his faith, is in shade and ease, while the disbeliever, by his disbelief, is in heat and hardship.

Then He mentioned another parable concerning the believer and the disbeliever, beyond the case of the blind and the seeing, since the blind may share with the seeing some kind of perception, whereas the disbeliever does not perceive in a beneficial way; he is like the dead. For this reason He repeated the verb, saying ﴿And the living are not equal, nor the dead﴾, as if He had placed it in the position of a question, and He repeated "lā" in what He mentioned to emphasize the opposition. Darkness opposes and contrasts with light, and shade and heat are likewise; but the blind and the seeing are not like that, because one and the same person may be seeing, then afterward blindness befalls him, so there is no opposition except from the standpoint of the attribute. The opposition between shade and heat is permanent, because what is meant by shade is the absence of heat and cold; since the opposition there is more complete, it was emphasized by repetition. As for the living and the dead, inasmuch as one and the same body may be a locus of life, then it becomes a locus of death, the opposition between them is more complete than the opposition between the blind and the seeing, because these two may share some kind of perception, whereas the living does not. The dead differs from the living in reality, not merely in attribute, as explained in the Divine Wisdom. The more noble was placed first in two examples, namely the shade and the living, and was placed last in two examples, namely the seeing and the light. This is not said for the sake of rhymed prose (saj'), because the miraculous nature of the Qur'an does not lie in mere wording, but in its meaning as well. The poet may advance and postpone for the sake of rhyme, whereas the Qur'an's meaning is sound and its wording eloquent. Before the mission they were in misguidance, so they were like the blind, and their path was darkness. When the Messenger came and some people were guided by him, they became seeing, and their path was light. He placed first what was earlier in the one characterized by disbelief and his way, over what was later in the one characterized by faith and his way. Then, when He mentioned the outcome and the final return, He placed what is connected with mercy before what is connected with wrath, as has come: "My mercy precedes My wrath." So He placed the shade before the heat.

Then the persistent disbeliever after the mission became more astray than the blind, and resembled the dead in not perceiving the truth. So He said ﴿And the living are not equal﴾, those who believed in what Allah sent down, ﴿nor the dead﴾, those to whom the clear verses were recited and who did not benefit from them. These were after the faith of those who believed, so He placed them later, because the life of the believers existed before the death of the disbeliever. He made the blind and the seeing singular, because He matched the genus with the genus, since among individuals of the blind there may be some who equal some individuals of the seeing, like a blind man who has such intelligence that he equals a dull seeing man. So the difference between the two genera is certain, not between individuals. The darknesses were made plural, because the paths of disbelief are many; and light was made singular, because monotheism and the truth are one, and the difference between each individual of those (plural) and this one is such that He said: the darknesses do not find in them anything equal to this light. As for the living and the dead, the difference between them is greater, since there is no dead person who equals a living one in perception. So He mentioned that the living are not equal to the dead, whether you match genus with genus or individual with individual. End of the words of Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi, with some abridgement.

Then He consoled His Messenger, saying ﴿Indeed Allah makes hear whom He wills﴾, meaning: the causing of these people to hear is subject to Our will, and by "hearing" He meant that by which response to faith occurs. When He had mentioned that ﴿the living are not equal nor the dead﴾, He said ﴿And you are not one who can make hear those in the graves﴾, meaning these people, because of their not listening to the hearing of the truth, are in the position of those who have died and then remain in their graves. Just as one who has died cannot accept from you the word of truth, so too are these, for they are dead of heart. Al-Ashhab and al-Hasan read "bi-musmi‘i man" with an idafa; the majority read it with tanwin.

﴿You are only a warner﴾, meaning: your duty is only to convey and warn. If the one warned is among those whom Allah wills to guide, he hears and is guided; and if he is among those whom Allah wills to misguide, then it is not upon you, for He, exalted is He, is the One who guides and misguides. "Bi'l-haqq" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the agent, meaning "being truthful"; or from the object, meaning "truthfully"; or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a sending with the truth," i.e., accompanied. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is related to "bashīr" and "nadhīr," so "nadhīr" is with respect to "bashīr" with the true promise, and "nadhīr" with the threat. End of quotation. It is not possible that "bi'l-haqq" relate to both "bashīr" and "nadhīr" together; rather his words should be interpreted as meaning that there is an omitted element, the sense being: a bringer of good tidings with the true promise, and a warner with the true threat, so he omitted the counterpart because its counterpart indicates it.

﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾. "Ummah" means a large group. The meaning is that the call to Allah has not ceased for any nation, either directly through their prophets, and what is transmitted up to the time of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ; and the verses indicating that Quraysh had not received a warner mean that no warner had come to them directly, nor had their nearer forefathers. Or it means that warning ceased, and then not. When the traces of warning began to fade, Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ; and what the scholars of kalam mention about the condition of the people of the intervals (al-fatarat) is by way of supposition, since that is actual, and there is no nation upon the face of the earth that has not known the call to Allah and His worship. He suffices with mentioning "nadhīr" without "bashīr," because it is accompanied by it in His saying ﴿as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, so this indicates that it is intended, and it was omitted for the sake of that indication.

﴿And if they deny you﴾ is a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ, and the discussion of the parallels to these sentences has preceded at the end of Al ʿImran. His saying ﴿then how was My denunciation?﴾ is a threat to Quraysh with what befell the deniers of their messengers.

(p-307) ﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation.﴾ ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah.﴾ ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls to its burden, nothing of it will be carried, even by a near relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer. Whoever purifies himself, purifies himself only for his own soul, and to Allah is the final return.﴾ ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike,﴾ ﴿nor are the darkness and the light,﴾ ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat.﴾ ﴿Nor are the living and the dead alike. Indeed Allah makes whom He wills hear, but you cannot make those in the graves hear.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner. And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had also denied. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with the Psalms, and with the Book that gives light.﴾ ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved, and how was My rejection!﴾

This is a verse of admonition and reminder, and that all people are in need of Allah's beneficence and favour in all their conditions. No one is independent of Him for even the blink of an eye, while He is absolutely independent of the whole creation. He described them as "the poor" (fuqara') in order to show them how intensely they are in need of Him, since they are the category of the poor. Even though the whole world is in need of Him, because of their weakness they are treated as if they were the entirety of this category. Had He used the indefinite form, the meaning would have been "you are [some] poor," but the definite form makes the poor stand in contrast to the Self-Sufficient. He is described as "the Praiseworthy" to indicate that He is generous and bountiful, so He is praised for the blessings He bestows and deserves to be praised.

Having stated that He is absolutely self-sufficient, He mentioned what indicates His independence from the creation and that He has no need of them, saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away﴾, meaning: if He wills to take you away, He will take you away. This contains a threat of destroying them.

﴿And that﴾, that is, taking you away and bringing a new creation, ﴿is not difficult﴾, meaning it is not impossible for Him, since He is characterised by complete power, so nothing He wills is impossible for Him. The meaning of ﴿a new creation﴾ is that He will replace you, in line with His saying ﴿And if you turn away, He will substitute a people other than you﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. Ibn 'Abbas said: He will create after you those who worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. This meaning has also come in connection with the mention of taking away after describing Him as self-sufficient, in His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can take you away and make successors after you of whomever He wills﴾ [al-An'am: 133]. The taking away is also linked, and concluded at the end of the verse, with the mention of the power that indicates this, in His saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others; and Allah is ever capable of that﴾ [al-Nisa': 133].

It is reported that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to some of the believers: "Disbelieve in Muhammad, and I will bear your burden," so this verse was revealed. Allah informed that no one carries another's burden. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: this verse concerns sins and crimes. It is said: "wazara al-shay'" means he carried the thing, and *wazira* (a bearer) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "a soul bearing [a burden]". He mentioned the adjective without mentioning the noun it qualifies, restricting himself to it, because the meaning is that every soul is seen only as bearing its own burden, not the burden of another. So He does not seize a soul for the sin of another soul, unlike the tyrants of this world who seize the neighbour for the neighbour, the friend for the friend, and the relative for the relative. Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever among the rulers goes to the extreme of seizing a relative for the crime of his relative, as the act of Ziyad and similar people, that is injustice, because the one seized may have helped the criminal through support and association, or by knowing of his condition and approving of it, and thus he has taken a share of the crime. End of quote. It seems Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted the actions of Ziyad and what he did in Islam; his conduct was close to that of al-Hajjaj. There is no contradiction between this verse and the one in al-'Ankabut, because that one concerns misguided people who misguide others: they bear the burdens of leading people astray together with the burdens of their own error, so all of that is their burden, and there is nothing of the burden of others in it. Do you not see His words: ﴿And they will not bear anything of their sins﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12]?

﴿And if a heavily laden soul calls﴾, that is, a soul weighed down by its load, ﴿to its burden, nothing of it will be carried﴾, meaning there will be no help or rescue on that day for one who seeks rescue, and no assistance, to the extent that a soul whose burdens have weighed it down, if it calls someone to lighten some of its burden, will not be answered, even if the one called is one of its close relatives, such as a father, son or brother. The previous verse is about the justice of Allah in His judgement and that He does not seize a soul for the sin of another, while this one is about negating assistance. *Al-himl* (load) originally means what is carried on the back in physical things, and it is extended metaphorically to abstract things such as sins and the like. Thus every burden is considered as attached to the back, as in His saying ﴿And they carry their burdens on their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31], just as every acquisition is attributed to the hand.

The majority of readers read ﴿yuḥmal﴾ (is carried) with a *ya'* and in the passive voice. Abu al-Sammal, on the authority of Talha, and Ibrahim ibn Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read it with a *ta'* at the beginning and a *kasra* on the *mim*. This reading requires that *shay'* be in the accusative, just as the majority reading requires it to be in the nominative. The subject of *yuḥmal* in this reading is a pronoun referring to the omitted object of *tad'u* (calls), meaning: "And if a heavily laden soul calls another soul to its burden, that other soul will not carry anything of it." The subject of *kāna* (the verb "to be") is a pronoun referring to the understood one called, from His saying ﴿And if he calls﴾. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement. He said: the called one was left unspecified so that it would include and cover every person called. He said: If you ask, "how can there be a pronoun for something implied, and how can a general noun be the close relative of the heavily laden one?" I say: this is of the generality that occurs by way of substitution. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the subject of *kāna* is an implied pronoun, its estimated form being "wa-law kāna" (even if there were). End of quote, meaning: even if the one called was a close relative of the one called upon, the one called will not carry anything of it. The pronoun is mentioned in agreement with the meaning, because His saying ﴿heavily laden﴾ does not refer only to the feminine form of meaning, but to every person, so it is as if it were said: "And if he calls a heavily laden person."

It was also read as *wa-law kāna dhu qurba* (even if there were a near relative), with *kāna* being complete (*tāmma*, i.e., used with the meaning "to occur, to exist"), meaning: "even if a near relative were present at that time and she called him, he would not carry anything of it." The Arabs say: "qad kāna laban," meaning "there came to be milk," i.e., it appeared and came about. Al-Zamakhshari said: the structure of the sentence fits incomplete *kāna* (*nāqisa*, i.e., used as a copula) better, because the meaning is: when the heavily laden soul calls someone to its burden, that person will not carry any of it, even if the one it calls is a near relative. This is a sound meaning and well connected. If you said "even if a near relative were found," it would fall apart and lose its coherence and cohesion. End of quote. This is a coherent construction under the interpretation we mentioned. Its explanation is *kāna*, which is in the active voice; the passive form is taken as an explanation of meaning, not as a synonym. Its synonyms are *ḥadatha* (happened), *ḥaḍara* (was present) or *waqa'a* (occurred), as the grammarians explained it.

When what contains the threat and some of the terrors of the Resurrection had preceded, that was a warning. So He mentioned that warning benefits and profits only those who fear Allah.

﴿Unseen﴾ (*bil-ghayb*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a grammatical term meaning the state of the subject or object at the time of the action) from the subject or the object: they fear their Lord while heedless of His punishment, or they fear His punishment while it is absent from them. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means in secret. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means, while He is in the state of being unseen by them, and what they have is only the message.

The majority read ﴿wa-man tazakkā﴾ (and whoever purifies himself) as a past-tense verb, and ﴿fa-innamā yatazakkā﴾ (then he purifies only) as a present-tense verb from *tazakkā*. The meaning is: whoever purifies himself by performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, the fruit of that returns to himself. His purification is only for himself and not for anyone else. *Tazakkī* includes fear and the establishment of prayer. Al-Abbas, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿wa-man yazzakkā fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with a *ya'* at the beginning and a doubled *zay* in both, and these are present-tense verbs whose original form is *wa-man yatazakkā*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*, just as it was assimilated into the *dhal* in His saying ﴿yadhdhakkarūn﴾ [al-An'am: 126]. Ibn Mas'ud and Talha read ﴿wa-manizzakkā﴾, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay* and a *hamzat al-wasl* (connecting hamza, a hamza used at the beginning of a word and dropped in continuous speech) added at the beginning. Talha also read ﴿fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*.

﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ is a promise to whoever purifies himself, of reward.

﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, the verse. It is a rebuke of the disbelievers and an illustration. The blind is the disbeliever and the seeing is the believer. Or the blind is the idol and the seeing is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, exalted, meaning that the one they worship and the one the believers worship are not alike. The darkness and the light, and the shade and the scorching heat, are illustrations of truth and falsehood and of the reward and punishment that each leads to. The living and the dead are an illustration of those who entered Islam and those who did not enter it. *Al-ḥarūr* is the intensity of the sun's heat. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-ḥarūr* is the samum (a hot, dry wind), except that the samum occurs by day, while *al-ḥarūr* occurs by night and day; it was also said: by night. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Ru'ba said: *al-ḥarūr* is by night, and *al-samum* by day, but that is not as he said. The matter is as al-Farra' and others related: that *al-samum* is specific to the day. It is said: *al-ḥarūr* is the heat of the night and the heat of the day. End of quote. Ru'ba's statement is not refuted, because language is taken from him, and he reported the language of his people. Some said: the shade here is Paradise, and the scorching heat is Hell. The verb *yastawī* (to be equal) is among those verbs that do not suffice with one subject. The repetition of *lā* (not) in the negation is for emphasis of its meaning, as in His saying ﴿The good deed and the bad deed are not equal﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the repetition of *lā* is only in the form of repetition, as if he said: "nor are the darkness and the light, nor the light and the darkness," so mention of the first items is sufficient without the second, and the mentioned part of the speech indicates what is left out. End of quote. What was mentioned does not need this supposition, because when He negates the equality of darkness and light, what is the benefit of supposing a second negation of their equality and adding two elisions? You say: "Zayd did not stand, nor 'Amr," so you emphasise the meaning of negation with *lā*; likewise here.

Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read ﴿wa-mā tastawī al-aḥyā'﴾ with the feminine *ta'*. The majority read it with a *ya'*. The ordering of these things negated as being equal is in the utmost eloquence. He mentioned the blind and the seeing as an example of the believer and the disbeliever. Then the seeing person, even if he is keen-sighted, sees only in light, so He mentioned what the disbeliever is in, namely the darkness of disbelief, and what the believer is in, namely the light of faith. Then He mentioned their outcome, which is the shade: the believer, by his faith, is in shade and ease, while the disbeliever, by his disbelief, is in heat and hardship.

Then He mentioned another parable concerning the believer and the disbeliever, beyond the case of the blind and the seeing, since the blind may share with the seeing some kind of perception, whereas the disbeliever does not perceive in a beneficial way; he is like the dead. For this reason He repeated the verb, saying ﴿And the living are not equal, nor the dead﴾, as if He had placed it in the position of a question, and He repeated "lā" in what He mentioned to emphasize the opposition. Darkness opposes and contrasts with light, and shade and heat are likewise; but the blind and the seeing are not like that, because one and the same person may be seeing, then afterward blindness befalls him, so there is no opposition except from the standpoint of the attribute. The opposition between shade and heat is permanent, because what is meant by shade is the absence of heat and cold; since the opposition there is more complete, it was emphasized by repetition. As for the living and the dead, inasmuch as one and the same body may be a locus of life, then it becomes a locus of death, the opposition between them is more complete than the opposition between the blind and the seeing, because these two may share some kind of perception, whereas the living does not. The dead differs from the living in reality, not merely in attribute, as explained in the Divine Wisdom. The more noble was placed first in two examples, namely the shade and the living, and was placed last in two examples, namely the seeing and the light. This is not said for the sake of rhymed prose (saj'), because the miraculous nature of the Qur'an does not lie in mere wording, but in its meaning as well. The poet may advance and postpone for the sake of rhyme, whereas the Qur'an's meaning is sound and its wording eloquent. Before the mission they were in misguidance, so they were like the blind, and their path was darkness. When the Messenger came and some people were guided by him, they became seeing, and their path was light. He placed first what was earlier in the one characterized by disbelief and his way, over what was later in the one characterized by faith and his way. Then, when He mentioned the outcome and the final return, He placed what is connected with mercy before what is connected with wrath, as has come: "My mercy precedes My wrath." So He placed the shade before the heat.

Then the persistent disbeliever after the mission became more astray than the blind, and resembled the dead in not perceiving the truth. So He said ﴿And the living are not equal﴾, those who believed in what Allah sent down, ﴿nor the dead﴾, those to whom the clear verses were recited and who did not benefit from them. These were after the faith of those who believed, so He placed them later, because the life of the believers existed before the death of the disbeliever. He made the blind and the seeing singular, because He matched the genus with the genus, since among individuals of the blind there may be some who equal some individuals of the seeing, like a blind man who has such intelligence that he equals a dull seeing man. So the difference between the two genera is certain, not between individuals. The darknesses were made plural, because the paths of disbelief are many; and light was made singular, because monotheism and the truth are one, and the difference between each individual of those (plural) and this one is such that He said: the darknesses do not find in them anything equal to this light. As for the living and the dead, the difference between them is greater, since there is no dead person who equals a living one in perception. So He mentioned that the living are not equal to the dead, whether you match genus with genus or individual with individual. End of the words of Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi, with some abridgement.

Then He consoled His Messenger, saying ﴿Indeed Allah makes hear whom He wills﴾, meaning: the causing of these people to hear is subject to Our will, and by "hearing" He meant that by which response to faith occurs. When He had mentioned that ﴿the living are not equal nor the dead﴾, He said ﴿And you are not one who can make hear those in the graves﴾, meaning these people, because of their not listening to the hearing of the truth, are in the position of those who have died and then remain in their graves. Just as one who has died cannot accept from you the word of truth, so too are these, for they are dead of heart. Al-Ashhab and al-Hasan read "bi-musmi‘i man" with an idafa; the majority read it with tanwin.

﴿You are only a warner﴾, meaning: your duty is only to convey and warn. If the one warned is among those whom Allah wills to guide, he hears and is guided; and if he is among those whom Allah wills to misguide, then it is not upon you, for He, exalted is He, is the One who guides and misguides. "Bi'l-haqq" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the agent, meaning "being truthful"; or from the object, meaning "truthfully"; or an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a sending with the truth," i.e., accompanied. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is related to "bashīr" and "nadhīr," so "nadhīr" is with respect to "bashīr" with the true promise, and "nadhīr" with the threat. End of quotation. It is not possible that "bi'l-haqq" relate to both "bashīr" and "nadhīr" together; rather his words should be interpreted as meaning that there is an omitted element, the sense being: a bringer of good tidings with the true promise, and a warner with the true threat, so he omitted the counterpart because its counterpart indicates it.

﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾. "Ummah" means a large group. The meaning is that the call to Allah has not ceased for any nation, either directly through their prophets, and what is transmitted up to the time of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ; and the verses indicating that Quraysh had not received a warner mean that no warner had come to them directly, nor had their nearer forefathers. Or it means that warning ceased, and then not. When the traces of warning began to fade, Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ; and what the scholars of kalam mention about the condition of the people of the intervals (al-fatarat) is by way of supposition, since that is actual, and there is no nation upon the face of the earth that has not known the call to Allah and His worship. He suffices with mentioning "nadhīr" without "bashīr," because it is accompanied by it in His saying ﴿as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾, so this indicates that it is intended, and it was omitted for the sake of that indication.

﴿And if they deny you﴾ is a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ, and the discussion of the parallels to these sentences has preceded at the end of Al ʿImran. His saying ﴿then how was My denunciation?﴾ is a threat to Quraysh with what befell the deniers of their messengers.

(p-307) ﴿O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation.﴾ ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah.﴾ ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls to its burden, nothing of it will be carried, even by a near relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer. Whoever purifies himself, purifies himself only for his own soul, and to Allah is the final return.﴾ ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike,﴾ ﴿nor are the darkness and the light,﴾ ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat.﴾ ﴿Nor are the living and the dead alike. Indeed Allah makes whom He wills hear, but you cannot make those in the graves hear.﴾ ﴿You are only a warner.﴾ ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner. And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, those before them had also denied. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with the Psalms, and with the Book that gives light.﴾ ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved, and how was My rejection!﴾

This is a verse of admonition and reminder, and that all people are in need of Allah's beneficence and favour in all their conditions. No one is independent of Him for even the blink of an eye, while He is absolutely independent of the whole creation. He described them as "the poor" (fuqara') in order to show them how intensely they are in need of Him, since they are the category of the poor. Even though the whole world is in need of Him, because of their weakness they are treated as if they were the entirety of this category. Had He used the indefinite form, the meaning would have been "you are [some] poor," but the definite form makes the poor stand in contrast to the Self-Sufficient. He is described as "the Praiseworthy" to indicate that He is generous and bountiful, so He is praised for the blessings He bestows and deserves to be praised.

Having stated that He is absolutely self-sufficient, He mentioned what indicates His independence from the creation and that He has no need of them, saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away﴾, meaning: if He wills to take you away, He will take you away. This contains a threat of destroying them.

﴿And that﴾, that is, taking you away and bringing a new creation, ﴿is not difficult﴾, meaning it is not impossible for Him, since He is characterised by complete power, so nothing He wills is impossible for Him. The meaning of ﴿a new creation﴾ is that He will replace you, in line with His saying ﴿And if you turn away, He will substitute a people other than you﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. Ibn 'Abbas said: He will create after you those who worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. This meaning has also come in connection with the mention of taking away after describing Him as self-sufficient, in His saying ﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, the Possessor of mercy. If He wills, He can take you away and make successors after you of whomever He wills﴾ [al-An'am: 133]. The taking away is also linked, and concluded at the end of the verse, with the mention of the power that indicates this, in His saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others; and Allah is ever capable of that﴾ [al-Nisa': 133].

It is reported that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to some of the believers: "Disbelieve in Muhammad, and I will bear your burden," so this verse was revealed. Allah informed that no one carries another's burden. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: this verse concerns sins and crimes. It is said: "wazara al-shay'" means he carried the thing, and *wazira* (a bearer) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "a soul bearing [a burden]". He mentioned the adjective without mentioning the noun it qualifies, restricting himself to it, because the meaning is that every soul is seen only as bearing its own burden, not the burden of another. So He does not seize a soul for the sin of another soul, unlike the tyrants of this world who seize the neighbour for the neighbour, the friend for the friend, and the relative for the relative. Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever among the rulers goes to the extreme of seizing a relative for the crime of his relative, as the act of Ziyad and similar people, that is injustice, because the one seized may have helped the criminal through support and association, or by knowing of his condition and approving of it, and thus he has taken a share of the crime. End of quote. It seems Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted the actions of Ziyad and what he did in Islam; his conduct was close to that of al-Hajjaj. There is no contradiction between this verse and the one in al-'Ankabut, because that one concerns misguided people who misguide others: they bear the burdens of leading people astray together with the burdens of their own error, so all of that is their burden, and there is nothing of the burden of others in it. Do you not see His words: ﴿And they will not bear anything of their sins﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12]?

﴿And if a heavily laden soul calls﴾, that is, a soul weighed down by its load, ﴿to its burden, nothing of it will be carried﴾, meaning there will be no help or rescue on that day for one who seeks rescue, and no assistance, to the extent that a soul whose burdens have weighed it down, if it calls someone to lighten some of its burden, will not be answered, even if the one called is one of its close relatives, such as a father, son or brother. The previous verse is about the justice of Allah in His judgement and that He does not seize a soul for the sin of another, while this one is about negating assistance. *Al-himl* (load) originally means what is carried on the back in physical things, and it is extended metaphorically to abstract things such as sins and the like. Thus every burden is considered as attached to the back, as in His saying ﴿And they carry their burdens on their backs﴾ [al-An'am: 31], just as every acquisition is attributed to the hand.

The majority of readers read ﴿yuḥmal﴾ (is carried) with a *ya'* and in the passive voice. Abu al-Sammal, on the authority of Talha, and Ibrahim ibn Zadan, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read it with a *ta'* at the beginning and a *kasra* on the *mim*. This reading requires that *shay'* be in the accusative, just as the majority reading requires it to be in the nominative. The subject of *yuḥmal* in this reading is a pronoun referring to the omitted object of *tad'u* (calls), meaning: "And if a heavily laden soul calls another soul to its burden, that other soul will not carry anything of it." The subject of *kāna* (the verb "to be") is a pronoun referring to the understood one called, from His saying ﴿And if he calls﴾. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement. He said: the called one was left unspecified so that it would include and cover every person called. He said: If you ask, "how can there be a pronoun for something implied, and how can a general noun be the close relative of the heavily laden one?" I say: this is of the generality that occurs by way of substitution. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the subject of *kāna* is an implied pronoun, its estimated form being "wa-law kāna" (even if there were). End of quote, meaning: even if the one called was a close relative of the one called upon, the one called will not carry anything of it. The pronoun is mentioned in agreement with the meaning, because His saying ﴿heavily laden﴾ does not refer only to the feminine form of meaning, but to every person, so it is as if it were said: "And if he calls a heavily laden person."

It was also read as *wa-law kāna dhu qurba* (even if there were a near relative), with *kāna* being complete (*tāmma*, i.e., used with the meaning "to occur, to exist"), meaning: "even if a near relative were present at that time and she called him, he would not carry anything of it." The Arabs say: "qad kāna laban," meaning "there came to be milk," i.e., it appeared and came about. Al-Zamakhshari said: the structure of the sentence fits incomplete *kāna* (*nāqisa*, i.e., used as a copula) better, because the meaning is: when the heavily laden soul calls someone to its burden, that person will not carry any of it, even if the one it calls is a near relative. This is a sound meaning and well connected. If you said "even if a near relative were found," it would fall apart and lose its coherence and cohesion. End of quote. This is a coherent construction under the interpretation we mentioned. Its explanation is *kāna*, which is in the active voice; the passive form is taken as an explanation of meaning, not as a synonym. Its synonyms are *ḥadatha* (happened), *ḥaḍara* (was present) or *waqa'a* (occurred), as the grammarians explained it.

When what contains the threat and some of the terrors of the Resurrection had preceded, that was a warning. So He mentioned that warning benefits and profits only those who fear Allah.

﴿Unseen﴾ (*bil-ghayb*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a grammatical term meaning the state of the subject or object at the time of the action) from the subject or the object: they fear their Lord while heedless of His punishment, or they fear His punishment while it is absent from them. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means in secret. It was also said: *bil-ghayb* means, while He is in the state of being unseen by them, and what they have is only the message.

The majority read ﴿wa-man tazakkā﴾ (and whoever purifies himself) as a past-tense verb, and ﴿fa-innamā yatazakkā﴾ (then he purifies only) as a present-tense verb from *tazakkā*. The meaning is: whoever purifies himself by performing acts of obedience and abandoning sins, the fruit of that returns to himself. His purification is only for himself and not for anyone else. *Tazakkī* includes fear and the establishment of prayer. Al-Abbas, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﴿wa-man yazzakkā fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with a *ya'* at the beginning and a doubled *zay* in both, and these are present-tense verbs whose original form is *wa-man yatazakkā*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*, just as it was assimilated into the *dhal* in His saying ﴿yadhdhakkarūn﴾ [al-An'am: 126]. Ibn Mas'ud and Talha read ﴿wa-manizzakkā﴾, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay* and a *hamzat al-wasl* (connecting hamza, a hamza used at the beginning of a word and dropped in continuous speech) added at the beginning. Talha also read ﴿fa-innamā yazzakkā﴾ with the *ta'* assimilated into the *zay*.

﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾ is a promise to whoever purifies himself, of reward.

﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, the verse. It is a rebuke of the disbelievers and an illustration. The blind is the disbeliever and the seeing is the believer. Or the blind is the idol and the seeing is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, exalted, meaning that the one they worship and the one the believers worship are not alike. The darkness and the light, and the shade and the scorching heat, are illustrations of truth and falsehood and of the reward and punishment that each leads to. The living and the dead are an illustration of those who entered Islam and those who did not enter it. *Al-ḥarūr* is the intensity of the sun's heat.
