It was also read with a fatha on the yā', a sukun on the ḥā', and a lightened lām, from ḥaliyat al-mar'ah, meaning the woman wore jewelry, so she is ḥāliyy; and it is said "jīd ḥālin" (a neck adorned) when it contains jewelry. The discussion of ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk﴾ was given earlier in Surat al-Hajj.

The majority read "al-ḥazan" with two fathas. It was also read with a damma on the ḥā' and a sukun on the zāy, reported by Janah ibn Ḥubaysh. "Al-ḥazan" encompasses all sorrows, and the commentators specified it here and gave many examples. It should be understood as an illustration rather than a precise specification. Abu al-Darda' said: al-ḥazan is the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and what befalls there from wronging oneself, of grief and sorrow. Samurah ibn Jundub said: the livelihood of this world, the good and similar. Qatadah said: the sorrow of this world is the fear that their deeds will not be accepted. Muqatil said: the sorrow of departure, which they say when they have settled there. al-Kalbi said: the fear of Satan. Ibn Zayd said: al-ḥazan is the injustice of the Hereafter, the standing before acceptance and rejection of acts of worship, and the long stay upon the Sirat. al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: al-ḥazan is the removal of distress, the turning of the heart, and the fear of the consequence. They have given many examples, to the point that some said: the rent of the house. The meaning is that it encompasses every sorrow of the religion and of the world, even this.

﴿Indeed our Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative﴾: "Ghafur" (All-Forgiving) contains an indication to the entry of the one who wronged himself into Paradise.

"Shakur" (All-Appreciative) contains an indication to the foremost, and that he has many good deeds. "Al-muqamah" (the abode of lasting residence) means "al-iqamah," that is, Paradise, because it is an abode of permanent residence from which one is not removed.

﴿From His bounty﴾: from His gift.

﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾: i.e., bodily exhaustion (nasab); ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾: i.e., weariness of the soul (lughub), which is a necessary consequence of bodily weariness. Qatadah said: al-lughub is "al-wad'" (putting down, relaxing). al-Zamakhshari said: al-nasab is the toil and hardship that afflicts one who exerts himself and labors at it; as for al-lughub, it is what befalls him of slackness and lassitude because of the toil. So nasab is the very hardship and burden, and lughub is its result, what arises from it of fatigue and languor. End of quote. If you ask: when the cause is negated, its effect is negated; so what is the ruling when the cause is negated and its effect is negated too? You say: "I did not get full and did not eat," and it is not good to say "I did not eat nor got full," because the negation of eating necessarily entails the negation of fullness, but not vice versa. So if this construction were used, it would be: "no hardship touches us therein and no fatigue"? The answer: He, exalted, explained the difference between Paradise and the abode of this world, for its places are of two kinds: a place where hardships and toils touch, like the deserts and wildernesses, and a place where exhaustion touches, like houses and dwellings where there are children. So He said: ﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾, because it is not a place of the toils of this worldly abode; ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾, meaning we do not go out from it to a place of toil and return to it so that exhaustion touches us there. The majority read "lughub" with a damma on the lām, while 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Sulami read it with a fatha. al-Farra' said: it is what one is exhausted by, like "al-futur" and "al-suhur," and it may be an adjective of a suppressed verbal noun, as if it were "lughub," like their saying "mawt ma'it" (dead death). Sahib al-Lawami said: it may be a verbal noun like "al-qabul," or if you wish you may make it an adjective of a hidden noun, meaning "amr lughub" (a lughub matter). Lughub is also used in other than this sense for a fool. A Bedouin said: "Indeed so-and-so is a lughub; he brought my letter and belittled it," meaning a fool. He was asked: "Why did you make it feminine?" He said: "Is it not a sahifah (sheet)?"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colours? And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying shades, and jet-black ones.﴾ ﴿And among people, beasts and cattle are those of varying colours. Thus, only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah, establish the prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, hope for a commerce that will never perish.﴾ ﴿That He may pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. Indeed, He is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative.﴾ ﴿And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming what is before it. Indeed, Allah is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿Then We made the Book an inheritance to those whom We chose from Our servants. Among them is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who outstrips others in good deeds by Allah's permission. That is the great bounty.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative."﴾ ﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty. No fatigue touches us therein, nor does weariness touch us therein.﴾

(p-311) When the Exalted established His oneness through proofs He brought near and parables He presented, He followed them with heavenly and earthly proofs, and said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾. This interrogative is confirmatory (taqriri), and it is used only for something extremely evident. The address is to the listener, and (tara) is from the sight of the heart, because the attribution of the sending down to Him, exalted is He, is not inferred except by reason that agrees with transmission. Although the sending down of rain is witnessed with the eye, the sight of the heart may be attributed to sight of the eye and to other things. The discourse shifts from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in His saying ﴿so We bring forth﴾, because of the grandeur in that, since it is attributed to the Great One who speaks. Also, the blessing of bringing forth is more complete than the blessing of sending down, because of the benefit of bringing forth, so the more complete is attributed to His own Self with the first-person pronoun, and what is less than it with the third-person pronoun. The apparent meaning is that "colours" (al-alwan), if what is meant is what the mind immediately grasps of redness, yellowness, greenness, blackness, and other things, then colours in this sense are broader and more numerous than colours in the sense of dyes. The majority read ﴿mukhtalifan alwanuha﴾ on the pattern of ikhtalafa alwanuha. Zayd ibn Ali read mukhtalifatun alwanuha, on the pattern of ikhtalafat alwanuha, and a broken plural may take the feminine ta' or not take it. The majority read ﴿judadun﴾ with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the dal, plural of judda. Ibn Bahr said: a piece, from your saying: jadadtu al-shay', I cut it. al-Zuhri read it like the reading of the majority. The author of al-Lawami' said: plural of judda, which is what differs from the path in the mountains in the colour of what is beside it. Also from him, with a damma on the jim and the dal: plural of jadida, judud and jada'id, as is said of the noun: safina, sufun and safa'in. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Dark-shouldered (jawn al-sarat), or are they four jada'id?"

Also from him, with a fatha on the jim and the dal, which Abu Hatim did not permit regarding meaning, nor did he authenticate it as a report. Others said: it is the clear, evident path, and it is put in the place of the paths and the clear lines, separate from one another. Abu Ubayda said: judad is said as the plural of jadid, and the meaning of "new" has no place in this verse. The author of al-Lawami' said: judad is the plural of jadid meaning: new traces, clear in colours. End. He said: ﴿mukhtalif alwanuha﴾, because whiteness and redness vary in intensity and weakness; a white does not resemble another white, and a red does not resemble another red, even if they share the common element, but this is problematic. The apparent reading is that ﴿wa gharabib﴾ is conjoined to ﴿humrun﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 50], the conjunction of one coloured thing to another coloured thing. al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined to (bidun) or to (judad), as if it were said: and among the mountains is a streaked one having streaks, and among them is one of a single colour. He said after that: there must be an elision of the genitive-governing noun in His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾, meaning: having streaks, white, red and black, until it returns to your saying: and among the mountains are those whose colours differ, as He said ﴿fruits of varying colours﴾.

﴿And among people, beasts and cattle are those of varying colours﴾, meaning: among them is a part of varying colour. Ibn al-Sumayqa read: alwanuha. End.

The apparent reading is that when He mentioned the gharabib, which is the intensely black, He did not mention in it "of varying colours", because insofar as it is made intensely black, meaning it reaches the utmost extent of blackness, it does not have varying colours; rather this is one colour, unlike the white and the red, which vary. The apparent reading is that His saying ﴿white and red﴾ are not both grouped under one streak; rather the meaning is: white streaks, red streaks, and black streaks. It is said: aswad halakuk (jet-black), and aswad gharbib, and by right the extreme of that colour, to be a follower. Ibn Atiyya said: the more eloquent description was placed first, and its right position was to come later, and it is the same in meaning, but the eloquent speech of the Arabs comes often in this way. al-Zamakhshari said: gharbib is an emphasis for aswad (black), and by right emphasis should follow what it emphasises, as in your saying: asfar faqi' (bright yellow), abyad yaqiq (very white), and what is similar to that; its manner is that the emphasised word appears before it, so what follows is an explanation of what was implied, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And the believer of the protected birds."

It is only done for increasing emphasis, when it indicates the one meaning by way of both explicit and implicit expression together. End. This is not valid except according to the view of those who permit omitting the emphasised word. Some grammarians prohibited that, and it is the choice of Ibn Malik. It was also said: it is by inversion, (p-312) meaning sud gharabib (black, jet-black). It was also said: sud is a substitute (badal) for (gharabib), and this is better; what makes it better is that (gharabib) does not necessarily have to be used as an emphasis. Of this is what came in the hadith: "Indeed, Allah dislikes the old man who dyes with black," meaning the one who dyes with black. The poet said:

"The eye is roving, the hand is swimming, the leg is gleaming, and the face is jet-black."

Another said:

"Among the wonders of Allah's creation is a mare, some of whose parts are a mixed grey and some jet-black."

The majority read ﴿wa al-dawabb﴾ with a doubled ba'; al-Zuhri read it with it lightened, disliking the doubling, since it involves the meeting of two unvocalised letters. Just as some read (wa la al-dallin) with a hamza, fleeing from the meeting of two unvocalised letters, so here the last of the two doubled letters is elided and the first of the two unvocalised letters is vowelled. And ﴿mukhtalifatun﴾ is an adjective of an elided noun, meaning: a creation whose colours vary, thus, that is, like the variation of fruits and mountains. Therefore this comparison is part of the speech before it, and stopping upon it is good. Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is part of the second speech, coming in the manner of a cause, as if he said: just as the power has come in all this.

﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾, that is, those sincere to these lessons, who reflect upon them. End. This possibility is not valid, because what follows (innama) cannot be connected to this genitive phrase before it. Even if it came in the manner of a cause, the construction would be: thus He is feared by His servants, meaning for that consideration, and reflection upon the creatures of Allah and the variation of their colours produces fear. But the construction came with (innama), which cuts this genitive phrase off from what follows it. The scholars (al-ulama') are those who know Him through His attributes and His oneness, and what is permissible for Him, what is obligatory for Him, and what is impossible for Him. So they magnify Him and esteem Him as He deserves, and fear Him as He should be feared. Whoever gains more knowledge of Him gains more fear of Him, and whoever has less knowledge of Him is more secure. Hadiths and reports have come about fear. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whose fear was manifest in him until it was recognised in him. Whoever claimed that (innama) indicates restriction said: the meaning is: none fear Allah except the scholars, so others do not fear Him; this is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya said: in this verse (innama) specifies the scholars rather than restricting, and it is a word that can signify restriction and also comes without it, and that depends on the meaning in which it occurs. End.

This sentence came after His saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾, since its apparent address is to the Messenger, in which He enumerated His signs, the marks of His power, the traces of His craftsmanship, and the varied natures He created, and what is used as evidence of Him and His attributes. So it is as if He said: only one like you, and one of your attributes, from among those who know Him in the truest knowing, fears Him. The majority read with the Name of Allah in the accusative and al-Ulama' in the nominative. It is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and Abu Hanifa the reverse of that. This reading was interpreted as meaning that fear is a metaphor for magnification, because whoever fears and holds in awe magnifies and exalts the one he fears and holds in awe. Perhaps that is not authentically transmitted from them both. We have seen books on the irregular readings, and they did not mention this reading; rather al-Zamakhshari mentioned it, and Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn Jubara mentioned it from Abu Haywa in his book al-Kamil.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Forgiving﴾: an explanation (ta'lil) for the fear, since might indicates the punishment and subjugation of the disobedient, and forgiveness indicates the turning back of the obedient and pardon for them.

﴿Indeed, those who recite﴾: its apparent meaning is "read", ﴿the Book of Allah﴾, that is, they persist in its recitation. Mutarrif ibn Abdullah ibn al-Shikhkhir said: this is the verse of the reciters, and they follow the Book of Allah, acting upon what is in it. From al-Kalbi: they take hold of what is in it. al-Suddi said: they are the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them. Ata' said: they are the believers. When the Exalted mentioned their description with fear, which is an action of the heart, He mentioned that they recite the Book of Allah, which is an action of the tongue.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾, which is an action of the limbs, and ﴿spend﴾, which is financial action. Establishing the prayer and spending are done seeking the Face of Allah, not for showing off or reputation.

﴿A commerce that will never perish﴾: will never become unsalable, and profit will not be hindered in it, but rather it is paid back in full with Allah.

﴿That He may pay them﴾: attached to (yarjuna) or to (lan tabur), or to an implied verb whose estimate is: they did that. These are the views. al-Zamakhshari said: if you wish, you may say: (yarjuna) is in the place of a circumstantial clause, as in "and they spend, hoping, that He may pay them", meaning they did all that for this purpose. The predicate of inna is His saying ﴿Indeed He is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative﴾ regarding their deeds, and appreciation is a metaphor for reward. End. Their rewards are those which the Exalted ordained for their deeds, and the increase is from His bounty. Abu Wa'il said: through His intercession for those whom they benefited. al-Dahhak said: through the widening of hearts. In a hadith: "through the multiplying of their good deeds." It was also said: through looking upon His Face. The Book is the Qur'an, and (min) is for specification, or for kind, or for partitive, which are readings al-Zamakhshari提出了.

﴿Confirming﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial (hal) ﴿what is before it﴾ of the divine scriptures: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and others. In this is an indication that it is a revelation, since he, peace be upon him, was not one who reads or writes, and he brought the explanation of what is in the books of Allah, and that could only be from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed Allah, of His servants, is All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾: knowing the subtleties of things and their inner aspects, seeing what appears of them. And since He made you fit for His revelation, and chose you with His message and His Book, Allah knows best where He places His messages.

Then We caused the Book to be inherited (thumma awrathna al-Kitab). The "thumma" (then) is said by some to mean "wa" (and), and by others to indicate a delay, either in time or in the report, as will be explained. As for "al-Kitab" (the Book), there are two opinions. The first is that the meaning is: We sent down the divine Books, and in this case "al-Kitab" is a noun of genus. As for "al-Mustafun" (the chosen ones), as will be explained, the meaning is the prophets and their followers, as stated by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are this Community, the Community of Muhammad ﷺ was made to inherit every Book that Allah sent down. Ibn Jarir said: He made them inherit faith, since the Books command following the Qur'an, so they believe in them and act in accordance with their requirements. This is indicated by ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the Truth﴾, and then He followed it with His words ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾. So we know that they are the Community of Muhammad ﷺ, since the meaning of inheritance is the transfer of something from one people to another, and no community had a Book transferred to it from a people who were before them other than his Community. If we say they are the prophets and their followers, the meaning would be: We made inherit every Book sent down to a prophet, that prophet and his followers. The second opinion is that the Book is the Qur'an, and the "chosen ones" are the Community of the Messenger. The meaning of "awrathna" (We caused to inherit), Mujahid said, is "a'tayna" (We gave), because inheritance is a gift.

Then He divided the inheritors into these three categories. Makki said: it was said they are those mentioned in al-Waqi'ah (surah 56). So the one who is foremost in good deeds is the one brought near (al-muqarrab), the one who is moderate is the companions of the right (ashab al-maymanah), and the one who wrongs himself is the companions of the left (ashab al-mash'amah). This is an opinion whose meaning is narrated from 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and Qatadah, who said: the pronoun in "minhum" (among them) refers to the servants. So the one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever and the hypocrite, the moderate is the believer who disobeys, and the foremost is the pious in the absolute sense. They said: this is similar to what is in al-Waqi'ah. Most scholars hold that these three are within the Community of the Messenger, and whoever was among the companions of the left, being a denier and astray, does not inherit the Book and was not chosen by Allah; what is in al-Waqi'ah is the various kinds of creation from the earliest and the latest. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: our foremost are the people of jihad, our moderate are the people of our settled places, and our wrongdoers are the people of our desert, who do not attend Friday prayer or congregational prayer. Mu'adh said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who died upon a major sin without repenting from it; the moderate is the one who died upon a minor sin and did not commit a major sin without repenting from it; and the foremost is the one who died repentant from a major or minor sin, or who did not commit that. It was said: the one who wrongs himself is the disobedient transgressor; the moderate is the one who avoids major sins; and the foremost is the pious in the absolute sense. al-Hasan said: the wrongdoer is the one whose good deeds are light; the moderate is the one whose deeds are balanced; and the foremost is the one whose deeds outweigh. al-Zamakhshari said: He divided them into a wrongdoer who is a sinner, and this is the one who is a postponer (murji') regarding the command of Allah; a moderate, who is the one who mixed a righteous deed with another evil one; and a foremost one among the foremost. End of quote. He mentioned in al-Tajrid forty-three opinions regarding these three categories. Abu 'Imran al-Hawfi, 'Umar ibn Abi Shu'ayb, and Ya'qub in one narration, and the reading narrated from Abu 'Amr, read "sabbaq" (intensive form); the majority read "sabiq". It was said: the wrongdoer was placed first because he relies only on the mercy of Allah. al-Zamakhshari said: to signal the great number of the sinners among them and their predominance, and that the moderate are few in comparison with them, and the foremost are fewer than the few. End of quote.

﴿By the permission of Allah﴾: by His facilitation and empowerment, meaning that their precedence is not from their own essence, but that is from Him, exalted is He. The apparent meaning is that the reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the inheriting of the Book and the choosing of this Community.

"Jannatu" (gardens) on this reading is the subject (mubtada'), and "yadkhulunaha" (they enter it) is the predicate (khabar). The reading of the majority is "Jannatu" in the plural with a nominative ending, and this would be informing of the number of those chosen. al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said "jannatu" is a substitute (badal) for "al-fadl" (the bounty). al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how is "jannatu 'adnin" made a substitute for "al-fadl al-kabir" (the great bounty), which is the precedence in good deeds referred to by "dhalika"? I say: since it is the cause of attaining the reward, it takes the place of the effect, as if it were the reward itself, so "jannatu 'adnin" was substituted for it. End of quote. What indicates that it is a subject is the reading of al-Jahdari and Harun from 'Asim: "jannati" in the accusative under the construction of the verb being suppressed, meaning they enter the gardens of Eden, they enter them. Raz'in, Hubaysh and al-Zuhri read "jannatun" in the singular. Abu 'Amr read "yudkhalunaha" in the passive voice, and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir and the majority in the active voice. The apparent meaning is that the raised pronoun in "yadkhulunaha" refers to the three categories. This is the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Abu al-Darda', 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, Abu Sa'id, 'A'ishah, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ja'far al-Sadiq, Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i and Ka'b al-Ahbar. 'Umar recited this verse, then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Our foremost is the foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven." As for the one who makes the three categories those of al-Waqi'ah, the pronoun in "yadkhulunaha" refers, in his view, to the moderate and the foremost. al-Zamakhshari said: it refers only to the foremost, and for this reason he made "dhalika" a reference to the precedence after the division, and then mentioned their reward. The silence about the other two contains what it contains of the obligation of caution: let the moderate beware, and let the one who wrongs himself be fearful, and both must seek sincere repentance that delivers from the punishment of Allah. Let him not be deceived by what 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Our foremost is the foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven," for the condition of that is the soundness of repentance. "Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness" (asa Allahu an yatuba 'alayhim). And His words: "Either He punishes them or He turns to them in forgiveness" have been expressed in the Qur'an in many places; whoever surveys them becomes aware of the reality of the matter and does not deceive himself. End of quote, and this is on the path of the Mu'tazilah.

The majority read ﴿yuhallawna﴾ with a damma on the yā' (y), a fatha on the ḥā' (ḥ), and a shadda on the lām (l), in the passive voice. It was also read with a fatha on the yā', a sukun on the ḥā', and a lightened lām, from ḥaliyat al-mar'ah, meaning the woman wore jewelry, so she is ḥāliyy; and it is said "jīd ḥālin" (a neck adorned) when it contains jewelry. The discussion of ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk﴾ was given earlier in Surat al-Hajj.

The majority read "al-ḥazan" with two fathas. It was also read with a damma on the ḥā' and a sukun on the zāy, reported by Janah ibn Ḥubaysh. "Al-ḥazan" encompasses all sorrows, and the commentators specified it here and gave many examples. It should be understood as an illustration rather than a precise specification. Abu al-Darda' said: al-ḥazan is the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and what befalls there from wronging oneself, of grief and sorrow. Samurah ibn Jundub said: the livelihood of this world, the good and similar. Qatadah said: the sorrow of this world is the fear that their deeds will not be accepted. Muqatil said: the sorrow of departure, which they say when they have settled there. al-Kalbi said: the fear of Satan. Ibn Zayd said: al-ḥazan is the injustice of the Hereafter, the standing before acceptance and rejection of acts of worship, and the long stay upon the Sirat. al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: al-ḥazan is the removal of distress, the turning of the heart, and the fear of the consequence. They have given many examples, to the point that some said: the rent of the house. The meaning is that it encompasses every sorrow of the religion and of the world, even this.

﴿Indeed our Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative﴾: "Ghafur" (All-Forgiving) contains an indication to the entry of the one who wronged himself into Paradise.

"Shakur" (All-Appreciative) contains an indication to the foremost, and that he has many good deeds. "Al-muqamah" (the abode of lasting residence) means "al-iqamah," that is, Paradise, because it is an abode of permanent residence from which one is not removed.

﴿From His bounty﴾: from His gift.

﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾: i.e., bodily exhaustion (nasab); ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾: i.e., weariness of the soul (lughub), which is a necessary consequence of bodily weariness. Qatadah said: al-lughub is "al-wad'" (putting down, relaxing). al-Zamakhshari said: al-nasab is the toil and hardship that afflicts one who exerts himself and labors at it; as for al-lughub, it is what befalls him of slackness and lassitude because of the toil. So nasab is the very hardship and burden, and lughub is its result, what arises from it of fatigue and languor. End of quote. If you ask: when the cause is negated, its effect is negated; so what is the ruling when the cause is negated and its effect is negated too? You say: "I did not get full and did not eat," and it is not good to say "I did not eat nor got full," because the negation of eating necessarily entails the negation of fullness, but not vice versa. So if this construction were used, it would be: "no hardship touches us therein and no fatigue"? The answer: He, exalted, explained the difference between Paradise and the abode of this world, for its places are of two kinds: a place where hardships and toils touch, like the deserts and wildernesses, and a place where exhaustion touches, like houses and dwellings where there are children. So He said: ﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾, because it is not a place of the toils of this worldly abode; ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾, meaning we do not go out from it to a place of toil and return to it so that exhaustion touches us there. The majority read "lughub" with a damma on the lām, while 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Sulami read it with a fatha. al-Farra' said: it is what one is exhausted by, like "al-futur" and "al-suhur," and it may be an adjective of a suppressed verbal noun, as if it were "lughub," like their saying "mawt ma'it" (dead death). Sahib al-Lawami said: it may be a verbal noun like "al-qabul," or if you wish you may make it an adjective of a hidden noun, meaning "amr lughub" (a lughub matter). Lughub is also used in other than this sense for a fool. A Bedouin said: "Indeed so-and-so is a lughub; he brought my letter and belittled it," meaning a fool. He was asked: "Why did you make it feminine?" He said: "Is it not a sahifah (sheet)?"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colours? And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying shades, and jet-black ones.﴾ ﴿And among people, beasts and cattle are those of varying colours. Thus, only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah, establish the prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, hope for a commerce that will never perish.﴾ ﴿That He may pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. Indeed, He is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative.﴾ ﴿And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming what is before it. Indeed, Allah is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿Then We made the Book an inheritance to those whom We chose from Our servants. Among them is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who outstrips others in good deeds by Allah's permission. That is the great bounty.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative."﴾ ﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty. No fatigue touches us therein, nor does weariness touch us therein.﴾

(p-311) When the Exalted established His oneness through proofs He brought near and parables He presented, He followed them with heavenly and earthly proofs, and said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾. This interrogative is confirmatory (taqriri), and it is used only for something extremely evident. The address is to the listener, and (tara) is from the sight of the heart, because the attribution of the sending down to Him, exalted is He, is not inferred except by reason that agrees with transmission. Although the sending down of rain is witnessed with the eye, the sight of the heart may be attributed to sight of the eye and to other things. The discourse shifts from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in His saying ﴿so We bring forth﴾, because of the grandeur in that, since it is attributed to the Great One who speaks. Also, the blessing of bringing forth is more complete than the blessing of sending down, because of the benefit of bringing forth, so the more complete is attributed to His own Self with the first-person pronoun, and what is less than it with the third-person pronoun. The apparent meaning is that "colours" (al-alwan), if what is meant is what the mind immediately grasps of redness, yellowness, greenness, blackness, and other things, then colours in this sense are broader and more numerous than colours in the sense of dyes. The majority read ﴿mukhtalifan alwanuha﴾ on the pattern of ikhtalafa alwanuha. Zayd ibn Ali read mukhtalifatun alwanuha, on the pattern of ikhtalafat alwanuha, and a broken plural may take the feminine ta' or not take it. The majority read ﴿judadun﴾ with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the dal, plural of judda. Ibn Bahr said: a piece, from your saying: jadadtu al-shay', I cut it. al-Zuhri read it like the reading of the majority. The author of al-Lawami' said: plural of judda, which is what differs from the path in the mountains in the colour of what is beside it. Also from him, with a damma on the jim and the dal: plural of jadida, judud and jada'id, as is said of the noun: safina, sufun and safa'in. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Dark-shouldered (jawn al-sarat), or are they four jada'id?"

Also from him, with a fatha on the jim and the dal, which Abu Hatim did not permit regarding meaning, nor did he authenticate it as a report. Others said: it is the clear, evident path, and it is put in the place of the paths and the clear lines, separate from one another. Abu Ubayda said: judad is said as the plural of jadid, and the meaning of "new" has no place in this verse. The author of al-Lawami' said: judad is the plural of jadid meaning: new traces, clear in colours. End. He said: ﴿mukhtalif alwanuha﴾, because whiteness and redness vary in intensity and weakness; a white does not resemble another white, and a red does not resemble another red, even if they share the common element, but this is problematic. The apparent reading is that ﴿wa gharabib﴾ is conjoined to ﴿humrun﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 50], the conjunction of one coloured thing to another coloured thing. al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined to (bidun) or to (judad), as if it were said: and among the mountains is a streaked one having streaks, and among them is one of a single colour. He said after that: there must be an elision of the genitive-governing noun in His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾, meaning: having streaks, white, red and black, until it returns to your saying: and among the mountains are those whose colours differ, as He said ﴿fruits of varying colours﴾.

﴿And among people, beasts and cattle are those of varying colours﴾, meaning: among them is a part of varying colour. Ibn al-Sumayqa read: alwanuha. End.

The apparent reading is that when He mentioned the gharabib, which is the intensely black, He did not mention in it "of varying colours", because insofar as it is made intensely black, meaning it reaches the utmost extent of blackness, it does not have varying colours; rather this is one colour, unlike the white and the red, which vary. The apparent reading is that His saying ﴿white and red﴾ are not both grouped under one streak; rather the meaning is: white streaks, red streaks, and black streaks. It is said: aswad halakuk (jet-black), and aswad gharbib, and by right the extreme of that colour, to be a follower. Ibn Atiyya said: the more eloquent description was placed first, and its right position was to come later, and it is the same in meaning, but the eloquent speech of the Arabs comes often in this way. al-Zamakhshari said: gharbib is an emphasis for aswad (black), and by right emphasis should follow what it emphasises, as in your saying: asfar faqi' (bright yellow), abyad yaqiq (very white), and what is similar to that; its manner is that the emphasised word appears before it, so what follows is an explanation of what was implied, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And the believer of the protected birds."

It is only done for increasing emphasis, when it indicates the one meaning by way of both explicit and implicit expression together. End. This is not valid except according to the view of those who permit omitting the emphasised word. Some grammarians prohibited that, and it is the choice of Ibn Malik. It was also said: it is by inversion, (p-312) meaning sud gharabib (black, jet-black). It was also said: sud is a substitute (badal) for (gharabib), and this is better; what makes it better is that (gharabib) does not necessarily have to be used as an emphasis. Of this is what came in the hadith: "Indeed, Allah dislikes the old man who dyes with black," meaning the one who dyes with black. The poet said:

"The eye is roving, the hand is swimming, the leg is gleaming, and the face is jet-black."

Another said:

"Among the wonders of Allah's creation is a mare, some of whose parts are a mixed grey and some jet-black."

The majority read ﴿wa al-dawabb﴾ with a doubled ba'; al-Zuhri read it with it lightened, disliking the doubling, since it involves the meeting of two unvocalised letters. Just as some read (wa la al-dallin) with a hamza, fleeing from the meeting of two unvocalised letters, so here the last of the two doubled letters is elided and the first of the two unvocalised letters is vowelled. And ﴿mukhtalifatun﴾ is an adjective of an elided noun, meaning: a creation whose colours vary, thus, that is, like the variation of fruits and mountains. Therefore this comparison is part of the speech before it, and stopping upon it is good. Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is part of the second speech, coming in the manner of a cause, as if he said: just as the power has come in all this.

﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾, that is, those sincere to these lessons, who reflect upon them. End. This possibility is not valid, because what follows (innama) cannot be connected to this genitive phrase before it. Even if it came in the manner of a cause, the construction would be: thus He is feared by His servants, meaning for that consideration, and reflection upon the creatures of Allah and the variation of their colours produces fear. But the construction came with (innama), which cuts this genitive phrase off from what follows it. The scholars (al-ulama') are those who know Him through His attributes and His oneness, and what is permissible for Him, what is obligatory for Him, and what is impossible for Him. So they magnify Him and esteem Him as He deserves, and fear Him as He should be feared. Whoever gains more knowledge of Him gains more fear of Him, and whoever has less knowledge of Him is more secure. Hadiths and reports have come about fear. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whose fear was manifest in him until it was recognised in him. Whoever claimed that (innama) indicates restriction said: the meaning is: none fear Allah except the scholars, so others do not fear Him; this is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya said: in this verse (innama) specifies the scholars rather than restricting, and it is a word that can signify restriction and also comes without it, and that depends on the meaning in which it occurs. End.

This sentence came after His saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾, since its apparent address is to the Messenger, in which He enumerated His signs, the marks of His power, the traces of His craftsmanship, and the varied natures He created, and what is used as evidence of Him and His attributes. So it is as if He said: only one like you, and one of your attributes, from among those who know Him in the truest knowing, fears Him. The majority read with the Name of Allah in the accusative and al-Ulama' in the nominative. It is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and Abu Hanifa the reverse of that. This reading was interpreted as meaning that fear is a metaphor for magnification, because whoever fears and holds in awe magnifies and exalts the one he fears and holds in awe. Perhaps that is not authentically transmitted from them both. We have seen books on the irregular readings, and they did not mention this reading; rather al-Zamakhshari mentioned it, and Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn Jubara mentioned it from Abu Haywa in his book al-Kamil.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Forgiving﴾: an explanation (ta'lil) for the fear, since might indicates the punishment and subjugation of the disobedient, and forgiveness indicates the turning back of the obedient and pardon for them.

﴿Indeed, those who recite﴾: its apparent meaning is "read", ﴿the Book of Allah﴾, that is, they persist in its recitation. Mutarrif ibn Abdullah ibn al-Shikhkhir said: this is the verse of the reciters, and they follow the Book of Allah, acting upon what is in it. From al-Kalbi: they take hold of what is in it. al-Suddi said: they are the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them. Ata' said: they are the believers. When the Exalted mentioned their description with fear, which is an action of the heart, He mentioned that they recite the Book of Allah, which is an action of the tongue.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾, which is an action of the limbs, and ﴿spend﴾, which is financial action. Establishing the prayer and spending are done seeking the Face of Allah, not for showing off or reputation.

﴿A commerce that will never perish﴾: will never become unsalable, and profit will not be hindered in it, but rather it is paid back in full with Allah.

﴿That He may pay them﴾: attached to (yarjuna) or to (lan tabur), or to an implied verb whose estimate is: they did that. These are the views. al-Zamakhshari said: if you wish, you may say: (yarjuna) is in the place of a circumstantial clause, as in "and they spend, hoping, that He may pay them", meaning they did all that for this purpose. The predicate of inna is His saying ﴿Indeed He is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative﴾ regarding their deeds, and appreciation is a metaphor for reward. End. Their rewards are those which the Exalted ordained for their deeds, and the increase is from His bounty. Abu Wa'il said: through His intercession for those whom they benefited. al-Dahhak said: through the widening of hearts. In a hadith: "through the multiplying of their good deeds." It was also said: through looking upon His Face. The Book is the Qur'an, and (min) is for specification, or for kind, or for partitive, which are readings al-Zamakhshari提出了.

﴿Confirming﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial (hal) ﴿what is before it﴾ of the divine scriptures: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and others. In this is an indication that it is a revelation, since he, peace be upon him, was not one who reads or writes, and he brought the explanation of what is in the books of Allah, and that could only be from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed Allah, of His servants, is All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾: knowing the subtleties of things and their inner aspects, seeing what appears of them. And since He made you fit for His revelation, and chose you with His message and His Book, Allah knows best where He places His messages.

Then We caused the Book to be inherited (thumma awrathna al-Kitab). The "thumma" (then) is said by some to mean "wa" (and), and by others to indicate a delay, either in time or in the report, as will be explained. As for "al-Kitab" (the Book), there are two opinions. The first is that the meaning is: We sent down the divine Books, and in this case "al-Kitab" is a noun of genus. As for "al-Mustafun" (the chosen ones), as will be explained, the meaning is the prophets and their followers, as stated by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are this Community, the Community of Muhammad ﷺ was made to inherit every Book that Allah sent down. Ibn Jarir said: He made them inherit faith, since the Books command following the Qur'an, so they believe in them and act in accordance with their requirements. This is indicated by ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the Truth﴾, and then He followed it with His words ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾. So we know that they are the Community of Muhammad ﷺ, since the meaning of inheritance is the transfer of something from one people to another, and no community had a Book transferred to it from a people who were before them other than his Community. If we say they are the prophets and their followers, the meaning would be: We made inherit every Book sent down to a prophet, that prophet and his followers. The second opinion is that the Book is the Qur'an, and the "chosen ones" are the Community of the Messenger. The meaning of "awrathna" (We caused to inherit), Mujahid said, is "a'tayna" (We gave), because inheritance is a gift.

Then He divided the inheritors into these three categories. Makki said: it was said they are those mentioned in al-Waqi'ah (surah 56). So the one who is foremost in good deeds is the one brought near (al-muqarrab), the one who is moderate is the companions of the right (ashab al-maymanah), and the one who wrongs himself is the companions of the left (ashab al-mash'amah). This is an opinion whose meaning is narrated from 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and Qatadah, who said: the pronoun in "minhum" (among them) refers to the servants. So the one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever and the hypocrite, the moderate is the believer who disobeys, and the foremost is the pious in the absolute sense. They said: this is similar to what is in al-Waqi'ah. Most scholars hold that these three are within the Community of the Messenger, and whoever was among the companions of the left, being a denier and astray, does not inherit the Book and was not chosen by Allah; what is in al-Waqi'ah is the various kinds of creation from the earliest and the latest. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: our foremost are the people of jihad, our moderate are the people of our settled places, and our wrongdoers are the people of our desert, who do not attend Friday prayer or congregational prayer. Mu'adh said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who died upon a major sin without repenting from it; the moderate is the one who died upon a minor sin and did not commit a major sin without repenting from it; and the foremost is the one who died repentant from a major or minor sin, or who did not commit that. It was said: the one who wrongs himself is the disobedient transgressor; the moderate is the one who avoids major sins; and the foremost is the pious in the absolute sense. al-Hasan said: the wrongdoer is the one whose good deeds are light; the moderate is the one whose deeds are balanced; and the foremost is the one whose deeds outweigh. al-Zamakhshari said: He divided them into a wrongdoer who is a sinner, and this is the one who is a postponer (murji') regarding the command of Allah; a moderate, who is the one who mixed a righteous deed with another evil one; and a foremost one among the foremost. End of quote. He mentioned in al-Tajrid forty-three opinions regarding these three categories. Abu 'Imran al-Hawfi, 'Umar ibn Abi Shu'ayb, and Ya'qub in one narration, and the reading narrated from Abu 'Amr, read "sabbaq" (intensive form); the majority read "sabiq". It was said: the wrongdoer was placed first because he relies only on the mercy of Allah. al-Zamakhshari said: to signal the great number of the sinners among them and their predominance, and that the moderate are few in comparison with them, and the foremost are fewer than the few. End of quote.

﴿By the permission of Allah﴾: by His facilitation and empowerment, meaning that their precedence is not from their own essence, but that is from Him, exalted is He. The apparent meaning is that the reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the inheriting of the Book and the choosing of this Community.

"Jannatu" (gardens) on this reading is the subject (mubtada'), and "yadkhulunaha" (they enter it) is the predicate (khabar). The reading of the majority is "Jannatu" in the plural with a nominative ending, and this would be informing of the number of those chosen. al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said "jannatu" is a substitute (badal) for "al-fadl" (the bounty). al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how is "jannatu 'adnin" made a substitute for "al-fadl al-kabir" (the great bounty), which is the precedence in good deeds referred to by "dhalika"? I say: since it is the cause of attaining the reward, it takes the place of the effect, as if it were the reward itself, so "jannatu 'adnin" was substituted for it. End of quote. What indicates that it is a subject is the reading of al-Jahdari and Harun from 'Asim: "jannati" in the accusative under the construction of the verb being suppressed, meaning they enter the gardens of Eden, they enter them. Raz'in, Hubaysh and al-Zuhri read "jannatun" in the singular. Abu 'Amr read "yudkhalunaha" in the passive voice, and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir and the majority in the active voice. The apparent meaning is that the raised pronoun in "yadkhulunaha" refers to the three categories. This is the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Abu al-Darda', 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, Abu Sa'id, 'A'ishah, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ja'far al-Sadiq, Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i and Ka'b al-Ahbar. 'Umar recited this verse, then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Our foremost is the foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven." As for the one who makes the three categories those of al-Waqi'ah, the pronoun in "yadkhulunaha" refers, in his view, to the moderate and the foremost. al-Zamakhshari said: it refers only to the foremost, and for this reason he made "dhalika" a reference to the precedence after the division, and then mentioned their reward. The silence about the other two contains what it contains of the obligation of caution: let the moderate beware, and let the one who wrongs himself be fearful, and both must seek sincere repentance that delivers from the punishment of Allah. Let him not be deceived by what 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Our foremost is the foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven," for the condition of that is the soundness of repentance. "Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness" (asa Allahu an yatuba 'alayhim). And His words: "Either He punishes them or He turns to them in forgiveness" have been expressed in the Qur'an in many places; whoever surveys them becomes aware of the reality of the matter and does not deceive himself. End of quote, and this is on the path of the Mu'tazilah.

The majority read ﴿yuhallawna﴾ with a damma on the yā' (y), a fatha on the ḥā' (ḥ), and a shadda on the lām (l), in the passive voice. It was also read with a fatha on the yā', a sukun on the ḥā', and a lightened lām, from ḥaliyat al-mar'ah, meaning the woman wore jewelry, so she is ḥāliyy; and it is said "jīd ḥālin" (a neck adorned) when it contains jewelry. The discussion of ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk﴾ was given earlier in Surat al-Hajj.

The majority read "al-ḥazan" with two fathas. It was also read with a damma on the ḥā' and a sukun on the zāy, reported by Janah ibn Ḥubaysh. "Al-ḥazan" encompasses all sorrows, and the commentators specified it here and gave many examples. It should be understood as an illustration rather than a precise specification. Abu al-Darda' said: al-ḥazan is the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and what befalls there from wronging oneself, of grief and sorrow. Samurah ibn Jundub said: the livelihood of this world, the good and similar. Qatadah said: the sorrow of this world is the fear that their deeds will not be accepted. Muqatil said: the sorrow of departure, which they say when they have settled there. al-Kalbi said: the fear of Satan. Ibn Zayd said: al-ḥazan is the injustice of the Hereafter, the standing before acceptance and rejection of acts of worship, and the long stay upon the Sirat. al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: al-ḥazan is the removal of distress, the turning of the heart, and the fear of the consequence. They have given many examples, to the point that some said: the rent of the house. The meaning is that it encompasses every sorrow of the religion and of the world, even this.

﴿Indeed our Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative﴾: "Ghafur" (All-Forgiving) contains an indication to the entry of the one who wronged himself into Paradise.

"Shakur" (All-Appreciative) contains an indication to the foremost, and that he has many good deeds. "Al-muqamah" (the abode of lasting residence) means "al-iqamah," that is, Paradise, because it is an abode of permanent residence from which one is not removed.

﴿From His bounty﴾: from His gift.

﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾: i.e., bodily exhaustion (nasab); ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾: i.e., weariness of the soul (lughub), which is a necessary consequence of bodily weariness. Qatadah said: al-lughub is "al-wad'" (putting down, relaxing). al-Zamakhshari said: al-nasab is the toil and hardship that afflicts one who exerts himself and labors at it; as for al-lughub, it is what befalls him of slackness and lassitude because of the toil. So nasab is the very hardship and burden, and lughub is its result, what arises from it of fatigue and languor. End of quote. If you ask: when the cause is negated, its effect is negated; so what is the ruling when the cause is negated and its effect is negated too? You say: "I did not get full and did not eat," and it is not good to say "I did not eat nor got full," because the negation of eating necessarily entails the negation of fullness, but not vice versa. So if this construction were used, it would be: "no hardship touches us therein and no fatigue"? The answer: He, exalted, explained the difference between Paradise and the abode of this world, for its places are of two kinds: a place where hardships and toils touch, like the deserts and wildernesses, and a place where exhaustion touches, like houses and dwellings where there are children. So He said: ﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾, because it is not a place of the toils of this worldly abode; ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾, meaning we do not go out from it to a place of toil and return to it so that exhaustion touches us there. The majority read "lughub" with a damma on the lām, while 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Sulami read it with a fatha. al-Farra' said: it is what one is exhausted by, like "al-futur" and "al-suhur," and it may be an adjective of a suppressed verbal noun, as if it were "lughub," like their saying "mawt ma'it" (dead death). Sahib al-Lawami said: it may be a verbal noun like "al-qabul," or if you wish you may make it an adjective of a hidden noun, meaning "amr lughub" (a lughub matter). Lughub is also used in other than this sense for a fool. A Bedouin said: "Indeed so-and-so is a lughub; he brought my letter and belittled it," meaning a fool. He was asked: "Why did you make it feminine?" He said: "Is it not a sahifah (sheet)?"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 35, verses 27–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colours? And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying shades, and jet-black ones.﴾ ﴿And among people, beasts and cattle are those of varying colours. Thus, only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah, establish the prayer, and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, hope for a commerce that will never perish.﴾ ﴿That He may pay them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. Indeed, He is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative.﴾ ﴿And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth, confirming what is before it. Indeed, Allah is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿Then We made the Book an inheritance to those whom We chose from Our servants. Among them is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who outstrips others in good deeds by Allah's permission. That is the great bounty.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾ ﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative."﴾ ﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty. No fatigue touches us therein, nor does weariness touch us therein.﴾

(p-311) When the Exalted established His oneness through proofs He brought near and parables He presented, He followed them with heavenly and earthly proofs, and said: ﴿Have you not seen﴾. This interrogative is confirmatory (taqriri), and it is used only for something extremely evident. The address is to the listener, and (tara) is from the sight of the heart, because the attribution of the sending down to Him, exalted is He, is not inferred except by reason that agrees with transmission. Although the sending down of rain is witnessed with the eye, the sight of the heart may be attributed to sight of the eye and to other things. The discourse shifts from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in His saying ﴿so We bring forth﴾, because of the grandeur in that, since it is attributed to the Great One who speaks. Also, the blessing of bringing forth is more complete than the blessing of sending down, because of the benefit of bringing forth, so the more complete is attributed to His own Self with the first-person pronoun, and what is less than it with the third-person pronoun. The apparent meaning is that "colours" (al-alwan), if what is meant is what the mind immediately grasps of redness, yellowness, greenness, blackness, and other things, then colours in this sense are broader and more numerous than colours in the sense of dyes. The majority read ﴿mukhtalifan alwanuha﴾ on the pattern of ikhtalafa alwanuha. Zayd ibn Ali read mukhtalifatun alwanuha, on the pattern of ikhtalafat alwanuha, and a broken plural may take the feminine ta' or not take it. The majority read ﴿judadun﴾ with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the dal, plural of judda. Ibn Bahr said: a piece, from your saying: jadadtu al-shay', I cut it. al-Zuhri read it like the reading of the majority. The author of al-Lawami' said: plural of judda, which is what differs from the path in the mountains in the colour of what is beside it. Also from him, with a damma on the jim and the dal: plural of jadida, judud and jada'id, as is said of the noun: safina, sufun and safa'in. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Dark-shouldered (jawn al-sarat), or are they four jada'id?"

Also from him, with a fatha on the jim and the dal, which Abu Hatim did not permit regarding meaning, nor did he authenticate it as a report. Others said: it is the clear, evident path, and it is put in the place of the paths and the clear lines, separate from one another. Abu Ubayda said: judad is said as the plural of jadid, and the meaning of "new" has no place in this verse. The author of al-Lawami' said: judad is the plural of jadid meaning: new traces, clear in colours. End. He said: ﴿mukhtalif alwanuha﴾, because whiteness and redness vary in intensity and weakness; a white does not resemble another white, and a red does not resemble another red, even if they share the common element, but this is problematic. The apparent reading is that ﴿wa gharabib﴾ is conjoined to ﴿humrun﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 50], the conjunction of one coloured thing to another coloured thing. al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined to (bidun) or to (judad), as if it were said: and among the mountains is a streaked one having streaks, and among them is one of a single colour. He said after that: there must be an elision of the genitive-governing noun in His saying ﴿and among the mountains are streaks﴾, meaning: having streaks, white, red and black, until it returns to your saying: and among the mountains are those whose colours differ, as He said ﴿fruits of varying colours﴾.

﴿And among people, beasts and cattle are those of varying colours﴾, meaning: among them is a part of varying colour. Ibn al-Sumayqa read: alwanuha. End.

The apparent reading is that when He mentioned the gharabib, which is the intensely black, He did not mention in it "of varying colours", because insofar as it is made intensely black, meaning it reaches the utmost extent of blackness, it does not have varying colours; rather this is one colour, unlike the white and the red, which vary. The apparent reading is that His saying ﴿white and red﴾ are not both grouped under one streak; rather the meaning is: white streaks, red streaks, and black streaks. It is said: aswad halakuk (jet-black), and aswad gharbib, and by right the extreme of that colour, to be a follower. Ibn Atiyya said: the more eloquent description was placed first, and its right position was to come later, and it is the same in meaning, but the eloquent speech of the Arabs comes often in this way. al-Zamakhshari said: gharbib is an emphasis for aswad (black), and by right emphasis should follow what it emphasises, as in your saying: asfar faqi' (bright yellow), abyad yaqiq (very white), and what is similar to that; its manner is that the emphasised word appears before it, so what follows is an explanation of what was implied, as in the saying of al-Nabigha:

"And the believer of the protected birds."

It is only done for increasing emphasis, when it indicates the one meaning by way of both explicit and implicit expression together. End. This is not valid except according to the view of those who permit omitting the emphasised word. Some grammarians prohibited that, and it is the choice of Ibn Malik. It was also said: it is by inversion, (p-312) meaning sud gharabib (black, jet-black). It was also said: sud is a substitute (badal) for (gharabib), and this is better; what makes it better is that (gharabib) does not necessarily have to be used as an emphasis. Of this is what came in the hadith: "Indeed, Allah dislikes the old man who dyes with black," meaning the one who dyes with black. The poet said:

"The eye is roving, the hand is swimming, the leg is gleaming, and the face is jet-black."

Another said:

"Among the wonders of Allah's creation is a mare, some of whose parts are a mixed grey and some jet-black."

The majority read ﴿wa al-dawabb﴾ with a doubled ba'; al-Zuhri read it with it lightened, disliking the doubling, since it involves the meeting of two unvocalised letters. Just as some read (wa la al-dallin) with a hamza, fleeing from the meeting of two unvocalised letters, so here the last of the two doubled letters is elided and the first of the two unvocalised letters is vowelled. And ﴿mukhtalifatun﴾ is an adjective of an elided noun, meaning: a creation whose colours vary, thus, that is, like the variation of fruits and mountains. Therefore this comparison is part of the speech before it, and stopping upon it is good. Ibn Atiyya said: it is possible that it is part of the second speech, coming in the manner of a cause, as if he said: just as the power has come in all this.

﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾, that is, those sincere to these lessons, who reflect upon them. End. This possibility is not valid, because what follows (innama) cannot be connected to this genitive phrase before it. Even if it came in the manner of a cause, the construction would be: thus He is feared by His servants, meaning for that consideration, and reflection upon the creatures of Allah and the variation of their colours produces fear. But the construction came with (innama), which cuts this genitive phrase off from what follows it. The scholars (al-ulama') are those who know Him through His attributes and His oneness, and what is permissible for Him, what is obligatory for Him, and what is impossible for Him. So they magnify Him and esteem Him as He deserves, and fear Him as He should be feared. Whoever gains more knowledge of Him gains more fear of Him, and whoever has less knowledge of Him is more secure. Hadiths and reports have come about fear. It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whose fear was manifest in him until it was recognised in him. Whoever claimed that (innama) indicates restriction said: the meaning is: none fear Allah except the scholars, so others do not fear Him; this is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya said: in this verse (innama) specifies the scholars rather than restricting, and it is a word that can signify restriction and also comes without it, and that depends on the meaning in which it occurs. End.

This sentence came after His saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾, since its apparent address is to the Messenger, in which He enumerated His signs, the marks of His power, the traces of His craftsmanship, and the varied natures He created, and what is used as evidence of Him and His attributes. So it is as if He said: only one like you, and one of your attributes, from among those who know Him in the truest knowing, fears Him. The majority read with the Name of Allah in the accusative and al-Ulama' in the nominative. It is narrated from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and Abu Hanifa the reverse of that. This reading was interpreted as meaning that fear is a metaphor for magnification, because whoever fears and holds in awe magnifies and exalts the one he fears and holds in awe. Perhaps that is not authentically transmitted from them both. We have seen books on the irregular readings, and they did not mention this reading; rather al-Zamakhshari mentioned it, and Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn Jubara mentioned it from Abu Haywa in his book al-Kamil.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Mighty, All-Forgiving﴾: an explanation (ta'lil) for the fear, since might indicates the punishment and subjugation of the disobedient, and forgiveness indicates the turning back of the obedient and pardon for them.

﴿Indeed, those who recite﴾: its apparent meaning is "read", ﴿the Book of Allah﴾, that is, they persist in its recitation. Mutarrif ibn Abdullah ibn al-Shikhkhir said: this is the verse of the reciters, and they follow the Book of Allah, acting upon what is in it. From al-Kalbi: they take hold of what is in it. al-Suddi said: they are the Companions of the Messenger (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them. Ata' said: they are the believers. When the Exalted mentioned their description with fear, which is an action of the heart, He mentioned that they recite the Book of Allah, which is an action of the tongue.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾, which is an action of the limbs, and ﴿spend﴾, which is financial action. Establishing the prayer and spending are done seeking the Face of Allah, not for showing off or reputation.

﴿A commerce that will never perish﴾: will never become unsalable, and profit will not be hindered in it, but rather it is paid back in full with Allah.

﴿That He may pay them﴾: attached to (yarjuna) or to (lan tabur), or to an implied verb whose estimate is: they did that. These are the views. al-Zamakhshari said: if you wish, you may say: (yarjuna) is in the place of a circumstantial clause, as in "and they spend, hoping, that He may pay them", meaning they did all that for this purpose. The predicate of inna is His saying ﴿Indeed He is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative﴾ regarding their deeds, and appreciation is a metaphor for reward. End. Their rewards are those which the Exalted ordained for their deeds, and the increase is from His bounty. Abu Wa'il said: through His intercession for those whom they benefited. al-Dahhak said: through the widening of hearts. In a hadith: "through the multiplying of their good deeds." It was also said: through looking upon His Face. The Book is the Qur'an, and (min) is for specification, or for kind, or for partitive, which are readings al-Zamakhshari提出了.

﴿Confirming﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial (hal) ﴿what is before it﴾ of the divine scriptures: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and others. In this is an indication that it is a revelation, since he, peace be upon him, was not one who reads or writes, and he brought the explanation of what is in the books of Allah, and that could only be from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed Allah, of His servants, is All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾: knowing the subtleties of things and their inner aspects, seeing what appears of them. And since He made you fit for His revelation, and chose you with His message and His Book, Allah knows best where He places His messages.

Then We caused the Book to be inherited (thumma awrathna al-Kitab). The "thumma" (then) is said by some to mean "wa" (and), and by others to indicate a delay, either in time or in the report, as will be explained. As for "al-Kitab" (the Book), there are two opinions. The first is that the meaning is: We sent down the divine Books, and in this case "al-Kitab" is a noun of genus. As for "al-Mustafun" (the chosen ones), as will be explained, the meaning is the prophets and their followers, as stated by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are this Community, the Community of Muhammad ﷺ was made to inherit every Book that Allah sent down. Ibn Jarir said: He made them inherit faith, since the Books command following the Qur'an, so they believe in them and act in accordance with their requirements. This is indicated by ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the Truth﴾, and then He followed it with His words ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾. So we know that they are the Community of Muhammad ﷺ, since the meaning of inheritance is the transfer of something from one people to another, and no community had a Book transferred to it from a people who were before them other than his Community. If we say they are the prophets and their followers, the meaning would be: We made inherit every Book sent down to a prophet, that prophet and his followers. The second opinion is that the Book is the Qur'an, and the "chosen ones" are the Community of the Messenger. The meaning of "awrathna" (We caused to inherit), Mujahid said, is "a'tayna" (We gave), because inheritance is a gift.

Then He divided the inheritors into these three categories. Makki said: it was said they are those mentioned in al-Waqi'ah (surah 56). So the one who is foremost in good deeds is the one brought near (al-muqarrab), the one who is moderate is the companions of the right (ashab al-maymanah), and the one who wrongs himself is the companions of the left (ashab al-mash'amah). This is an opinion whose meaning is narrated from 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and Qatadah, who said: the pronoun in "minhum" (among them) refers to the servants. So the one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever and the hypocrite, the moderate is the believer who disobeys, and the foremost is the pious in the absolute sense. They said: this is similar to what is in al-Waqi'ah. Most scholars hold that these three are within the Community of the Messenger, and whoever was among the companions of the left, being a denier and astray, does not inherit the Book and was not chosen by Allah; what is in al-Waqi'ah is the various kinds of creation from the earliest and the latest. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: our foremost are the people of jihad, our moderate are the people of our settled places, and our wrongdoers are the people of our desert, who do not attend Friday prayer or congregational prayer. Mu'adh said: the one who wrongs himself is the one who died upon a major sin without repenting from it; the moderate is the one who died upon a minor sin and did not commit a major sin without repenting from it; and the foremost is the one who died repentant from a major or minor sin, or who did not commit that. It was said: the one who wrongs himself is the disobedient transgressor; the moderate is the one who avoids major sins; and the foremost is the pious in the absolute sense. al-Hasan said: the wrongdoer is the one whose good deeds are light; the moderate is the one whose deeds are balanced; and the foremost is the one whose deeds outweigh. al-Zamakhshari said: He divided them into a wrongdoer who is a sinner, and this is the one who is a postponer (murji') regarding the command of Allah; a moderate, who is the one who mixed a righteous deed with another evil one; and a foremost one among the foremost. End of quote. He mentioned in al-Tajrid forty-three opinions regarding these three categories. Abu 'Imran al-Hawfi, 'Umar ibn Abi Shu'ayb, and Ya'qub in one narration, and the reading narrated from Abu 'Amr, read "sabbaq" (intensive form); the majority read "sabiq". It was said: the wrongdoer was placed first because he relies only on the mercy of Allah. al-Zamakhshari said: to signal the great number of the sinners among them and their predominance, and that the moderate are few in comparison with them, and the foremost are fewer than the few. End of quote.

﴿By the permission of Allah﴾: by His facilitation and empowerment, meaning that their precedence is not from their own essence, but that is from Him, exalted is He. The apparent meaning is that the reference of "that" (dhalika) is to the inheriting of the Book and the choosing of this Community.

"Jannatu" (gardens) on this reading is the subject (mubtada'), and "yadkhulunaha" (they enter it) is the predicate (khabar). The reading of the majority is "Jannatu" in the plural with a nominative ending, and this would be informing of the number of those chosen. al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah said "jannatu" is a substitute (badal) for "al-fadl" (the bounty). al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how is "jannatu 'adnin" made a substitute for "al-fadl al-kabir" (the great bounty), which is the precedence in good deeds referred to by "dhalika"? I say: since it is the cause of attaining the reward, it takes the place of the effect, as if it were the reward itself, so "jannatu 'adnin" was substituted for it. End of quote. What indicates that it is a subject is the reading of al-Jahdari and Harun from 'Asim: "jannati" in the accusative under the construction of the verb being suppressed, meaning they enter the gardens of Eden, they enter them. Raz'in, Hubaysh and al-Zuhri read "jannatun" in the singular. Abu 'Amr read "yudkhalunaha" in the passive voice, and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir and the majority in the active voice. The apparent meaning is that the raised pronoun in "yadkhulunaha" refers to the three categories. This is the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Abu al-Darda', 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, Abu Sa'id, 'A'ishah, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ja'far al-Sadiq, Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i and Ka'b al-Ahbar. 'Umar recited this verse, then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Our foremost is the foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven." As for the one who makes the three categories those of al-Waqi'ah, the pronoun in "yadkhulunaha" refers, in his view, to the moderate and the foremost. al-Zamakhshari said: it refers only to the foremost, and for this reason he made "dhalika" a reference to the precedence after the division, and then mentioned their reward. The silence about the other two contains what it contains of the obligation of caution: let the moderate beware, and let the one who wrongs himself be fearful, and both must seek sincere repentance that delivers from the punishment of Allah. Let him not be deceived by what 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Our foremost is the foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven," for the condition of that is the soundness of repentance. "Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness" (asa Allahu an yatuba 'alayhim). And His words: "Either He punishes them or He turns to them in forgiveness" have been expressed in the Qur'an in many places; whoever surveys them becomes aware of the reality of the matter and does not deceive himself. End of quote, and this is on the path of the Mu'tazilah.

The majority read ﴿yuhallawna﴾ with a damma on the yā' (y), a fatha on the ḥā' (ḥ), and a shadda on the lām (l), in the passive voice. It was also read with a fatha on the yā', a sukun on the ḥā', and a lightened lām, from ḥaliyat al-mar'ah, meaning the woman wore jewelry, so she is ḥāliyy; and it is said "jīd ḥālin" (a neck adorned) when it contains jewelry. The discussion of ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk﴾ was given earlier in Surat al-Hajj.

The majority read "al-ḥazan" with two fathas. It was also read with a damma on the ḥā' and a sukun on the zāy, reported by Janah ibn Ḥubaysh. "Al-ḥazan" encompasses all sorrows, and the commentators specified it here and gave many examples. It should be understood as an illustration rather than a precise specification. Abu al-Darda' said: al-ḥazan is the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and what befalls there from wronging oneself, of grief and sorrow. Samurah ibn Jundub said: the livelihood of this world, the good and similar. Qatadah said: the sorrow of this world is the fear that their deeds will not be accepted. Muqatil said: the sorrow of departure, which they say when they have settled there. al-Kalbi said: the fear of Satan. Ibn Zayd said: al-ḥazan is the injustice of the Hereafter, the standing before acceptance and rejection of acts of worship, and the long stay upon the Sirat. al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: al-ḥazan is the removal of distress, the turning of the heart, and the fear of the consequence. They have given many examples, to the point that some said: the rent of the house. The meaning is that it encompasses every sorrow of the religion and of the world, even this.

﴿Indeed our Lord is All-Forgiving, All-Appreciative﴾: "Ghafur" (All-Forgiving) contains an indication to the entry of the one who wronged himself into Paradise.

"Shakur" (All-Appreciative) contains an indication to the foremost, and that he has many good deeds. "Al-muqamah" (the abode of lasting residence) means "al-iqamah," that is, Paradise, because it is an abode of permanent residence from which one is not removed.

﴿From His bounty﴾: from His gift.

﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾: i.e., bodily exhaustion (nasab); ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾: i.e., weariness of the soul (lughub), which is a necessary consequence of bodily weariness. Qatadah said: al-lughub is "al-wad'" (putting down, relaxing). al-Zamakhshari said: al-nasab is the toil and hardship that afflicts one who exerts himself and labors at it; as for al-lughub, it is what befalls him of slackness and lassitude because of the toil. So nasab is the very hardship and burden, and lughub is its result, what arises from it of fatigue and languor. End of quote. If you ask: when the cause is negated, its effect is negated; so what is the ruling when the cause is negated and its effect is negated too? You say: "I did not get full and did not eat," and it is not good to say "I did not eat nor got full," because the negation of eating necessarily entails the negation of fullness, but not vice versa. So if this construction were used, it would be: "no hardship touches us therein and no fatigue"? The answer: He, exalted, explained the difference between Paradise and the abode of this world, for its places are of two kinds: a place where hardships and toils touch, like the deserts and wildernesses, and a place where exhaustion touches, like houses and dwellings where there are children.
