Moreover, the substitute is intended as a repetition of the governing element, and that is not possible here, because there is no governing element in ﴿Have you considered﴾ to imagine it entering upon ﴿Show me﴾. We have already discussed ﴿Have you considered﴾ at length in (the chapter of) al-Anʿam. What I hold is that ﴿Have you considered﴾ means "Inform me," and it requires two objects: one is in the accusative, and the other contains an interrogative. The Arabs say: "Have you considered Zayd, what he did?" So the first here is ﴿your partners﴾, and the second is ﴿what they created﴾. ﴿Show me﴾ is a parenthetical clause containing emphasis and reinforcement of the speech. It may also be that this is from the pattern of "working" (iʿmāl): both ﴿Have you considered﴾ and ﴿Show me﴾ have come upon ﴿what they created﴾, because ﴿Show me﴾ has been attached to its object in their saying: "Do you not see?", meaning "do you see here?", and the second has been made to govern according to the preferred view of the Basrans (al-Baṣriyyūn).

It was said: ﴿Have you considered﴾ may be a real interrogative, and ﴿Show me﴾ an imperative of challenge (amr taʿjīz) for clarification, meaning: "Do you know these you call upon as they are and in the state of incapacity they are in? Or do you imagine in them some power? If you know them to be incapable, how do you worship them? Or if you imagined for them power, then show me their power in what it is: is it on the earth?" As some of them said: "God is a god in the heaven, and these are gods on the earth." They said: and in it there are the stars and idols and their images. "Or is it in the heavens?" As some of them said: "The heaven was created with the assistance of the angels, so the angels are partners in its creation, and these idols are their images." "Or is their power in intercession for you?" As some of them said: "The angels did not create anything, but they are near to God, so we worship them so that they may intercede for us." "So is there with them from God a Book in which is His permission for them to intercede?" End of quote.

The partners were attributed to them because they made them partners of God; that is, the idols have no partnership in any way except by their saying and their making. It was said: it may be "your partners" in the Fire, according to His saying ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 98]. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿We have given them﴾ returns to the partners, (p-318) so that the pronouns are consistent. That is: "Is there with one who made partners for God a Book from God in which it is said that He has intercession with Him? For He does not intercede except by His permission." It was said: it returns to the polytheists, and it is an iltifāt (shift) from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence, turning away from them and treating them as the absent one who is not addressed. Its meaning: the worship of these is either by reason, and there is no reason for one who worships what does not create a single part of the earth, nor has a share in the heaven; or by transmission, and We did not give the polytheists a Book in which there is a command to worship these. So this is worship that is neither rational nor transmitted. End of quote.

Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, Hamza, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir, Hafs and Aban from ʿAsim read ﴿ʿalā bayyinah﴾ (upon evidence) in the singular; and the remaining seven read it in the plural.

When He, exalted is He, made clear the corruption of the affair of the idols and established the proof against their falsehood, He followed it by mentioning His greatness and power, so that the matter would be made clear by its opposite, and the lowliness of the idols would be emphasised by mentioning the greatness of God. So He said: ﴿Indeed God holds the heavens and the earth lest they should cease﴾. The apparent meaning is that its meaning is: lest they move from their places and the heavens fall from their heights. It was said: its meaning is: lest they cease from revolving. End of quote. It is not correct that the earth does not revolve. It appears from the saying of Ibn Masʿud that the heaven does not revolve, but rather the stars move within it. He said: "It is enough of a cessation that it revolves; for if it revolved, it would have ceased." ﴿Lest they should cease﴾ is in the place of the object of purpose (mafʿūl lah), and it was estimated as: "so that they do not cease," and "for fear that they cease." Al-Zajjaj said: "holds" means "prevents them from ceasing," so it is a second object by omission of the preposition, and it may be a substitute, meaning: He prevents the cessation of the heavens and the earth, as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl).

**Surah 35, verses 36–41 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And if they should cease﴾. The particle *in* (إنْ) usually introduces a possible condition. If its governing verb is understood as referring to something possible, then this refers to the Day of Resurrection, when the heaven is folded up and the mountains are blown away. That is possible, and it will indeed occur according to the true report. The meaning is: "And if the time of their cessation comes." It is also possible that this is meant hypothetically, that is, "And if We suppose their cessation," in which case it has the meaning of *law* ("if").

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *wa-law zālatā* ("and even if they should cease"), with *in* as a negative particle (*in nāfiyah*). The verb *amsakahumā* ("He holds them") in the sense of the present tense is the answer to an implied oath that precedes the preparatory *lam* (لام التوطئة, the *lam* of preparation) in *la-in*. It has the sense of the present because of the conditional *in* (إنْ الشرطية) that follows it, as in His words ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], meaning "they would not follow." Likewise, His words ﴿And if We sent a wind and they saw it turned yellow, they would surely remain disbelievers﴾ [al-Rum: 51], meaning "they would surely remain." All of this is parsed as the present tense because of the conditional *in*. The answer to the conditional *in* in these constructions is omitted, because the answer to the oath indicates it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*In amsakahā* ("if He holds them") is the answer to the oath in ﴿And if they should cease﴾; it takes the place of both answers." He concluded. He means that it indicates the omitted answer. If his words are taken literally, they are not correct, because if it took the place of both, it would have a grammatical position (*iʿrab*, grammatical analysis) as the answer to the condition, but it would have no grammatical position as the answer to the oath. One and the same thing cannot be both governed and not governed.

The *min* (مِن) in ﴿anyone﴾ (*min aḥad*) is for emphasizing the comprehensiveness of the negation. The *min* in ﴿after Him﴾ (*min baʿdihi*) indicates the starting point, meaning "after His withholding them."

Ibn ʿAbbas asked a man who had come from al-Sham: "Whom did you meet?" He said: "Kaʿb." He said: "And what did you hear him say?" He said: "That the heavens are upon the shoulder of an angel." He said: "Kaʿb lied. Has he not yet abandoned his Judaism?" Then he recited this verse.

Ibn Masʿud said to Jundub al-Bajali, who was ... i.e., Kaʿb al-Ahbar (كعب الأحبار, the Rabbi Kaʿb al-Ahbar), in a discussion whose conclusion was: Judaism never settled in a heart without nearly leaving it.

Another group said: His attribute of forbearance and forgiveness in this verse is only an indication that the heaven was nearly about to cease, and the earth likewise, because of the association of the disbelievers. So He holds them back by His judgment concerning the polytheists, and He waits so that He may forgive those among them who believe, just as He said in another verse ﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from it﴾ [Maryam: 90].

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Forbearing, Forgiving﴾ means not hastening punishment, in that He holds them back, while they were worthy of being shaken, so that the word of polytheism would shake the bones, as He said ﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from it﴾ [Maryam: 90], and so on.

(p-316) When he mentioned the state of the believers and their abode, he mentioned the state of the disbelievers. This indicates that those three (groups) are in Paradise. ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ are their counterparts. ﴿It will not be decreed upon them﴾, meaning they will not be finished off so that ﴿they die﴾, because if they died, their senses would cease and they would find rest. Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿fa-yamutu﴾ (so they die) with the nun omitted and the verb in the subjunctive, as a response to a negation (jawab al-nafy). This is one of the two meanings of the subjunctive (al-nasb): the meaning is that the decree is negated, and so its consequence is negated. That is, ﴿it will not be decreed upon them﴾ and ﴿they will not die﴾. It is like your saying: "You do not come to us so that you speak to us," meaning: there is no conversation, the coming is negated, and so the conversation is negated. It is not correct for it to be on the second meaning of the subjunctive, because the meaning would be: "You do not come to us speaking to us; rather you come and do not speak." The meaning here is not: "It will not be decreed upon them while they are dead," rather: "It will be decreed upon them, but they will not die."

ʿIsa and al-Hasan read ﴿fa-yamutuna﴾ (so they die) with the nun, its reading being that it is coordinated (ma‘tufah) with ﴿lā yuqḍā﴾. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is a weak reading." Abu ʿUthman al-Mazini said: it is a coordination, meaning "so they do not die," in accordance with His saying ﴿nor will they be given leave to make excuse﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36], meaning "so they do not make excuse." ﴿Nor will their punishment be lightened for them﴾, the type of their punishment itself admits that they might be brought to life and made happy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ʿAbd al-Warith, from Abu ʿAmr, read ﴿wa-lā yukhaffaf﴾ with the fa' sukun, treating the separate (word) like the joined, as in his saying:

*"So today I drink without being subjected to blame"*

Al-Jumhur read ﴿najzī kulla﴾ (We recompense every) in the active voice, with ﴿kull﴾ in the accusative. Abu ʿAmr and Abu Hatim, from Nafi‘, read it with the ya' in the passive voice, with ﴿kullu﴾ in the nominative.

﴿Wa-hum yaṣṭariḥūna﴾ (And they will cry out for help). It is formed from al-ṣarkh (a cry), the pattern yaftaʿilu. The ta' was changed to a ṭa', and its origin is yaṣrikhūna. Al-ṣurākh is the intensity of shouting. The poet said:

*"A pregnant woman cried out, when her tribe abandoned her."*

It is used for seeking help, with the voice of the one seeking help being directed toward its source. The poet said:

*"And the prolonged crying out of a man in the depth of its pit, and the effort of a wretch who has long wailed in the Fire."*

﴿Our Lord, bring us out﴾, meaning saying: "Our Lord, bring us out of it," that is, out of the Fire, and return us to the world.

﴿We will do righteousness﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "We will say: There is no god but God," ﴿other than what we used to do﴾, meaning of shirk (associating others with God); and we will obey the commands of the messengers, so we will believe instead of disbelief and obey instead of disobedience.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Did He suffice with ṣāliḥan (righteousness), as He sufficed with it in (Return us, so we may do righteousness)? And what is the benefit of adding ﴿other than what we used to do﴾, given that it suggests they would do a different righteousness from the righteousness they had done?" I say: its benefit is increasing the regret over what they did of non-righteousness, together with acknowledging it. As for the suggestion, it is removed by the manifestation of their state in disbelief and their engaging in sins; and because they used to do good deeds, so they said: "Bring us out, so we may do righteousness other than what we used to consider righteous, and then do it." End of quote.

It was narrated that they will be answered after a period equal to the life of this world: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough...﴾. It is an interrogative of reproach, censure and affirmation. The ma is verbal-temporal (maṣdariyyah ẓarfiyyah), meaning: "a duration in which one would remember." Al-Jumhur read ﴿what one who would remember could remember therein﴾. Al-Aʿmash read mā yadhdhakkaru fīhi man idhdhakkara, with idgham (assimilation) and with a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) pronounced in continuous speech. This duration, al-Hasan said, is puberty, meaning that it is the first state of remembrance. It was said: seventeen years. Qatada said: eighteen years. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said: twenty. Ibn ʿAbbas said: forty; and it was said: fifty. ʿAli said: sixty, and this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿And there came to you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough...﴾, because its meaning is: "We indeed gave you life," as in His saying ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 18], and His saying ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1], then He said ﴿And you remained among us﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 18], and He said ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ [al-Sharh: 2], because the meaning is: "We had nurtured you and expanded (your breast)."

﴿The warner﴾ is a collective noun, and they are the prophets, each prophet being a warner to his community. It was read as al-nudhur (plural). It was said: the warner is grey hair (al-shayb), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Sufyan, Waki‘, al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl, al-Farra’ and al-Tabari. It was said: the death of family and relatives; and it was said: the completion of old age.

﴿So taste﴾, meaning the punishment of Hell. Janah ibn Ḥubaysh read ʿālimun (knowing) with tanwin, with ghayba in the accusative; and al-Jumhur read it in the genitive construct (iḍāfah). The placement of this sentence after what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, mentioned that the disbelievers are punished continually for the duration of their disbelief, which was a short and finite duration; then He informed that He, exalted is He, is ﴿Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, so nothing hidden in the breasts is concealed from Him. He knew about the disbeliever that disbelief had become firmly established in his heart, such that if it lasted forever he would never have believed in God or worshipped Him.

Khalāʾif is the plural of khalīfah, and khulafāʾ is the plural of khalīf. Both khalīfah and khalīf are used for one who is made a successor. In this there is an admonition that He, exalted is He, made them successors in place of those before them, yet they did not take warning from the state of those who came before them, the deniers of the messengers, and the destruction that befell them; nor did they learn from those who disbelieved, nor did they heed those who came before them.

﴿Then upon him is his disbelief﴾, meaning the punishment for his disbelief. The apparent meaning is that it is a general address; and it was said: it is addressed to the people of Makkah. Al-maqt is the most extreme contempt, hatred and anger; and al-khasār is the loss of life. As though life were capital: if it passes in other than obedience to God, then he has lost it, and has taken in exchange, in place of profit, what he does of acts of obedience, the displeasure and wrath of God, to the point that they went to the Fire.

﴿Say: Have you considered your partners﴾. Al-Ḥawfi said: the alif of the interrogative there is for affirmation. In al-Taḥrīr: "Have you considered" – what is meant by it is "Inform me," because the interrogative requires that. One says: "Have you considered what Zayd did?" and the listener says: "He sold and bought." Were it not that it includes the meaning of "Inform me," the answer would be "yes" or "no." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Have you considered" takes the place of "Inform me" according to Sibawayh. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Show me﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿Have you considered﴾, because the meaning of "Have you considered" is "Inform me." It is as if He said: "Inform me about these partners, and about what they deserved by which they were given divinity and partnership. Show me what part of the parts of the earth they independently created apart from God; or do they have a partnership with God in the creation of the heavens? Or is there with them a Book from God that speaks that they are His partners, so that they have a proof and evidence from that Book?" Or the pronoun in ﴿We have given them﴾ refers to the polytheists, according to His saying ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority?﴾ [al-Rum: 35], ﴿Or have We given them a Book before it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21].

﴿Nay, the wrongdoers promise one another only delusion﴾, the wrongdoers being the leaders, ﴿one another﴾ being the followers, ﴿only delusion﴾, which is their saying: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18]. End of quote.

As for his saying that ﴿Show me﴾ is a substitute for ﴿Have you considered﴾, this is not correct, because when a substitute is made from what the interrogative has entered upon, the particle must enter upon the substitute as well. Also, substituting a clause for a clause is not attested in their language. Moreover, the substitute is intended as a repetition of the governing element, and that is not possible here, because there is no governing element in ﴿Have you considered﴾ to imagine it entering upon ﴿Show me﴾. We have already discussed ﴿Have you considered﴾ at length in (the chapter of) al-Anʿam. What I hold is that ﴿Have you considered﴾ means "Inform me," and it requires two objects: one is in the accusative, and the other contains an interrogative. The Arabs say: "Have you considered Zayd, what he did?" So the first here is ﴿your partners﴾, and the second is ﴿what they created﴾. ﴿Show me﴾ is a parenthetical clause containing emphasis and reinforcement of the speech. It may also be that this is from the pattern of "working" (iʿmāl): both ﴿Have you considered﴾ and ﴿Show me﴾ have come upon ﴿what they created﴾, because ﴿Show me﴾ has been attached to its object in their saying: "Do you not see?", meaning "do you see here?", and the second has been made to govern according to the preferred view of the Basrans (al-Baṣriyyūn).

It was said: ﴿Have you considered﴾ may be a real interrogative, and ﴿Show me﴾ an imperative of challenge (amr taʿjīz) for clarification, meaning: "Do you know these you call upon as they are and in the state of incapacity they are in? Or do you imagine in them some power? If you know them to be incapable, how do you worship them? Or if you imagined for them power, then show me their power in what it is: is it on the earth?" As some of them said: "God is a god in the heaven, and these are gods on the earth." They said: and in it there are the stars and idols and their images. "Or is it in the heavens?" As some of them said: "The heaven was created with the assistance of the angels, so the angels are partners in its creation, and these idols are their images." "Or is their power in intercession for you?" As some of them said: "The angels did not create anything, but they are near to God, so we worship them so that they may intercede for us." "So is there with them from God a Book in which is His permission for them to intercede?" End of quote.

The partners were attributed to them because they made them partners of God; that is, the idols have no partnership in any way except by their saying and their making. It was said: it may be "your partners" in the Fire, according to His saying ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 98]. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿We have given them﴾ returns to the partners, (p-318) so that the pronouns are consistent. That is: "Is there with one who made partners for God a Book from God in which it is said that He has intercession with Him? For He does not intercede except by His permission." It was said: it returns to the polytheists, and it is an iltifāt (shift) from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence, turning away from them and treating them as the absent one who is not addressed. Its meaning: the worship of these is either by reason, and there is no reason for one who worships what does not create a single part of the earth, nor has a share in the heaven; or by transmission, and We did not give the polytheists a Book in which there is a command to worship these. So this is worship that is neither rational nor transmitted. End of quote.

Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, Hamza, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir, Hafs and Aban from ʿAsim read ﴿ʿalā bayyinah﴾ (upon evidence) in the singular; and the remaining seven read it in the plural.

When He, exalted is He, made clear the corruption of the affair of the idols and established the proof against their falsehood, He followed it by mentioning His greatness and power, so that the matter would be made clear by its opposite, and the lowliness of the idols would be emphasised by mentioning the greatness of God. So He said: ﴿Indeed God holds the heavens and the earth lest they should cease﴾. The apparent meaning is that its meaning is: lest they move from their places and the heavens fall from their heights. It was said: its meaning is: lest they cease from revolving. End of quote. It is not correct that the earth does not revolve. It appears from the saying of Ibn Masʿud that the heaven does not revolve, but rather the stars move within it. He said: "It is enough of a cessation that it revolves; for if it revolved, it would have ceased." ﴿Lest they should cease﴾ is in the place of the object of purpose (mafʿūl lah), and it was estimated as: "so that they do not cease," and "for fear that they cease." Al-Zajjaj said: "holds" means "prevents them from ceasing," so it is a second object by omission of the preposition, and it may be a substitute, meaning: He prevents the cessation of the heavens and the earth, as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl).

**Surah 35, verses 36–41 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿And if they should cease﴾. The particle *in* (إنْ) usually introduces a possible condition. If its governing verb is understood as referring to something possible, then this refers to the Day of Resurrection, when the heaven is folded up and the mountains are blown away. That is possible, and it will indeed occur according to the true report. The meaning is: "And if the time of their cessation comes." It is also possible that this is meant hypothetically, that is, "And if We suppose their cessation," in which case it has the meaning of *law* ("if").

Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *wa-law zālatā* ("and even if they should cease"), with *in* as a negative particle (*in nāfiyah*). The verb *amsakahumā* ("He holds them") in the sense of the present tense is the answer to an implied oath that precedes the preparatory *lam* (لام التوطئة, the *lam* of preparation) in *la-in*. It has the sense of the present because of the conditional *in* (إنْ الشرطية) that follows it, as in His words ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], meaning "they would not follow." Likewise, His words ﴿And if We sent a wind and they saw it turned yellow, they would surely remain disbelievers﴾ [al-Rum: 51], meaning "they would surely remain." All of this is parsed as the present tense because of the conditional *in*. The answer to the conditional *in* in these constructions is omitted, because the answer to the oath indicates it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*In amsakahā* ("if He holds them") is the answer to the oath in ﴿And if they should cease﴾; it takes the place of both answers." He concluded. He means that it indicates the omitted answer. If his words are taken literally, they are not correct, because if it took the place of both, it would have a grammatical position (*iʿrab*, grammatical analysis) as the answer to the condition, but it would have no grammatical position as the answer to the oath. One and the same thing cannot be both governed and not governed.

The *min* (مِن) in ﴿anyone﴾ (*min aḥad*) is for emphasizing the comprehensiveness of the negation. The *min* in ﴿after Him﴾ (*min baʿdihi*) indicates the starting point, meaning "after His withholding them."

Ibn ʿAbbas asked a man who had come from al-Sham: "Whom did you meet?" He said: "Kaʿb." He said: "And what did you hear him say?" He said: "That the heavens are upon the shoulder of an angel." He said: "Kaʿb lied. Has he not yet abandoned his Judaism?" Then he recited this verse.

Ibn Masʿud said to Jundub al-Bajali, who was ... i.e., Kaʿb al-Ahbar (كعب الأحبار, the Rabbi Kaʿb al-Ahbar), in a discussion whose conclusion was: Judaism never settled in a heart without nearly leaving it.

Another group said: His attribute of forbearance and forgiveness in this verse is only an indication that the heaven was nearly about to cease, and the earth likewise, because of the association of the disbelievers. So He holds them back by His judgment concerning the polytheists, and He waits so that He may forgive those among them who believe, just as He said in another verse ﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from it﴾ [Maryam: 90].

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Forbearing, Forgiving﴾ means not hastening punishment, in that He holds them back, while they were worthy of being shaken, so that the word of polytheism would shake the bones, as He said ﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from it﴾ [Maryam: 90], and so on.

[p. 319]

The pronoun in ﴿They swore﴾ refers to the Quraysh. Having explained their denial of *tawhid* (the oneness of God), Abu Hayyan now explains their rejection of the Messengers. It is said: they used to curse the Jews and the Christians for rejecting their messengers, and they said: "If a messenger comes to us, we will surely be better guided than any one of the nations." When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they rejected him.

﴿If a warner came to them﴾ is a report of the meaning of their statement, not of its exact wording. Had it been their exact wording, the construction would have been "If a warner came to us from one of the nations," meaning: from a nation that is guided, or from the nation that is called "one of the nations," as a way of preferring it over others. This is like their saying: "He is one of the two ones" (*aḥad al-aḥadayn*), and "He is the one of the one" (*aḥad al-aḥad*), meaning preference in cunning and intellect, to the point that he has no equal. The poet said:

*Until they consulted me, the one of the ones,*
*a witness whose weapons are sought by Maʿadd.*

﴿When a warner came to them﴾: this is Muhammad (ﷺ). This is what Ibn ʿAbbas said, and it is the apparent meaning. Muqatil said: it is the splitting of the moon.

﴿It only increased them﴾: that is, he, or his coming, only increased them.

﴿In aversion﴾: distance from the truth and flight from it. Attributing the increase to him is a metaphor, because he was the cause of their increasing in aversion, as in His saying ﴿so it added to them filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], and they became more astray than they had been. The answer to (*lamma*, "when") is ﴿it only increased them﴾, and this is clear evidence that (*lamma*) is a particle (*ḥarf*) and not an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), since if it were an adverb it would not be permissible for it to precede its governing negated element (*ʿāmil*) with *mā*. We have mentioned this in His saying ﴿when We decreed death for him, nothing showed them﴾ [Saba': 14], and in His saying ﴿and when they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them at all﴾ [Yusuf: 68].

Apparently ﴿arrogance﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*), meaning: the cause of the aversion is arrogance. ﴿And the evil scheming﴾ is coordinated with ﴿arrogance﴾, so it is also an object of purpose, meaning: what drives them to keep away from the truth is arrogance. ﴿The evil scheming﴾ is the deceit you intend against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the plotting against him. Qatada said: the evil scheming is polytheism. It was also said that ﴿arrogance﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿aversion﴾; this was said by al-Akhfash. It was said that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: arrogant and scheming against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers. The phrase ﴿evil scheming﴾ is an idafa of a qualified noun to its adjective, and for this reason it comes in its original form in ﴿and the evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its people﴾. It was also said that it is permissible for ﴿and evil scheming﴾ to be coordinated with ﴿aversion﴾.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *wa-makra al-sayyi'*, with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Aʿmash and Hamza read it with the hamza sukun. This is either treating the connection as a pause (*ijrāʾ al-waṣl mujrā al-waqf*), or sukun to avoid successive vowels and treating the separated as if it were joined, like His saying: *lanā ibilān* (we have two camels). Al-Zajjaj claimed that this reading is a solecism (*laḥn*). Abu Jaʿfar said: it became a solecism because it omitted the grammatical inflection (*iʿrāb*) from it. Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) claimed that this is not permissible in either prose or poetry, because the vowels of inflection were introduced to distinguish meanings. Some grammarians found it too grave that al-Aʿmash should read this way, and said: he only paused at the point of one who transmitted from him. The evidence for this is that the first (word) is a complete utterance, and the second, since it is not a complete utterance, is inflected. The vowel on the second is heavier than on the first, because it is a *damma* between two *kasras*.

Al-Zajjaj also said: Hamza's reading *wa-makra al-sayyi'* with two *yā's*, when stopping at it according to the experts, is a solecism that is not permissible, and it is only permissible in poetry due to necessity. Abu ʿAli (al-Farisi) gave many citations and arguments in his *al-Hujja* for the sukun, on account of successive vowels, necessity, and connecting with the intention of stopping. He said: when what we have mentioned of interpretation in this reading is admissible, it cannot be said that it is a solecism. Ibn al-Qushayri said: whatever has been established through widespread transmission (*istifāḍa*) or mass transmission (*tawātur*) as having been recited is necessarily permissible, and it cannot be called a solecism. Al-Zamakhshari said: perhaps he elided the vowel and it was thought to be sukun, or he paused briefly and then began with ﴿and it does not encompass﴾.

It is reported from Ibn Kathir: *wa-makra al-sa'y*, with a sukun hamza after the sin and a *yā'* after it with a kasra, and this is an inverted form (*maqlūb*) of the lightened *al-sayyi'* from *al-sayyi'*, as the poet said:

*They do not repay good with evil,*
*nor do they repay harshness with gentleness.*

Ibn Masʿud read: *wa-makran sayyi'an* (and a scheme that is evil), coordinating an indefinite noun with an indefinite noun.

﴿And it does not encompass﴾: that is, it surrounds and befalls. It is only used for what is disliked. It is also read *yuḥīq* with a *ḍamma*, meaning with the *yā'* vowelled with *ḍamma*, and *al-makra* is in the accusative case: ﴿and it does not encompass God, except its people.﴾ In this world, the consequence of that falls upon its people.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: If you say: we often see the schemer benefit from his scheming and overcome his opponent by scheming, while the verse indicates otherwise. The answer has several aspects. First: the scheming in the verse is the scheming against the Messenger, which is the resolve to kill and expel him, and it only befalls them, as they were killed at Badr. Second: it is general, and this is the more correct view, for he (peace be upon him) forbade scheming and said: "Do not scheme, nor help a schemer, for He, the Exalted, says: ﴿and the evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its people﴾." So on this basis, the one who is schemed against is the one who deserves it, and so he does not increase in loss. Third: affairs are judged by their outcomes. Whoever is schemed against by another and that scheme is carried out against him, appearing to succeed immediately, is in reality the winner, while the schemer is the one who perishes. End of quote.

Ka'b said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "In the Torah: whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it." Ibn ʿAbbas said to him: "We found this in the Book of God: ﴿and the evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its people﴾." End of quote.

In the proverbs of the Arabs: "Whoever digs a well for his brother falls into it headfirst." And *sunnat al-awwalīn* (the way of the former peoples) means the sending down of punishment upon those among the nations who disbelieved in their messengers. Their awaiting it is made as if it were an expectation of it from them. In *sunnat al-awwalīn* the verbal noun is an idafa. In ﴿for the way of God﴾ there is an idafa to the agent: it was first attributed to them because it is a way that applies to them, and second to Him because He is the one who established it. The Exalted explained the vengeance against the deniers of the Messengers as a customary practice (*ʿāda*) that He does not change for another, nor transfer to other than its people, though that is inevitable. He cited as evidence what they used to witness in their travels and trade journeys, in their trips to Syria, Iraq and Yemen, of the traces of the bygone ones and the signs of their destruction and their dwellings, such as the dwellings of Thamud and the like. The discussion of a parallel of this sentence has preceded in Surat al-Rum. There, ﴿they were stronger than them in power﴾ [al-Rum: 9] is a resumptive report about what they were like, and here ﴿and they were﴾ means "and indeed they had been," so the clause is a circumstantial clause. Thus these are two purposes.

﴿And God was not to be frustrated﴾: that is, to escape Him or outpace Him, ﴿by anything﴾: any thing, and *min* (by) is for the comprehensiveness of things. ﴿Indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾: by His knowledge He knows all things, so nothing is hidden from His knowledge, and by His power nothing is beyond Him.

Then the Exalted mentioned His forbearance toward His servants in not hastening punishment, and said: ﴿And if God were to take the people to account for what they earned﴾: that is, for polytheism and denying the Messengers. This is the meaning in the verse in al-Nahl, namely His saying ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾. The discussion of the parallel of this verse has preceded in al-Nahl, where there it reads ﴿upon it﴾, and here it reads ﴿upon its back﴾. The pronoun refers to the earth, except that there the context indicates it, while here it may refer to something explicitly mentioned, namely His saying ﴿in the heavens nor on the earth﴾. Since it carries those who are upon it, the back is borrowed for it, like a beast of burden carrying loads, and also because the back is the outward part, unlike its inward part. ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Seeing﴾ is a warning to the deniers, meaning: He will recompense them for their deeds.

This is like their saying: "He is one of the two ones" (*aḥad al-aḥadayn*), and "He is the one of the one" (*aḥad al-aḥad*), meaning preference in cunning and intellect, to the point that he has no equal. The poet said:

*Until they consulted me, the one of the ones,*
*a witness whose weapons are sought by Maʿadd.*

﴿When a warner came to them﴾: this is Muhammad (ﷺ). This is what Ibn ʿAbbas said, and it is the apparent meaning. Muqatil said: it is the splitting of the moon.

﴿It only increased them﴾: that is, he, or his coming, only increased them.

﴿In aversion﴾: distance from the truth and flight from it. Attributing the increase to him is a metaphor, because he was the cause of their increasing in aversion, as in His saying ﴿so it added to them filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], and they became more astray than they had been. The answer to (*lamma*, "when") is ﴿it only increased them﴾, and this is clear evidence that (*lamma*) is a particle (*ḥarf*) and not an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), since if it were an adverb it would not be permissible for it to precede its governing negated element (*ʿāmil*) with *mā*. We have mentioned this in His saying ﴿when We decreed death for him, nothing showed them﴾ [Saba': 14], and in His saying ﴿and when they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them at all﴾ [Yusuf: 68].

Apparently ﴿arrogance﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*), meaning: the cause of the aversion is arrogance. ﴿And the evil scheming﴾ is coordinated with ﴿arrogance﴾, so it is also an object of purpose, meaning: what drives them to keep away from the truth is arrogance. ﴿The evil scheming﴾ is the deceit you intend against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the plotting against him. Qatada said: the evil scheming is polytheism. It was also said that ﴿arrogance﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿aversion﴾; this was said by al-Akhfash. It was said that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning: arrogant and scheming against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers. The phrase ﴿evil scheming﴾ is an idafa of a qualified noun to its adjective, and for this reason it comes in its original form in ﴿and the evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its people﴾. It was also said that it is permissible for ﴿and evil scheming﴾ to be coordinated with ﴿aversion﴾.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *wa-makra al-sayyi'*, with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Aʿmash and Hamza read it with the hamza sukun. This is either treating the connection as a pause (*ijrāʾ al-waṣl mujrā al-waqf*), or sukun to avoid successive vowels and treating the separated as if it were joined, like His saying: *lanā ibilān* (we have two camels). Al-Zajjaj claimed that this reading is a solecism (*laḥn*). Abu Jaʿfar said: it became a solecism because it omitted the grammatical inflection (*iʿrāb*) from it. Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) claimed that this is not permissible in either prose or poetry, because the vowels of inflection were introduced to distinguish meanings. Some grammarians found it too grave that al-Aʿmash should read this way, and said: he only paused at the point of one who transmitted from him. The evidence for this is that the first (word) is a complete utterance, and the second, since it is not a complete utterance, is inflected. The vowel on the second is heavier than on the first, because it is a *damma* between two *kasras*.

Al-Zajjaj also said: Hamza's reading *wa-makra al-sayyi'* with two *yā's*, when stopping at it according to the experts, is a solecism that is not permissible, and it is only permissible in poetry due to necessity. Abu ʿAli (al-Farisi) gave many citations and arguments in his *al-Hujja* for the sukun, on account of successive vowels, necessity, and connecting with the intention of stopping. He said: when what we have mentioned of interpretation in this reading is admissible, it cannot be said that it is a solecism. Ibn al-Qushayri said: whatever has been established through widespread transmission (*istifāḍa*) or mass transmission (*tawātur*) as having been recited is necessarily permissible, and it cannot be called a solecism. Al-Zamakhshari said: perhaps he elided the vowel and it was thought to be sukun, or he paused briefly and then began with ﴿and it does not encompass﴾.

It is reported from Ibn Kathir: *wa-makra al-sa'y*, with a sukun hamza after the sin and a *yā'* after it with a kasra, and this is an inverted form (*maqlūb*) of the lightened *al-sayyi'* from *al-sayyi'*, as the poet said:

*They do not repay good with evil,*
*nor do they repay harshness with gentleness.*

Ibn Masʿud read: *wa-makran sayyi'an* (and a scheme that is evil), coordinating an indefinite noun with an indefinite noun.

﴿And it does not encompass﴾: that is, it surrounds and befalls. It is only used for what is disliked. It is also read *yuḥīq* with a *ḍamma*, meaning with the *yā'* vowelled with *ḍamma*, and *al-makra* is in the accusative case: ﴿and it does not encompass God, except its people.﴾ In this world, the consequence of that falls upon its people.

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: If you say: we often see the schemer benefit from his scheming and overcome his opponent by scheming, while the verse indicates otherwise. The answer has several aspects. First: the scheming in the verse is the scheming against the Messenger, which is the resolve to kill and expel him, and it only befalls them, as they were killed at Badr. Second: it is general, and this is the more correct view, for he (peace be upon him) forbade scheming and said: "Do not scheme, nor help a schemer, for He, the Exalted, says: ﴿and the evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its people﴾." So on this basis, the one who is schemed against is the one who deserves it, and so he does not increase in loss. Third: affairs are judged by their outcomes. Whoever is schemed against by another and that scheme is carried out against him, appearing to succeed immediately, is in reality the winner, while the schemer is the one who perishes. End of quote.

Ka'b said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "In the Torah: whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it." Ibn ʿAbbas said to him: "We found this in the Book of God: ﴿and the evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its people﴾." End of quote.

In the proverbs of the Arabs: "Whoever digs a well for his brother falls into it headfirst." And *sunnat al-awwalīn* (the way of the former peoples) means the sending down of punishment upon those among the nations who disbelieved in their messengers. Their awaiting it is made as if it were an expectation of it from them. In *sunnat al-awwalīn* the verbal noun is an idafa. In ﴿for the way of God﴾ there is an idafa to the agent: it was first attributed to them because it is a way that applies to them, and second to Him because He is the one who established it. The Exalted explained the vengeance against the deniers of the Messengers as a customary practice (*ʿāda*) that He does not change for another, nor transfer to other than its people, though that is inevitable. He cited as evidence what they used to witness in their travels and trade journeys, in their trips to Syria, Iraq and Yemen, of the traces of the bygone ones and the signs of their destruction and their dwellings, such as the dwellings of Thamud and the like. The discussion of a parallel of this sentence has preceded in Surat al-Rum. There, ﴿they were stronger than them in power﴾ [al-Rum: 9] is a resumptive report about what they were like, and here ﴿and they were﴾ means "and indeed they had been," so the clause is a circumstantial clause. Thus these are two purposes.

﴿And God was not to be frustrated﴾: that is, to escape Him or outpace Him, ﴿by anything﴾: any thing, and *min* (by) is for the comprehensiveness of things. ﴿Indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾: by His knowledge He knows all things, so nothing is hidden from His knowledge, and by His power nothing is beyond Him.

Then the Exalted mentioned His forbearance toward His servants in not hastening punishment, and said: ﴿And if God were to take the people to account for what they earned﴾: that is, for polytheism and denying the Messengers. This is the meaning in the verse in al-Nahl, namely His saying ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾. The discussion of the parallel of this verse has preceded in al-Nahl, where there it reads ﴿upon it﴾, and here it reads ﴿upon its back﴾. The pronoun refers to the earth, except that there the context indicates it, while here it may refer to something explicitly mentioned, namely His saying ﴿in the heavens nor on the earth﴾. Since it carries those who are upon it, the back is borrowed for it, like a beast of burden carrying loads, and also because the back is the outward part, unlike its inward part. ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Seeing﴾ is a warning to the deniers, meaning: He will recompense them for their deeds.
